Listed mattress brand Wakefit reported a net profit of ₹15.9 Cr in second quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), almost flat from nearly ₹16 Cr in the year-ago quarter. However, on a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the bottom line tanked 32% from ₹23.4 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company attributed the sequential decline in profitability to rising commodity prices, geopolitical disruptions and the “challenging” operating environment. “The operating environment remained challenging during the quarter, with crude-linked raw materials, particularly Polyol and TDI, continuing to remain elevated, with further price increases witnessed in recent months. Geopolitical disruptions in West Asia also impacted raw material availability and logistics across the industry…,” said Wakefit cofounder and executive director Chaitanya Ramalingegowda. Despite this, operating revenue rose nearly 20% to a record ₹452 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹376.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, the top line also rose 11.6% from ₹404.9 Cr in the preceding quarter. While mattresses brought in 66% of revenue, furniture, furnishings and decor contributed the remaining 38%. Including other income of ₹16 Cr, Wakefit’s total income stood at ₹468 Cr in Q2 FY27. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter under review also shot up 19% to ₹441.4 Cr compared to ₹370.5 Cr in Q2 FY26. The listed company also incurred additional tax expenses of ₹10.7 Cr during the quarter. “The company recorded a deferred tax charge of ₹6.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, compared with nil in Q2 FY26 and ₹7.3 Cr in Q1 FY27. This is attributable to two factors: (i) normal-course reversal of timing differences relating to depreciation and provisions as they unwind through the P&L, and (ii) the unwinding of the deferred tax asset on carried-forward losses,” said the company in a statement. In its investor presentation, the company said that its operating EBITDA rose 25.8% to ₹30.5 Cr in the quarter under review compared to ₹24.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. Operating EBITDA margin also improved to 6.7% from 6.4% in the year-ago quarter. On the operational front, Wakefit opened 41 new offline stores in Q2 FY27, taking its total company-owned store count to 205 across 137 cities. It also had a presence across 2,589 multi-brand outlets spanning 787 towns and cities. Wakefit said that its own channels contributed 70% of its sales in Q2 FY27, while external channels accounted for the remaining 30%. The company also noted it operated a 1.6 Lakh sq. ft. mother warehouse in Hosur, 10 inventory holding points and 26 points of delivery at the end of September 2026. “Our planned FY27 capex of around ₹100 Cr to ₹120 Cr remains on track, with nearly 80% allocated towards retail expansion, particularly our jumbo store format. Construction of our first jumbo store in Bengaluru is progressing, and we are targeting its launch in Q2 FY28,” added Ramalingegowda. Shares of Wakefit closed Thursday's trading session 1.1% lower at ₹138.75 on the BSE.

'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
Jury sees video of Pleterski begging for his life at trial of alleged kidnappers
Warning: This story contains distressing details about torture and graphic images
Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described being beaten with a gun and tortured with knives and a lighter in the back of a truck as he began his testimony at the trial of his alleged kidnappers Friday in Toronto.
"[I was] very scared, scared I'm going to die, scared for my life, in survival mode essentially," Pleterski told the Ontario Superior Court about how he felt at the time.
The Crown played a 13-second video for the jury, which showed Pleterski on his knees begging for his life while a man pointed a gun at him and counted down from three.
Before reaching one, the man appears to fire the gun beside Pleterski's head.
"It didn't hit me, but I know it was very loud and there was a constant ringing in my left ear," Pleterski testified. "When he shot the firearm I didn't know if I was shot or not."
Akil Heywood, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry are all charged with kidnapping and extorting Pleterski over the course of three days in early December 2022.
Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearms offences, the aggravated assault of Pleterski, assaulting him with a weapon, and assault causing bodily harm over that same period. All three men have pleaded not guilty.
Pleterski, 27, was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf, but he's yet to be sentenced.
He told the court that Heywood invested between $300,000 and $400,000 and allegedly started threatening him in texts and phone calls about getting that money back in the beginning to the middle of 2022.
Pleterski also testified that Heywood was appointed as one of the five creditor inspectors tasked with overseeing his bankruptcy proceeding.
'Driving force'
In its opening statement, the Crown alleged Heywood was the "driving force" behind the plan to kidnap Pleterski and that evidence would show another man — who is not part of the trial — was the lead kidnapper and that Paladino and Henry carried it out alongside him.
Pleterski identified Heywood, Paladino and Henry in the courtroom Friday as Crown prosecutor Julia De Vuono walked him through the events leading to the alleged kidnapping and what Pleterski said happened to him during it.
From left to right, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, Instagram/atlanticmastoronto)
Pleterski described how he met a man he was introduced to as "Slime" a couple of weeks before the alleged kidnapping who said he wanted help converting cryptocurrency into cash. The pair began communicating and organized a meeting at the Ritz Carlton hotel in downtown Toronto in late 2022, according to Pleterski.
He testified that "Slime" attended the meeting with two other men, including one he later pointed out as Henry in the courtroom.
A couple of days later, on Dec. 5, Pleterski said he received a message from "Slime" asking to meet up about the cryptocurrency. Pleterski testified "Slime" picked him up in downtown Toronto in a Dodge Ram but this time, after he got in the backseat, "Slime" got in beside him and pulled out a gun.
He said Henry was on the other side of him in the backseat and also had a pistol on his lap. Pleterski identified Paladino as the driver.
Sandeep Gupta, Pleterski's former landlord, testified on Tuesday and Thursday at the trial of three men accused of kidnapping the self-described 'Crypto King.' (Pam Davies/CBC)
Pleterski said he was zip-tied and reusable garbage bags were put over his head at various points. He testified the truck got on the Gardiner Expressway and that, while in transit, "Slime" made a call.
"I knew instantly it was AK, or Akil Heywood," said Pleterski, about hearing the voice on the phone, which he testified was on speaker.
Pleterski testified that Heywood said "Where the F is my money, pussy?" and told him: "You're either going to pay with your money or you're going to pay with your life."
From there Pleterski explained how he told the kidnappers that his former landlord Sandeep Gupta was "hiding a bunch of assets, [I] just need to call him." Although in court, Pleterski said that was not true.
On Tuesday, the jury heard audio of a 911 call Gupta made during a phone call with Pleterski. Pleterski testified "Slime" was instructing him on what to say during that call, including telling him he needed $2-3 million from Gupta.
The Crown asked Pleterski why he didn't tell Gupta he was kidnapped.
"If I told him on the phone that I was kidnapped, I was scared that they would kill me," he replied.
Pleterski wasn't sure whether the phone call with Gupta happened before or after he was taken to a field, where the video of him on his knees was allegedly taken.
In that video, after the gun appears to be fired, Pleterski says "Sandeep has it all."
Gupta testified at the trial Tuesday and Thursday and denied any involvement in Pleterski's Ponzi scheme and denied hiding any money or assets for him.
Pleterski's testimony continued Friday afternoon.

The world’s largest, most comprehensive source of information for scientists and doctors to assess diseases and health worldwide is the Global Burden of Diseases study. Yet its dozens of parameters do not include one on a leading cause of disability worldwide: pain.
But it is too easy to blame the study for this oversight: “For pain, there are no medical biomarkers and the best we can do is to ask a person about their subjective experience,” Matthew Fillingim, a researcher at McGill University, Canada, said.
Dr. Fillingim, along with 98 researchers from 63 institutions worldwide, gathered data and studied subjective experiences of pain from 6.1 million individuals from 118 countries, aged 5-100 years, between 1995 and 2005. They recently published their findings in Nature Medicine.

India has had decades of unchanged high anaemia prevalence in women and children that has historically been thought to be due to iron deficiency. This has led firstly to an iron and folic acid (IFA) tablet supplementation targeted at women and children, and secondly to fitful implementation of mandatory fortification of staple foods. IFA is a ‘precision’ strategy, applying as it does to the vulnerable population it is intended for, while fortification is a broad strategy that applies to the entire population. The latter works in controlled settings such as clinical trials, but has not worked in real-world settings, and might have adverse effects when given to those it is unintended for.
The reason for pivoting: anaemia is mistakenly conflated with iron deficiency In India. The evidence is otherwise: in national Indian surveys, it has been shown that iron deficiency is not the major cause of anaemia. Indeed, fully one-third of anaemia cases demonstrate no micronutrient deficiency or obvious cause. Even so, giving iron should have sorted out those who did have iron deficiency anaemia, and reduced the general anaemia prevalence. While this could be a problem with inefficient programme implementation, two important questions arise: is there is really a deficiency in dietary iron intake in India? And is the administered iron being adequately absorbed and utilised for haemoglobin formation?

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Owono undecided over future following De Miguel death
- Published
FC Andorra manager Carles Manso says goalkeeper Jesus Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during a Spanish second division match on 2 November, with the Tenerife forward passing away the following day in hospital.
Manso said the goalkeeper, 25, is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return.
"What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him," Manso said.
"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.
"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that [he will do so]."
Andorra released a statement on behalf of Owono on 4 November, with the Equatorial Guinea keeper saying he was experiencing "the most difficult days of my life".
He added: "I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."
On Thursday, De Miguel's family released a statement via the Spanish Footballers' Association thanking those who had contributed to a crowdfunding page which has surpassed £170,000.
Fran Sol, a forward for Spanish third-tier side Hercules, set up the campaign with all proceeds going to relatives of De Miguel.
"We would like to express our heartfelt thanks for all the expressions of affection and support we have received," De Miguel's family said.
"We have been deeply moved to see so many of you rally behind this initiative."
Andorra will return to action for the first time since the forward's death on Saturday when they face Almeria in the Spanish second division.

Indian women’s hockey team head coach Sjoerd Marijne says he is working on “creating more depth” in the squad with the focus being on shaping versatile players, who can adapt to different positions and situations during the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy in Bhopal next week.
Besides India, the high-profile continental tournament, scheduled from November 19 to 28, will feature Paris Olympics silver medallists China, along with Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.
India offered a glimpse of its growing versatility at the recent Asian Games in Japan, where it defeated China to clinch gold and secure automatic qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Three-time Asian Champions Trophy winner India will now have another opportunity to underline that its Asian Games triumph was no flash in the pan when it faces China again on home turf in Bhopal.
“We are busy creating more depth, which also makes training sessions more competitive. The players are also aware of that,” said Marijne, who is in his second stint with the Indian women’s team after previously coaching the side from 2017 to 2021.
“We want the players to be able to play in different positions. It’s to create more depth in the squad. It becomes helpful if a player gets injured, especially in a tournament like the Olympics, and it’s very helpful for the development of the players,” added Marijne.
Citing the examples of Ishika and Rutuja Dadaso Pisal, Marijne said the idea was to make players comfortable in roles beyond their primary positions. Ishika, for instance, is primarily a forward but is now also being groomed to operate in midfield.
“Ishika normally plays as a striker and now sometimes plays as a midfielder as well; it’s the same with Rutuja (Dadaso Pisal). So, they have to learn to adapt to playing in other positions and we want to see if this adds something to the game we want to play, to the improvements we want to see in the team,” he added.
Marijne said India would concentrate on its own game rather than get caught up in analysing opponents, their combinations or individual players.
“The main thing is what I’ve said the whole year, and it will be the same for this tournament: we have to focus on ourselves, what we want to improve after the Asian Games, what we want to do better. That is where the main focus is for us. And then it doesn’t matter who is the opponent.
“We have worked on those topics in the camp in Bengaluru, and now it’s time to see how they perform under pressure in a tournament,” he added.
The coach also sees the tournament as an opportunity for young players Pooja Sahu and Jyoti Singh to make their mark, while forward Mumtaz Khan’s return adds another option to the attacking line.
“There are youngsters like Pooja who will get a chance, Jyoti Singh for the first time and Mumtaz is back after a long time. I think this is a good platform for all of them to show what they are capable of.”
After ACT, India’s focus will shift to the Pro League, which begins early next year.
The team qualified for the competition after winning the FIH Nations Cup in June. Marijne expects it to be a challenging road ahead.
“Playing against Argentina and Germany in February immediately after the small break following a tournament like Hockey India League is not easy. It’s always a tough period to come back into the international rhythm because the competition level on the international stage is very, very different.”
“But that’s not only with India, that’s the same with every country. You need time to adapt. So, that will be a big challenge for us: how fast we can get the girls back in that zone,” said Marijne.

A Japanese team said that it has become the first in the world to create hybrid plant-animal cells, dubbed “planimal” cells, by fusing a unicellular alga called Cyanidioschyzon merolae into cultured animal cells.
According to the team from the University of Tokyo, the Institute of Science Tokyo, Kindai University and others, all of C. merolae’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.
But the hybrid cells were, in terms of function, animal cells because C. merolae’s DNA was suppressed and chloroplasts, which conduct photosynthesis, were degraded during fusion.
“We hope to introduce chloroplasts and activate C. merolae genes to generate oxygen through photosynthesis,” said Sachihiro Matsunaga, professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Frontier Sciences.
The team’s findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications.
Matsunaga had been working on the production of planimal cells since he proposed the creation of such a hybrid in 2018.
If cells that produce useful animal and plant proteins can be cultured in large quantities using photosynthesis, it could provide a new means of producing drugs and cultured meat. In this experiment, the cultured animal cells were derived from Chinese hamster ovaries, which are used to produce drugs and other products.
While plant cells have walls outside the cell membrane, C. merolae has no cell walls because it is primitive. In addition, its genome is very small.
Matsunaga and other members of the team fused C. merolae into cultured animal cells using a conventional method involving polyethylene glycol, in order to put the alga’s DNA into the animal cell nucleus.
Although the success rate was low, they produced planimal cells in which all of the alga’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.
The integrated DNA was frozen by a mechanism called methylation, acting as an “off” switch for gene expression. Like ordinary cultured animal cells, the planimal cells continued to divide and multiply for more than 150 generations.

BYD admits wheel assembly error on its flagship electric SUV
Some Great Tang SUVs had their wheels installed the wrong way.
BYD has apologized for an assembly mistake affecting some units of its newly released Great Tang — or Datang, as it's called in China — electric SUV. According to Bloomberg, several owners complained that the wider wheel rims that were supposed to be installed on the rear of the vehicle were installed on the front. Meanwhile, the narrower wheel rims for the front of the car were installed on the back instead.
The Chinese electric automaker has posted its apology on social network Weibo, explaining that it launched an investigation after getting complaints from owners. Apparently, it traced the problem to its Hubei-based wheel mesh assembly supplier. BYD said it has already fixed the issue, and the supplier has also added a visual inspection mechanism on the production line, so that future vehicles will no longer be affected.
BYD didn't say how many vehicles were affected by the assembly error, but it said that there was no safety risk associated with the wheels being installed the wrong way. Even so, it will replace the wheel rims of the those vehicles for free and will also offer their owners a replacement vehicle or compensation for what they will spend on transportation while their Great Tang SUVs are being repaired. In addition, the company will restart their vehicle's warranty period.
The company unveiled the Great Tang SUV in March, with prices starting at around $40,000. It received 150,000 orders in its home country. BYD is planning to release the electric vehicle in European and Asian markets outside China by the end of this year or in early 2027.

Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.
After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other users around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.
The outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with users reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.
The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.
“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson says in a statement. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”
The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.
As Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, users will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.
Microsoft said it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, users may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.
The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.
Ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” says Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.
Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.
On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.
The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.
In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.
Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.
It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation.
The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.
Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.
"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.
The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.
A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.
While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.
Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, a claim spread online that U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was threatening to withhold committee assignments for any of his caucus members who didn't support him for speaker of the House.
The rumor circulated on X and Threads, and Snopes readers wrote in to ask us to verify it.
This claim originated from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about "friendly advice with very stark consequences" he allegedly received from senior House Democrats in regard to supporting Jeffries' bid for speaker. Social media posts appear to have taken Leonard's comments somewhat out of context. There's no evidence that Jeffries has literally threatened to withhold committee assignments from anyone who does not support him as speaker.
Jeffries and Leonard's offices did not immediately return requests for more information. Here's what we know:
Leonard's allegations
Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who flipped a Republican-held seat, posted a video on Nov. 9 claiming that top House Democrats said his life will become a "living hell" if he doesn't support Jeffries. 
Leonard says in the video that he will not support Jeffries as speaker without the New York Democrat's commitments to two issues: ending U.S. support for Israeli military actions, including the war in Iran, and a constitutional amendment that would reverse Citizens United, a Supreme Court decision that gives free-speech protections to corporate money in politics.
Here's the transcript from that video (emphasis ours):
Tonight, I met with — we'll call 'em senior members of the Democratic House — who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues: No. 1, getting a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United, and No. 2, ending U.S. support for the war in Iran, and the country, Israel, that led us into it — that that would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election in two years.
You know, we kinda knew this stuff was coming. It's part of the stuff you see in the movies. You know, we're searching our hearts tonight as to how we can reach Leader Jeffries and help him be a better speaker. At the end of the day, the big "D" Democratic Party needs some little "d" democracy and I'm just a stubborn SOB, so we'll continue meeting with our fellow members of Congress and members-elect and try and see if we can build support for what we're trying to do here. On Nov. 11, TMZ posted a video in which a reporter with the tabloid asks Leonard about his comments. In that video, Leonard expands on what "living hell" could mean and says committee assignments could be withheld. However, he also makes it clear that the conversation he was referencing did not directly involve Jeffries, nor was it meant to be threatening.
As such, it's unclear whether anyone actually told Leonard that Jeffries would withhold committee assignments from him or any other Democrat who does not support Jeffries as speaker.
Here's a transcript of the TMZ interview (emphasis ours):

LEONARD: What's out of a movie is the consequences of it, right? And the consequences are very real. Committee assignments will be withheld. TMZ: Is this not what people criticize Trump for? It sounds very similar.
LEONARD: Yeah, I know, I think, you know, well, welcome to Washington, D.C., right? I mean, it's — I'm not shocked, but I'm —
TMZ: Sounds a little shocking. I think you're a little —
LEONARD: — I'm disappointed.
TMZ: Yeah, well listen. We can say — you already said what you had to say. And it's gone viral. But I think we gotta go the next step further, here, just for Americans. Who were these people who said it to you?
LEONARD: Yeah, no, that's how we build relationships and sustain them going forward. But I appreciate it.
TMZ: You don't want to get in trouble, hey man, I appreciate it.
Axios reportedly asked Leonard about the conversation, per a Nov. 11 story, and he emphasized that it was a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" conversation with senior House Democrats. Here's how he described it to Axios:

The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk.

Politico reported that California Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, who is running unopposed for House majority whip, said he didn't know which Democrats Leonard was referring to.
"It's my belief that he will be overwhelmingly selected to lead this caucus. I don't lose any sleep over that," Aguilar reportedly said of Jeffries. "Members could have ideas and interests, and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question."

Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?
- Published
Harry Kane is now England's most-capped men's player as well as his country's record goalscorer, but harder to quantify is where these achievements place him among the Three Lions' greatest ever players.
This is a tricky debate with so many variables and a timescale as old as the game itself and, to my mind, not merely a determination of a player's individual ability but also a measure of their impact upon the nation's psyche.
Ballon d'Or winners Stanley Matthews, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen would surely have a shout if the criteria was such, not to mention genius technicians such as Glenn Hoddle, Chris Waddle and John Barnes.
Likewise, if any England boss managed to extract the best from Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard they would be surely making a classic late dart from midfield.
But to qualify as one of the greatest England players of all time, you need the above ability combined with an impactful overall contribution - those memorable moments and an element of longevity - in a Three Lions shirt.
It might be controversial then to leave out Geoff Hurst, who produced the most recognisable performance in England history, while the man he replaced, Jimmy Greaves, would be a shoo-in were it not for injury earlier in the tournament.
It is also hard to rank the contribution of those whose best football came outside of major tournaments and before the dawn of continental competitions - see Eddie Hapgood, Tom Finney, Nat Lofthouse, Dixie Dean et al.
There are only 10 spots, after all, so here we go.
10. David Beckham
Spice Boy. Celebrity. Galactico. There is no argument David Beckham is one of the most iconic England players of all time, but he backed it up on the pitch, too.
Beckham was the face of the Three Lions for a generation, and to his credit managed to overcome the vicious fallout of his red card against Argentina in 1998.
At times he seemed to single-handedly carry England, most notably scoring a 93rd-minute free-kick against Greece to qualify for the 2002 World Cup.
Beckham's former team-mate Gary Neville called him the "most influential player out of England in transforming football".
It's true. On top of 115 caps, Beckham was part of Manchester United's 1999 Treble-winning outfit - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up - before joining Real Madrid.
His profile was truly global with spells at LA Galaxy, AC Milan and Paris St-Germain.
9. Paul Gascoigne
There's arguably no England star fans forged an emotional attachment with more than Gazza - crying with him in 1990, rejoicing in his spectacular effort against Scotland and desperately willing him to connect during that Euro 96 semi-final defeat by Germany.
Gascoigne won 57 caps and scored 10 goals. At his peak, he was captivating - transcending football as a cultural phenomenon during the summers of '90 and '96, having joined a star-studded Serie A between those tournaments.
Creative, unpredictable, vulnerable. He was a loveable but flawed genius.
He suffered long-term injuries as England missed out on Euro 92 and the World Cup in the USA, but helped the Three Lions qualify for France 98 before being dropped from the final squad, famously wrecking boss Glenn Hoddle's office.
8. Billy Wright
Goalscorers often grab the headlines but I've tried to credit players across positions and eras. From a defensive point of view Ashley Cole, arguably England's best-ever full-back, was close to making it.
But instead it's the great Billy Wright, the first men's player to surpass a century of international caps, including a remarkable 70 successive appearances over eight years.
Wright captained his country on 90 occasions, a joint-record recently broken by Kane, taking in three World Cups with impressive longevity for his era.
He was a true one-club man, winning three league titles, the FA Cup and becoming unofficial "world champions" with Wolves in 1954 - helping inspire the birth of the European Cup - while finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up to Alfredo di Stefano in 1957.
7. Jude Bellingham
It feels a little premature to include a 23-year-old with the bulk of his England career ahead of him, but that shows the impact Jude Bellingham has already made for England and Real Madrid.
A Champions League winner, the midfielder has also appeared at four major tournaments for the Three Lions, becoming the youngest player to do so at the delayed Euro 2020, aged 17.
But his role in helping carry England to the final two years ago and a third-place finish at last summer's World Cup really make him stand out.
Bellingham has delivered those moments a nation collectively remembers. The last-gasp overhead kick against Slovakia in 2024, a quickfire double at the Azteca against Mexico this summer and 93rd-minute quarter-final winner against Norway.
His seven goals at this World Cup were more than any previous Three Lions player in a single edition, the solo effort against France a thing of beauty.
The former Birmingham and Dortmund man doesn't turn 24 until June but has already collected 61 England caps and netted 14 times. As Roy Keane put it, Bellingham has the potential to be one of the "greatest of all time".
6. Wayne Rooney
In terms of natural ability, Wayne Rooney is among England's greatest ever talents.
Bursting on to the scene at Euro 2004 as an electric 18-year-old, having become England's youngest player and scorer the previous year, convinced fans and media the teen sensation could carry the Three Lions to glory in Portugal.
He bounced World Cup winner Lilian Thuram around in England's opener against France in a glimpse of his precocious strength, before scoring twice against both Switzerland and Croatia.
Who knows how far England would have gone had Rooney not been injured against Portugal in the quarter-final?
He was unable to replicate the impact of his first Euros - a red card at World Cup 2006, suspension for the Euro 2012 group stage, seven goals across six major tournaments - but was an all-rounder who brought more than just goals.
Rooney also won it all with Manchester United, becoming the club's all-time top scorer, and finished his 15-year England career with 53 goals from 120 caps.
5. Gordon Banks
There has to be a place for a goalkeeper, and Gordon Banks is the safest pair of hands.
A World Cup winner in 1966, his save from Pele four years later against Brazil is one of the most iconic of all time. Pele called him a "goalkeeper with magic".
Banks spent the majority of his career at Leicester and Stoke, winning a League Cup with each, and earned 73 England caps overall between 1963 and 1972.
His incredible athleticism and reflexes saw the shot-stopper named Fifa's best goalkeeper for five successive years between 1966 and 1971.
4. Gary Lineker
Gary Lineker's early club career did not deliver the silverware as his goals deserved, netting 40 times but finishing league and FA Cup runner-up in his one season at Everton before joining Barcelona.
He scored a Clasico hat-trick and won the Copa del Rey and Cup Winner's Cup, however, before adding an FA Cup with Tottenham in 1991.
Lineker netted 283 club goals (and famously no cards) in total across spells with Leicester, Everton, Barcelona, Spurs and Nagoya Grampus Eight.
But as a player Lineker is most renowned for his contribution in an England shirt, winning the Golden Boot as they reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1986 - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up that year - before netting another four as the Three Lions reached the semi-finals in 1990.
Lineker equalised against West Germany before England crashed out on penalties.
However, having missed a spot-kick against Brazil, he finished one short of Bobby Charlton's elusive goal record when his international career ended after Euro 92.
3. Harry Kane
Harry Kane is undoubtedly England's most important and influential player of a generation - it is hard to imagine how this Three Lions side functions once the skipper hangs up his boots.
The Bayern Munich striker, complete with Ballon d'Or, has been scoring goals for his country for almost 12 years, the first just 79 seconds into his debut after coming off the bench against Lithuania in March 2015.
Rooney's goalscoring benchmark is long in his rear view mirror - you wouldn't bank against Kane doubling his nearest rival's figure once his England days are over.
They have come on the biggest stage, too - 21 in 36 appearances from three World Cups and European Championships apiece, winning the World Cup Golden Boot in 2018.
Kane has come closer to winning a major tournament than any England men's captain since Bobby Moore - losing two World Cup semi-finals and back-to-back Euros finals. Team-mate Bellingham called him the "greatest player that has ever played for England".
"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10, 15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved," said ex-England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.
2. Bobby Moore
In many ways, Bobby Moore would be the complete modern-day defender. Cool as you like under pressure, elegant in possession, a great passing range off both feet and, as his West Ham and England team-mate Geoff Hurst said: "Nobody out-ran him and nobody out-jumped him."
Moore's positioning and timing was perfect, that iconic tackle on Jairzinho at the 1970 World Cup the finest example of his poise and precision when defending.
He was also a composed and influential leader. A player built for the big occasions. England boss Sir Alf Ramsey called him: "My lieutenant on the field, a cool, calculated footballer I could trust with my life."
The Barking-born centre-back won the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup with West Ham but his finest moment was leading England to glory in 1966. He was only 25 at the time, having become his country's youngest captain three years earlier.
In 1970, after the Bogota bracelet incident, Moore was imperious as England reached the quarter-finals before bowing out to West Germany.
It was, however, the final group game against Brazil, the most exciting side on the planet, that produced some of the most recognisable and renowned images in sporting history - not only Moore's tackle and Banks' save but the defender swapping shirts with Pele after the final whistle.
"The greatest defender I ever played against," was the Brazilian's verdict.
1. Sir Bobby Charlton
For more than a generation, Sir Bobby's England goalscoring record remained unmatched. It took 55 years from his 49th and final strike against Colombia in 1970 until Rooney surpassed him with his half century in 2015.
Charlton was, as Alan Shearer put it, "not only a great goalscorer but a scorer of great goals" and played a pivotal part of the Three Lions' World Cup success in 1966, netting three times on the way to the final.
A scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark long-range strike into the corner at Wembley gave England's campaign lift-off against Mexico, before he scored twice against Eusebio's Portugal in the semi-finals.
Manager Ramsey called the buccaneering midfielder his "lynchpin" as England triumphed over West Germany in the showpiece and those performances helped Charlton win the Ballon d'Or later that year.
He'd be runner-up in successive years after that, too.
Charlton won 106 England caps and was a star for Manchester United, with Rooney also the one to pip his club-record 249 goals for the Old Trafford outfit.
A survivor of the Munich air disaster on 6 February 1958, which killed 23 people including eight players and three members of the club's staff, Charlton won three league titles, an FA Cup and most poignantly the European Cup in 1968.
"England's greatest ever player," Lineker previously told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He was unique. Wherever you go in the world, even if they didn't speak the language, they knew two words - Bobby Charlton."

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.
Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.
The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.
For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, December 13 as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.
Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-September 2026.
Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.
Temwa Chawinga
Age: 28 Country: Malawi
Club: Kansas City Position: Forward
Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.
Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.
Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.
Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.
Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.
Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.
Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.
Ewa Pajor
Age: 29 Country: Poland
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.
Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.
The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.
Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.
On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland as is the team's leading goalscorer.
Alexia Putellas
Age: 32 Country: Spain
Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder
Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.
After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.
Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.
Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.
Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.
Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.
Alessia Russo
Age: 27 Country: England
Club: Arsenal Position: Forward
Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.
She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.
Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.
It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.
Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.
She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.
Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw
Age: 29 Country: Jamaica
Club: Manchester City Position: Forward
After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.
The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.
Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.
They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.
She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.
Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

Fintech major Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed ₹5,000-6,000 Cr IPO, sources told Inc42. The offering is expected to value the company at around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027, the sources added. The IPO is expected to comprise a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale (OFS). However, the proposed split could not be ascertained. The Economic Times first reported the development. Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. It filed its IPO papers through the confidential route in June, targeting a valuation of $5 Bn to $6 Bn, below the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021. Ahead of the listing, Razorpay shifted its domicile from the US to India. The company slipped into the red in FY25, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs linked to the move. Operating revenue rose 65% to ₹3,783 Cr during the year. Razorpay’s Growing AI Offerings Alongside its IPO preparations, Razorpay has been expanding its AI offerings across payments, marketing, and business operations. Last month, it announced an expanded partnership with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT. Under the partnership, its growth marketing platform, Razorpay Engage, will enable brands to prepare product catalogues and launch and manage campaigns on ChatGPT Ads. Razorpay has also launched Vulcan, a transformer-based AI foundation model for digital payments. The company claims the model can improve payment reliability and safety by scoring payment routes in real time and identifying fraud patterns across multiple merchants once deployed. Built using NVIDIA and AWS technology, Vulcan combines Razorpay’s payments data with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AWS’ cloud infrastructure. The fintech major has also been developing Agent Studio, a platform for deploying task-specific AI agents for businesses. Around 200 businesses were using the platform in beta as of August, with use cases spanning reconciliation, abandoned-cart recovery, subscription recovery, and finance operations. Razorpay has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors including Y Combinator, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump wrote a social media post chastising Vice President JD Vance, including an order to change the vice president's name, circulated in November.
People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a social media post attributed to Trump that claimed, "I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!"
(X user @miribobs)
The alleged post was dated Nov. 5 and inspired readers to reach out about its authenticity. It circulated after Democrats enjoyed major victories in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
It read in full:
I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!
Nobody gave JD more than President Trump. I took him from the sidelines and gave him the biggest job of his life—and now he thinks he can DOUBLE CROSS THE BOSS and run for President in 2028 without my blessing?
EHHH!
WRONG!
You don't walk into the Trump Family, eat at the table, kiss the ring, and then decide you're the new Boss!
There is only ONE person who can make America Great Again the RIGHT WAY, and everybody knows who that is.
JD, you may have forgotten who made you—but I NEVER forget!
THE PRESIDENT HAS SPOKEN.
The post was fake, however.
A search of the president's Truth Social account and an online archive of his social media posts revealed no such post.
The fake Trump post circulated as an apparent response, likely satirical, to a Nov. 4 X post by Vance addressing the Republican turnout at the polls for the midterm elections. Vance wrote: "The main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026." His post sparked rumors that he's angling for a 2028 bid for the White House.
The engagement metrics displayed on the fake post — 14.3K reposts, 56.7K likes — exactly match those of other debunked Trump posts, suggesting it may have been generated using a template or a fake post generator. Note that the timestamp is written out as "11/5/26," while authentic Truth Social posts show dates written as "Nov 5, 2026."
The president made multiple posts on Truth Social on that date, but nothing about Vance or a rumored bid for the White House.
For further reading, check out Snopes' collection of alleged Trump social media posts we've debunked.

On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang resigned from the company that had become, in many ways, synonymous with its chief executive.
Less than an hour later, when the markets opened, Nvidia’s stock had lost roughly $546 billion in market value. Though it has rebounded somewhat, the last weeks of scandal—including a reported second affair with an Nvidia employee—have tanked the chip maker’s valuation by more than $1 trillion.
Huang’s very public downfall began in late October, when the The New York Times reported that the CEO had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed and alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. (The two are not known to be related.) At that time, Nvidia’s market cap was around $5.2 trillion.
On November 8, Nvidia announced it was investigating its CEO, after Jensen publicly acknowledged the affair. By the following morning, roughly $1 trillion had been erased since the scandal started.
If you hang out with a certain type of person who thinks of themselves as a day trader, they might have talked about “buying the dip” over drinks last weekend. If you believe Nvidia can thrive without Huang, there’s still time! The dip has dipped even further. But the early consensus seems to be that this could be more of a prolonged plunge.
“Huang is irreplaceable,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, told WIRED last week. “He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution.”
There are very real questions about what the end of Huang means for the global economy. Not only are Nvidia’s chips used to train most major AI models, the company has invested billions in a number of other tech companies. As of an August regulatory filing, Nvidia owned nearly $30 billion worth of Intel stock and roughly $21 billion of SpaceX stock.
For now, Nvidia’s loss is other chipmakers’ gain. AMD shares are up 28 percent over the last five days, and Broadcom is up nearly 16 percent. Nothing to see here.
More Numbers That Illuminate Huang’s Value:
- Nvidia’s market share of chips used in training frontier AI models: Roughly 90 percent
- AI companies in which Nvidia has invested at least $100 million: 8, as of its August filing.
- Huang’s pay last year: $36 million
- Portion of Nvidia owned by Huang: 3.5 percent, as of March—which means the scandal has devalued Huang’s own share of the company by more than $50 billion.
- Reported affairs: 2 (so far)
- PR firms hired with expertise in sex scandals: At least one
- Huang relatives employed by Nvidia: One son, one daughter, and one son-in-law
- Leather jackets owned: Several, including a $960,000 Tom Ford number. (But not that vintage Saint Laurent jacket everyone was talking about on X.)

Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder, a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.
The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose and design studies of the drug.
Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy and most other psychedelic drugs.
Veterans organisations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.
Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.
“That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process,” Kennedy said. “We’re going to have, I think, a record drug approval process.”
Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.
Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and “best-in-class research.”
“For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce,” Collins said.
Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.
Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.
Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the Food and Drug Administration. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.
Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.
The little data currently available mostly comes from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.
Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: “Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let’s do it.”

In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.
The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.
In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.
The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
All matters are still before the courts.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.
Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.
“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”
The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.
A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse – is traded.
Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.
It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.
The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.
There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”

Mumbai: YES Bank has asked the Supreme Court to review its 15 October order upholding a Bombay High Court ruling against the write-down of ₹8,415 crore of additional tier-1 (AT-1) bonds, a move that could prolong the wait for bondholders. “The Bank has filed a review petition under Article 137 of the Constitution of India before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India seeking review of its judgment and order dated October 15, 2026 in relation to the write-down of additional tier-1 bonds aggregating to ₹8,415 crore,” the lender said in a late Friday disclosure to the stock exchanges. In its 15 October ruling, the Supreme Court dismissed appeals by YES Bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Centre, upholding a Bombay High Court order that held that the bank’s administrator had no authority to write down the bonds as part of the lender’s 2020 rescue. The case relates to the perpetual AT-1 bonds that were written down as part of the YES Bank Reconstruction Scheme, 2020. Bondholders and the trustee, Axis Trustee Services, challenged the decision before the Bombay High Court, which quashed the write-down in January 2023. The Supreme court directed YES Bank to restore the bonds to bondholders with immediate effect. However, with the lender yet to act on the judgment, the YES Bank AT-1 Bond Holders Association, which represents around 400-450 affected investors, and Axis Trustee Services have written to the bank seeking restoration of the bonds and payment of pending interest dues. “The bank will take all such steps and measures as are necessary and permissible under applicable law,” including consequential actions, available legal remedies and other steps that may appropriately be taken in accordance with the law, it said in a letter to Axis Trustee dated 30 October. The lender has reiterated the same in other public disclosures, and has also informed stakeholders that it is continuing to evaluate and assess the matter Shares of YES Bank ended 0.3% lower at ₹17.42 on the National Stock Exchange on Friday. Reinstating the bonds is expected to have a significant capital and margin impact for the lender. In the earnings call, managing director and chief executive director Vinay Tonse had said that reinstatement of the AT-1 principal amount is expected to have a pro forma impact of approximately 240 basis points on the bank’s common equity tier-1 ratio, including profits. As of 30 September, the bank’s capital adequacy ratio was 14.5% and the common equity tier-1 ratio was 13.7%. “Our overall Tier 1 capital ratio is expected to remain around 13.7% on a pro forma basis. We recognize that the distinction between CET-1 and overall Tier 1 capital is important. We will continue to assess the implications for our capital structure, regulatory buffers, balance Sheet strength, and future growth plans,” Tonse had said.
