Hyderabad cricket has heard many speeches, but few came with a tractor.
In the six months since Ambati Rayudu promised to change the culture, the former India batter has been seen at pitch-side at dawn, at the soil vendor’s door in the rain and, by his own count, five to seven kilos lighter.
The initial results suggest the effort is paying off. The first phase of this Ranji Trophy season has wrapped up with Hyderabad winning three matches and playing out one draw, enough to sit on top of the Elite Group B table with 20 points. From players to coaches, the delight is evident.
Rayudu, the Director of Cricket Operations at the Hyderabad Cricket Association, shares it, but he is wary of premature celebrations. He takes his pride instead from the system underneath.
“I wouldn’t read too much into the results as of now, but I’m very happy with the way the systems are set. And most importantly, the boys are very confident and glad there is something to look forward to,” he told Sportstar.
It is a long way from May 5, when he walked into a hall of cameras and vowed to take Hyderabad cricket to the next level. Plenty of men have said as much in those corridors. What followed, Rayudu says, was quieter than the promise: basics, done properly, every single day.
First, he filled the calendar. Hyderabad’s age-group sides now play far more than the league demands, close to a thousand match days this season. It is how his own generation grew up.
“When they wake up, if they don’t have a game, they need to be worried: ‘What am I going to do today?’ We wanted to get that feeling back.”
Wasim Jaffer’s arrival as mentor has reinforced that change, bringing a cricketing culture to players and coaches alike. Open trials now let district players walk into Gymkhana and chase a State cap.
From the grassroots to the selection room, no corner of the system escaped a rethink.
“The first point on our agenda while picking selectors was: Do they have the integrity required? Because beyond that, we will take care of whatever comes. And because they come with such integrity, they are quite adamant and stubborn in their decision making as well. That is a welcome sign because we don’t want them to be yes-men. And they have done a fantastic job, so no complaints at all. All due credit to Jeevan Reddy (HCA secretary) or anybody else, they have never questioned the team selections.”
His Cricket Operations Committee (COC) had only stepped in when choosing who to lead the side.
Every pick and every omission is done through a signed sheet, filed with the Single Member Committee (SMC) headed by retired Justice P. Naveen Rao, Jeevan and the COC.
“The sheets have all the details about why a player was selected. In case any issue comes up, everything can be checked. It’s a way to avert any bad calls. It’s just like a Decision Review System (DRS), which helps us avoid blunders. If something comes up in the future, there is always documentation, which over a few years also helps us gather data on what could have been better.”
Digging in
From a cricket development perspective, Hyderabad’s flat tracks are no one’s first choice. They weren’t Rayudu’s either. International fixtures returning to the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium meant domestic hosting duties were solely granted to the iconic Gymkhana ground in Secunderabad.
Rayudu had ideas, but had to deal with some anticipated roadblocks first.
“There were so many apprehensions. Funds weren’t getting released sometimes. Tenders were not being opened.”
The system dragged its feet but Rayudu and head curator Mukesh Kumar did not. Priority was finding the right soil to redo the pitches.
They waited on vendors who vanished when the rains came, paid extra for earthmovers and chased labour that never turned up. When no tractors could enter the city, Rayudu sent for his own.
ALSO READ | Ranji Trophy 2026-27: “Both stressed and happy,” Anirudh Singh on Hyderabad’s last-gasp win
“Once everything came to the ground, we did not get labour sometimes. There were no tractors that were coming into the city, among other issues. So I brought my own tractor and the person who works on my farm. He is the one who has done all the banks that you see in Gymkhana now.”
Picking the soil, too, was just as elaborate and involved early morning trips to neighbouring districts.
“We’ve put in three types of soil. Even the mixed soil used is a natural mix. The soil near Vikarabad naturally gets mixed with red and black, so that is one of the soils that we picked up. There’s also a black soil pitch which is a proper seaming track which, I am sure, will come in handy in the future.”
His benchmark comes from seven seasons at Motibaug with Baroda. A good Ranji pitch, he explained, lets teams bat about 90 overs and keeps all four innings alive. The toss should not decide the outcome.
This surge was hardly without resistance. Ticking deadlines, noncooperative arms of bureaucracy and funding trouble came and went but the COC persevered. On the field, backing local league performers for the newly introduced Super League places drew backlash from those used to doing it differently.
Rayudu shrugged off the risk. “What is the worst thing that can happen? They would have all signed a petition to remove us! But by the time that happens, we would have already done a lot of good work.”
Rayudu sits now with the satisfaction of a productive start under his belt.
“It was a crazy experience, but we were not going to stop for anybody. It’s not just me. Even Wasim bhai, Mukesh and COC members P.S. Niranjan and M.P. Arjun, they have put in a lot of effort behind the scenes to make all this happen. It’s been a painstaking and stressful one, but for the first time in HCA’s history, I think good is winning over evil.”
Systems to outlast
The next phase moves beyond Gymkhana. Academies have been planned in Mahabubnagar and Karimnagar, along with a high-performance centre at Uppal, possibly run by an outside body under a public-private model. Rayudu hopes to get work started within a month or two. HCA-run teams may also enter different league divisions, so that talent found at open trials has somewhere competitive to play.
Women’s cricket will follow.
“We didn’t have time to go into women’s cricket this season,” Rayudu admitted, adding, “It’s just a matter of time that everything will follow in women’s cricket as well. SMC and even Jeevan are very eager to get everything done in the women’s game as well.”
Less than a decade ago, Rayudu took to social media and did not mince his words in criticising the way HCA was run. And he admitted that he never saw himself coming to bring out the change he longed to see.
“I thought that there was no hope left. But as they say in India, justice is always delayed, but it is never denied. I wouldn’t say things are perfect right now, not at all. There’s still a long way to go from here, but the processes are being set, there are a lot of systems and protocols that have come into place. Eventually at the end of the season we will release a document on the systems and processes. Once it all gets ratified and if followed, a lot of good will happen in the future.”
ALSO READ | Fast bowler needs pace and bounce: Siraj embraces New Zealand challenge
Rayudu, who said his desire is to see HCA among India’s top five associations in administration as well as cricket, said he is taking it all one year at a time. He has had the support of the SMC and Jeevan during this time, something he constantly credits for what he’s managed to do in the opening months of his tenure.
“I told myself that I’ll give everything to Hyderabad cricket for a year. I wanted to sacrifice a year for Hyderabad, which has done so much for me in terms of my cricketing career. Beyond this, I want to set up systems and protocols. The main thing is that SMC needs to be there for at least two or three years. That is very, very important, and along with him Jeevan should be around. I think with them and with these systems, even if I am there or not, it will all run very well.”
It’s been a decade since Hyderabad made the Ranji knockouts. They’ve even had a taste of life in the Plate division since. Three wins in four fixtures is a good start, but it’s just that – a start. Rayudu and his team have picked their Everest. But the first steps look promising.

Subsequently, customs officials held shipments belonging to several companies, including Pernod Ricard India, Diageo, Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers.
The industry has objected to a memorandum issued by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), which classified imported Scotch whisky as alcoholic beverage concentrate rather than finished whisky. This triggered a dispute over the applicable HS code and customs duty. The issue has also been described as a technical complication in the implementation of the India-UK FTA.
ANI reported, citing sources, that the Commerce Secretary assured industry representatives that the government would take a decision on the matter soon.
The HS code determines the applicable customs duty and rules. The DRI's position is that the imported products should be classified as alcoholic beverage concentrate rather than finished Scotch whisky because they enter India at a higher alcohol strength and are diluted later at a domestic facility. This classification could alter the duty calculation and raise questions about the accuracy of the original declarations.
The DRI says the imported concentrate has an alcohol content of 62–66%, compared with 42–46% for finished Scotch whisky. Since the two products fall under different HSN codes, the companies maintain that their imports qualify under the code eligible for concessions under the FTA.
DRI officials are examining whether some bulk Scotch whisky imports by the companies were classified in a manner that allowed them to claim lower customs duties under the India-UK trade agreement.
The sources clarified that the probe does not amount to a fresh increase in customs duty or establish any wrongdoing by the companies. Instead, authorities are examining which categories of Scotch imports qualify for the lower rate introduced under the India-UK trade agreement on July 15, 2026. Under the pact, the duty on eligible imports was reduced from 150% to 75%, effectively halving the rate.
However, the DRI has argued that the reduced duty applies only to finished products, including bottled, ready-to-drink Scotch, and not to bulk Scotch concentrates used in the manufacture of whisky brands.
Reuters recently reported that it had reviewed a confidential DRI memorandum dated November 4, which instructed customs officials across the country to continue applying the 150% duty on bulk Scotch imports. The memo described importers' claims for benefits under the trade agreement as "incorrect", stating that the products were concentrates or compound preparations requiring further manufacturing. It also flagged the potential for large-scale and recurring revenue implications arising from misclassification.
The classification dispute has also resulted in Scotch whisky shipments being held up at Indian ports. Reuters reported that Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers awaiting clearance, while Bacardi has five containers on hold. The companies are reportedly reluctant to pay the 150% duty, and prolonged delays could disrupt supplies.
Bulk shipments account for nearly 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume. These imports are subsequently used to produce Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL), in which Scotch is blended with other spirits and ingredients.
India's Scotch whisky imports were valued at $335 million in 2024. The Scotch Whisky Association has projected that the India-UK trade agreement could increase the value of bilateral trade by $1.34 billion over five years.

SpiceJet crisis: Understanding flight cancellations, passenger rights
Social media platforms have been flooded with posts from passengers, complaining about last-minute cancellations
When a Bengaluru-bound passenger arrived at Delhi airport for a SpiceJet flight on November 5, she discovered at the last moment that it had been cancelled. In a post on X, the passenger quoted a help desk person blaming fewer aircraft and a financial crisis for the cancellation.
On November 11, another X user wrote that her father-in-law’s flight from Kolkata to Mumbai was cancelled on November 6 with no information via email or WhatsApp. The user questioned who would hold SpiceJet accountable and said last-minute flight cancellations, prolonged delays, refund issues, and complaints of poor treatment at airports were causing serious distress.
Social media platforms have been flooded with posts from aggrieved passengers, complaining about last-minute cancellations, lack of information, and difficulties in securing refunds.
On November 12 (Thursday), Dubai Airports, which owns and operates Dubai International Airport and Al Maktoum International Airport, stopped cash-strapped SpiceJet’s check-in services over non-payment of around 14 million UAE dirhams (approximately ₹35.85 crore), even as the airline said it was working to resolve the issue without specifying how.
The action forced the airline to cancel four flights to Amritsar, Jaipur, Mumbai and Delhi on November 12. Other departures from Dubai were cancelled until the issue was resolved.
A SpiceJet spokesperson said the airline is resolving the matter with the concerned authorities. “We have adequate bank guarantee cover in place and are working to ensure that the issue is sorted out at the earliest.”
In a November 13 (Friday) communication, the airline informed BSE Limited about a meeting of the Board of Directors of the company on Wednesday (November 18) to consider and approve the proposal to raise fresh capital, including by issuing equity shares, preference shares, debt securities and/or other permissible instruments.
Operational difficulties, shrunk fleet
SpiceJet has been facing mounting financial and operational difficulties. Its fleet has shrunk to around 12 aircraft, with only nine operational, Mint reported on November 12. The airline’s domestic market share fell to 0.6% in September, down from 3.9% in January. It flew around 73,000 domestic passengers in September, compared with nearly 592,000 in January.
Data from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) showed that SpiceJet cancelled 20.29% of its scheduled flights in September. Its on-time performance at major airports fell to 16.6%. The carrier has struggled to clear supplier dues. ₹63.03 crore owed to small businesses remained unpaid beyond the stipulated 45-day period during April-September 2026, according to regulatory filings.
In the fiscal year that ended March 2026, the Ajay Singh-promoted SpiceJet flew 6.24 million passengers (17,352 passengers daily on average), including international, through 46,063 departures (an average of 126.2 daily). It had a market share of 4.7%, as per provisional DGCA data.
From April to September 2026, departures dipped to 13,422, including international (74 daily on average). The number of passengers declined to 1.8 million, including international (2,043.87 passengers daily on average), according to DGCA data.
Neither the Civil Aviation Ministry nor the aviation regulator DGCA has announced the weekly flights each domestic carrier will operate in the ongoing winter schedule (October 25-March 2027).
A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that SpiceJet filed around 550 arrivals and departures weekly (around 80 flights per day) under its winter schedule. But the aircraft fleet tracking website planespotter.net said the airline had only 11 aircraft (including two regional jets) in its fleet as of November 12, and 38 of them were on the ground.
Considering that one aircraft can operate an average of seven domestic flights daily, an airline roughly requires a fleet of 11-12 aircraft with some in buffer in case of a glitch.
Outstanding dues
People aware of the matter said the airline has failed to clear outstanding dues to vendors, including aircraft and engine lessors, jet fuel suppliers, and airport operators, amid a cash crunch. They added that the airline has failed to pay salaries to a majority of its employees for months.
Oil companies and air operators have put the struggling carrier on a pay-as-you-fly mode. As long as payments are not made, flights are not allowed to depart, resulting in delays and sometimes in last-minute cancellations.
The airline is struggling with an inadequate operational fleet, financial constraints, and mounting payment obligations. These factors appear to have affected its ability to operate flights as scheduled, resulting in cancelled flights, prolonged delays, uncertainty, and, in some cases, difficulties in securing refunds.
Rights and protections
The 2019 Ministry of Civil Aviation Passenger Charter, which outlines key rights and protections for air travellers and is enforced through DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements, mandates that airlines must inform passengers about a flight cancellation at least two weeks before the scheduled departure time. Airlines must arrange an alternate flight or refund, based on what the customer accepts.
The compensation includes free meals and a monetary component ranging from ₹5,000-10,000 depending on scenarios, including the nature of delay, the flight’s block time, or the booked one-way basic fare plus airline fuel charge, whichever is lower.
If a flight is delayed, passengers who have checked in on time are entitled to free meals and refreshments, depending on the waiting time.
For domestic flights expected to be delayed by over six hours, the airline must offer an alternative flight within six hours or a full refund. If the total delay exceeds 24 hours, or six hours for flights scheduled to depart between 8 pm and 3 am, the airline must provide hotel accommodation, including transfers, where applicable.
If an airline fails to provide the prescribed compensation or facilities, passengers can first approach the airline. They can also lodge a complaint through the government’s AirSewa portal or app. If they are dissatisfied with the resolution, they can approach the appropriate statutory body or court.
Airlines are exempt from paying compensation when cancellations or delays result from extraordinary circumstances beyond their control, such as adverse weather, security risks, certain Air Traffic Control restrictions, or other qualifying force majeure events.

New Zealand defeated India by a massive 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui after bowling them out for just 89 while defending a target of 334.
Matt Henry starred with a sensational six-wicket haul, including three wickets in the opening over, which triggered India’s batting collapse.
Henry explained that his bowling strategy was to keep things simple, target the stumps and make the most of the new-ball conditions. He said the sharp movement in the opening over put Indian batters under immediate pressure, particularly those facing their first deliveries.
“Well, especially with the way the wind was going, I wasn’t too worried about the swing. So from ball one it was just about trying to have the strengths and bring the stumps in play, really. We knew that there was a small window there with the new ball that you could put the batters under pressure. So just trying to be as simple as possible, obviously, and when it moves sharply like that in the first over, when people are facing the first ball, it’s pretty tough,” Matt Henry said after the match.
Matt Henry (6/27) wreaked havoc on India’s top order, dismissing Rohit Sharma (0), Virat Kohli (0) and Shreyas Iyer (0) in a sensational opening over to leave the visitors reeling at 0/3. The Kiwi pacer returned to dismantle the lower order, removing Ishan Kishan, Kuldeep Yadav (1) and Gurnoor Brar (2) to register career-best ODI figures and bowl India out for just 89 in 26.4 overs.
Henry continued his impressive record against India in ODIs. The Kiwi pace spearhead has now claimed 27 wickets in 12 matches at an outstanding average of 17.33, including two five-wicket hauls.
Speaking on his impressive record against India in ODIs, Henry acknowledged Men in Blue’s world-class quality and cautioned against reading too much into one victory, stressing that the team would need to maintain its focus ahead of the next match.
“Oh, I don’t want to get too carried away. No, they’re a world-class outfit, and I think that’s the message that we were saying right through. They can bat deep, and yeah, look, it’s one game, and we’ve got another one coming up soon that hopefully we can level the series,” he added.
It proved to be a decisive result as the hosts trimmed India’s series lead to 2-1 heading into the final fixture on Sunday.

A Mexican Singer Gives Old Ballads New Heroines
Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.
Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba.
Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers.
Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife.
“I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!”
On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.

Uttarakhand releases draft voter list after SIR, 72.78 lakh names included
Uttarakhand released its draft electoral roll listing 72,78,035 voters after a special revision. Claims and objections remain open until December 11, ahead of final publication on January 4.
The draft electoral roll for Uttarakhand was released on November 12, with 72,78,035 voters listed following a Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. Voters can submit claims and objections, including applications for inclusion, deletion or correction of names, until December 11, 2026.
Additional Chief Electoral Officer Vijay Kumar Jogdande announced the figures at a press conference, saying the draft roll includes 34,84,447 women, 37,93,373 men and 215 third-gender voters. The state also has 86,028 service voters, comprising 83,352 men and 2,676 women.
The release follows a special campaign conducted between October 4 and October 31, during which more than one lakh new voters were added to the electoral roll. The Election Commission had earlier released figures on October 3, showing 71,58,949 voters in the state.
This marks an increase of 1,19,086 voters compared with the October 3 figures.
The electoral department also received 6,130 applications for deletion of names under Form 7, which were processed in accordance with the prescribed rules.
12,498 POLLING STATIONS IN UTTARAKHAND
Jogdande said the state now has 12,498 polling stations following the reorganisation of polling centres.
Young people who will turn 18 by January 1, 2027, can also apply to have their names included in the electoral roll. Those whose names are missing from the draft list can submit Form 6 by December 11.
Applications can be submitted offline through Booth Level Officers (BLOs). Voters can also apply online through the Election Commission's ECINET app and its official website.
HOW TO CHECK YOUR NAME IN THE DRAFT VOTER LIST
Voters can check their names on the Election Commission's website, www.voter.eci.gov.in, and the Chief Electoral Officer, Uttarakhand's website, www.ceo.uk.gov.in.
The draft electoral roll is also available at the offices of District Election Officers (DEOs) and Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), as well as through local BLOs.
The Election Commission has provided soft copies of the draft roll to recognised national political parties. Hard copies are also being made available at the district level.
FINAL ELECTORAL ROLL ON JANUARY 4
The claims and objections process will remain open from November 12 to December 11, 2026. The election department will scrutinise and dispose of the applications by December 28.
After completing the process, the final electoral roll will be published on January 4, 2027.
The previous electoral roll, released on October 3 following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), had listed 71,58,949 voters. It included 34,21,036 women, 37,37,701 men and 212 third-gender voters.

Abhimanyu Mishra had welcomed the chance to play Magnus Carlsen twice when the Total Chess draw was announced. On Thursday, the youngest Grandmaster in the field emerged from those encounters unbeaten, even leaving the world No. 1 defending an inferior position in their return game.
The 17-year-old American drew both games in the third and fourth rounds of the Fast Classic group stage, making Carlsen wait for his first victory after four successive draws.
Mishra, rated 2644 against Carlsen’s 2823, was secure with Black in their first encounter. An Italian Game remained balanced despite Carlsen’s bishop sacrifice on h6, and the game ended in a draw following a rook exchange on move 50.
The return game offered Mishra considerably more. Carlsen chose the Scandinavian Defence, but his position deteriorated after he moved his king to d7 on move 26. Mishra’s knight manoeuvre to h5 allowed him to collect the g7 and h6 pawns, giving him a substantial advantage.
Carlsen nevertheless steered the game towards an opposite-coloured bishop ending. Mishra’s advantage slipped away as the kingside pawns advanced, and the Norwegian established a defensive barrier. The American continued probing before agreeing to a draw after 80 moves.
Before tournament began, Mishra had told Sportstar that the strength of the field was central to his decision to accept the invitation.
“What really convinced me to come here is the sheer number of the world’s elite,” he said.
He had particularly welcomed two games against Carlsen as a learning opportunity, alongside meetings with Anish Giri and Ian Nepomniachtchi.
The draws took Mishra to three points in Group C. Carlsen had four, while Nepomniachtchi and Haik Martirosyan shared the lead on six, with six games remaining. Nepomniachtchi drew twice with Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, while Martirosyan and Giri exchanged victories.
Arjun recovers; Praggnanandhaa, Vaishali lose twice
Bibisara Assaubayeva delivered the day’s biggest rating upset by defeating Arjun Erigaisi with Black in round three. The Kazakh, rated 2532 against Arjun’s 2746, secured her first Fast Classic victory after two opening-day draws.
Arjun responded by winning the return encounter, also with Black. The split results left both players on five points in Group D, with Arjun third ahead of Assaubayeva on the preliminary blitz tie-break.
R. Vaishali lost both games to Hans Niemann, leaving her last with one point. Niemann joined Maxime Vachier-Lagrave on eight after the Frenchman beat Wesley So and drew the return game.
R. Praggnanandhaa also endured two defeats, against Fabiano Caruana, and remained bottom of Group B on two points. Caruana led with 10, followed by Liem Le on eight after a win and a draw against Vincent Keymer.
Alireza Firouzja led Group A with eight points after beating Jorden van Foreest and drawing their second game. Jan-Krzysztof Duda followed on seven after trading wins with Nodirbek Abdusattorov.

In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks
The Kremlin, taking a hard line, is pushing to widen negotiations to overhaul European security structures.
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.
The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, the envoys were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.
Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw the European security architecture are addressed.
The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some of its positions.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces were again facing restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked the United States for information.

Delhi NCR-based gaming startup Zupee has nothing more to lose. For one, it has laid off its entire workforce. Then, its announcement of a pivot towards AI has failed to see the light of day. According to sources, the startup has provided severance pay to the affected employees, covering the period until January 2027, and its October pivot was a veiled attempt to present the impending closure. The final round of layoffs coincided with Zupee’s public announcement of its foray into AI, Inc42 has learnt. On October 16, the startup said it was positioning its existing technological capabilities as the foundation for its AI ambitions. However, it did not disclose its new gig. Further, the October layoffs followed two earlier rounds of job cuts. Zupee sacked around 200 employees 10 months before its October layoff and nearly 170 employees before that. At its peak, the startup employed close to 500 employees. Inc42 reached out to Zupee for comment but did not receive a response. Zupee Disguises Shutdown? On October 16, Zupee announced that it was exiting the gaming business and would focus on building AI-led ventures. The ailing startup said it would leverage its experience of serving over 200 Mn users to develop AI products for Indian consumers. “There was no AI plan. It was a damage control exercise to hide the fact that Zupee was winding down its operations. Currently, they have no employees left, barring 3-4 who are working with the founders,” sources told Inc42. Meanwhile, Zupee has also shut down its astrology platform, NeoAstro, and its microdrama venture, Zupee Studio, as part of its restructuring in October. The closure of these businesses suggest that Zupee may have already been winding down. Zupee entered the microdrama segment as part of this diversification strategy. It was in advanced discussions to acquire Vertical TV. “However, the proposed acquisition eventually fell through,” sources said. Inc42 could not independently ascertain the reasons behind this. What Happens To Zupee's $120 Mn Warchest? Founded in 2018 by Dilsher Singh Malhi and Siddhant Saurabh, Zupee built its business around mobile versions of traditional Indian games, including Ludo, Snakes and Ladders and Carrom. Over the years, it had raised over $120 Mn from investors, including Z47, Orios Venture Partners, Nepean Capital, WestCap Group, Tomales Bay Capital and AJ Capital. With its gaming business discontinued and its other consumer ventures reportedly shut down, questions remain about the startup’s remaining cash reserves, assets and outstanding liabilities. Inc42 reached out to Zupee’s investors, including Z47 Partners and Nepean Capital, to understand whether they were informed about the impending shutdown and workforce reduction, and whether the AI pivot was presented to them as a genuine business strategy. Investors have also been asked about the current status of their investment, the possibility of recovering unutilised capital and whether the management has initiated discussions around a potential shutdown or liquidation. However, none of the investors responded to Inc42’s queries. For a startup that raised close to $120 Mn and built a consumer platform with a claimed user base of over 200 Mn, the developments mark a significant reversal from its earlier growth ambitions.

- There are a total of 9 NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters.
- NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters can be hired to aid you or open a Rift for you and your party.
- Epic will add more NPCs to the Fortnite Treasure Hunters map as the storyline progresses.
Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season has introduced several new NPCs to the island, with two being carried over from Chapter 7 Override. Each of them has a story to tell and offers some service. That said, here’s where to find all NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season and what to expect from them.
All Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season NPC Locations and Services
There are a total of 9 NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season, with most of them being centered in and around POIs. You have to eventually visit all of them, be it to complete quests or merely to explore the entirety of the Fortnite Treasure Hunters map.
Unlike the bosses in Fortnite Treasure Hunters, you can approach these NPCs without the fear of being attacked. They are friendly and do not attack unless provoked. That said, here is where to find all Fortnite Treasure Hunters NPCs and what they provide in terms of services:
| NPC Name | Location | Services Offered | 
|---|---|---|
| Treasure Hunter Hope | Lantern Landing | Hire | 
| Charlotte-Sensei | The $.$. Rocky | Hire | 
| Buccaneer Brigand Jones | Windmill Village | Hire | 
| Kawaii Team Leader | Lil’ Uzi’s Stronghold | Hire | 
| Nami | South of Windmill Village | Rift | 
| Roronoa Zoro | Arlong Park | Rift | 
| Monkey D. Luffy | Loguetown | Rift | 
| Sanji | Busy Bay | Rift | 
| Usopp | Loguetown | Rift | 
Out of the 9 NPCs in Fortnite, only 4 of them can be hired to aid you in combat. If you plan on hunting for new Sprites in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season, it’s always good to have more party members. The rest provide a “Rift” service, which is used to rotate. That said, we’ve provided a map to help you get a better idea of where they are located.
Keep in mind that the list of NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters can change as the Mini Season progresses. However, as of the Fortnite Treasure Hunters update 43.10, this is where each NPC can be found on the island.
How to Hire an NPC in Fortnite
You can hire one NPC per player, for a total of three when playing in a squad. With the Fortnite Pirate Shop benefiting the entire team, playing together now makes more sense. That said, follow these steps to hire an NPC in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season:
- Check the map to see where the NPC is located and go to the general area.
- Once you are near an NPC that can be hired, look for the hire marker on top of the NPC’s head to confirm it’s a hireable NPC.
- Approach and talk to the Fortnite NPC using the interact button (E on the keyboard, Square on PlayStation, X on Xbox).
- Click on “Hire NPC” and confirm the service.
Once you hire the NPC, they follow you around wherever you go. Keep in mind that they can get eliminated, so try to protect them as best you can. They are rather nifty during a Battle Royale match, especially if you’re trying to complete One Piece Quests in Fortnite.
Where Did Gold Bars Go in Fortnite?
By now you’ve probably noticed that you don’t need to spend Gold Bars to hire an NPC or use any service since they’re all free. Epic Games has officially vaulted Gold Bars as of Fortnite update 43.00. This is rather odd since the theme is “Treasure Hunters” and everyone revolves around loot.
That’s about everything you need to know about NPCs in Fortnite Treasure Hunters. Remember to visit them as soon as you can to hear some interesting lore and use their services on the island to your advantage.

As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.

The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.
It is that time of the year where our conversations will be accompanied by sore throats and respiratory problems.
But who is responsible for this?

BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

Sovereign function: MEA on visa cancellations for foreign speakers at Congress event
The MEA defended reported visa denials and revocations for foreign Bharat Summit invitees. Congress questioned the move after Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng's clearance was cancelled.
The Ministry of External Affairs on Friday said visa matters were the sovereign function of any government, amid reports that visas of several foreign speakers were denied or revoked ahead of the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
Those affected reportedly included Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng, who was scheduled to speak at the summit. The Congress, which organised the event on November 13 and 14, questioned the government's decision.
“Visa matters are sovereign functions of any country or any government. So that is what I have to say,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a regular media briefing, according to PTI.
He was responding to a question about reports that the government had denied or revoked visas for more than 100 foreign invitees to the summit while granting clearance to over 300 others.
Lyng, an independent journalist from Norway, had briefly drawn media attention during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Oslo in May after asking the Indian side a question about press freedom.
In a post on X, Lyng asked Home Minister Amit Shah why her visa, granted by the Indian embassy in Norway, was cancelled minutes before she was due to leave for the airport. She said she hoped Shah would allow her to visit the world's largest democracy.
“I got a visa to India and was supposed to leave this morning to attend the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad. I had been invited as a panelist and speaker on the future of media and press freedom,” she said.
“But ‘orders from above’ in the Ministry of Home Affairs have cancelled my visa. Here is my message for Amit Shah,” she added while asking why the visa had been cancelled.
The Congress reacted strongly and asked why the government was afraid of questions.
“You may remember — a journalist in Norway asked Modi a question, and Modi was seen running away. Now that same journalist, Helle Lyng, was due to attend the ‘Bharat Summit’ being held in Telangana, but her visa was cancelled before she could even get there,” the party posted on X on Thursday.
“Why are Modi and his government so afraid of questions,” it added.
The MEA maintained that visa decisions were a sovereign function of the government as questions continued over the reported denial or cancellation of visas for foreign invitees to the Bharat Summit.

The Mundka monitoring station of the Delhi Pollution Control Board recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on the Diwali night, which is 60 times the standard measure. Yes, you read it right. 60 times. Reports emerged the next day that 93 of the top 100 cities with worst AQI were from India following Diwali celebrations on November 8. AIIMS pulmonologist Vijay Hadda told ANI on November 9, “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival.”
In any country with a functional government, this would warrant the environment minister to at least make a statement, even if not take direct accountability. Not in India.
Union minister of environment, forest and climate change, Bhupender Yadav, has remained conspicuously silent on the country’s deteriorating air quality before or after Diwali.
From the days preceding Diwali to four days after the festival when this article is being written, Yadav neither issued a single public appeal urging citizens to responsibly engage in celebrations, nor used his social media handles to spread awareness about the environmental consequences of bursting firecrackers or to address the mounting pollution crisis affecting major parts of the country.
Did Bhupender Yadav go Missing from Public Platforms?
Far from it. Yadav remained active on social media throughout this period. Between November 1 and November 12, he made 29 posts on his X account. Not one of them addressed the worsening air pollution, deteriorating air quality across Indian cities, or the need for public awareness and precautionary measures.
The days before Diwali are also crucial because pollution levels skyrocketing on the day of the festival and immediately after has become an annual phenomenon. It is reasonable to expect the minister holding the environment and climate change portfolio to make a public appeal ahead of Diwali, more so because firecracker pollution has been a matter of contention and has reached the Supreme Court in recent years.
Clearly, the Alwar MP thinks otherwise.
Modi Reigns Supreme on Yadav’s X Timeline
On November 7, observed as Chhoti Diwali, and November 8, the main day of Diwali, Yadav shared nine posts. These included amplification of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Diwali greetings to citizens, Modi’s Diwali celebrations and interactions with jawans at the CoBRA (Commando Battalion for Resolute Action) Operations Base in Karanpur, in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, as well as Yadav’s own festive greetings.
On November 7, Yadav shared a video of Narendra Modi greeting fellow citizens with wishes for Diwali and shared that, like every year, he would celebrate Diwali with the “veer jawans” of the country.

Updates on Political Assignments etc
A review of Yadav’s remaining social media activity during this period shows that he continued to document his political engagements, meetings with public representatives, participation in political programmes and official engagements.
On November 1, Yadav attended the “Save democracy, remove anarchy” rally alongside the Maharashtra chief minister and deputy chief minister. The following day, he met the Governor of Uttarakhand. On November 3, he met Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami and Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary in Delhi.
On November 5, he shared another post about his participation in the ‘Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy’ protest in Darbhanga, Bihar. On November 9, he attended the funeral of Dr Jaswant Yadav, the MLA from Bahror and former Member of Parliament, alongside the Rajasthan Chief Minister Bhajanlal Sharma.
His latest post, on November 12, documented an interaction chaired by him with Indian LeadIT (Leadership Group for Industry Transition) member companies and project partners in New Delhi.
In addition to these engagements, five of Yadav’s posts during the November 1–12 period were dedicated to sharing decisions taken by the Union Cabinet on various policy matters.
Despite maintaining a steady stream of updates on his political engagements, official meetings and public appearances, the environment Mminister’s X account offered no indication of concern over the environmental consequences of the widespread bursting of firecrackers during Diwali. Neither before it. Nor after.
Incidentally, on October 30, Yadav posted about an integrated command and control centre in Delhi to review and monitor air pollution real-time across Delhi-NCR.
The Firecracker Pollution Debate was Raging Since October 25
As early as October 25, Delhi Police had shared a video on its X handle urging citizens not to burst crackers this Diwali. The post said: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.” Soon after it was posted, social media users predicted that it would be taken down. Delhi Police proved them right, deleting the post within hours.
The episode sparked a debate, with a section of the Right-wing putting forward what has become its usual pre-Diwali stance on firecracker pollution: that any call to shun firecrackers or celebrate with restraint is an affront to Hindu faith.
