Why Apple's HomeView relies so heavily on your iPhone
It all comes down to convenience and personalization without sacrificing privacy.
"There's no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone."
That's the statement newly minted Apple CEO John Ternus made during his opening remarks at his first iPhone event this year. It should be no surprise then, that the device holding so much of your data would play a vital role with a separate "intelligent personal hub" that stays inside your home.
This week marks the arrival of the HomeView, Apple's long-rumored smart display that was announced last month. As I explained in detail in my review, it's basically a combination of several gadgets in one. It's both a visual interface and a smart speaker that is always listening for your Siri queries. It's a smart home hub for a range of connected devices. It's a sous chef in the kitchen, and it's a FaceTime station when you need to catch up with friends and family. Heck, it's even a digital photo frame.
The HomeView doesn't run apps though. It performs all those functions, and more, by mirroring the apps that you have on your iPhone or iPad. Instead of allowing you to download software from the App Store, the HomeView's system works like CarPlay does in your car. It shows you the compatible apps you've already installed on your phone or tablet, as well as Apple's core suite, including Calendar, Messages, Reminders and Weather.
This is just one of the reasons an iPhone (or iPad) needs to be close by for the HomeView to work.
"When we design home products, we always keep three things in mind," Cecilia Dantas, a member of Apple's Home product marketing team, told me. "They have to be intelligent, personal and private."
Since Siri AI needs all those apps to be able to provide the very personal context that makes its answers more intelligent and conversational, Apple needed a way to grant it that access that didn't compromise your privacy. Having your iPhone be the only container for that information and requiring it to be around for your data to be accessible helps keep it safe from prying eyes when you're away.
As a more general home hub, the HomeView has to work for every member of your household so they can turn lights off or see who's at the door. But it shouldn't be showing them every text message you get from your parents or revealing your calendar invites and inadvertently ruining surprises. This privacy is why, in addition to the built-in face and voice recognition, the HomeView relies so heavily on an iPhone or iPad.
"Everything that feels natural on a phone is now available in a subtle, glanceable device that gives you what you need in the moment," VP of hardware engineering Matthew Costello said. "It recognizes you and shows you your information, but when you step away, it's gone."
Costello further explained that the HomeView offers the best combination of personal information with the convenience of a dedicated communal device. Since the iPhone is a user's hub for their personal content — and really, their life — it only made sense to "extend and link that intelligence" into products like the HomeView.
If the HomeView doesn't recognize a user, it will only allow them to perform basic tasks. And even if you are a recognized user, you'll need to have your recently unlocked iPhone or iPad nearby for the smart display to show things like your Messages or Calendar.
"Personal information only surfaces once you've been recognized by your face, and [if] your paired iPhone is present and recently unlocked," Costello noted. "We thought building on the contextual information and the intelligence, but also the privacy, was super critical and also very unique."
By tying what shows up for you on the HomeView to your phone, your data is displayed while you're interacting with the device and disappears with you when you do. As Costello explained, it's not "posted on or housed on the device in any way."
The heavy reliance on an iPhone or an iPad has additional benefits. Like you can on a HomePod, the HomeView allows you to hand off music, FaceTime calls and more. One of the device's best features is recipe integration in Safari that makes cooking easier. It's also powered by the hand off action, so you need that other Apple device to kickstart the process. But Dantas explained that Apple doesn't see reliance on your phone or tablet as a hindrance.
"It's not just dependency, it's also part of this ecosystem," she said. The HomeView's similarity to your phone doesn't just enable familiar apps, but also a familiar method of interaction.
Speaking of interaction, there's a reason why there aren't any buttons on the HomeView. Apple intentionally built it like this. I found it odd, considering the device is a bit of a hybrid of an iPad (touchscreen), an Apple Watch (square shape) and a HomePod (speaker), two of which have physical buttons. But Costello said touch input was always meant to be secondary.
"We always envisioned it as something that was voice first, then touch second," he explained. "As we [designed] the product, that's how we thought about it, so that eliminated buttons and physical controls."
For Dantas, one of the main challenges during the product development phase was restraint. The process of bringing a new product and new software to life was obviously a tall task, but the engineering team also had to determine which parts of Apple's existing devices and services to include and which ones to leave behind.
"We've had home products for a while, and we built on that foundation," she said. "I think it was really, really challenging to go through and decide what do we bring and what do we not bring [to the HomeView]. That was very intentional to deliver this experience that's powerful and that's simple."

WHO’s ‘Together for Science and Health’ movement finds strong support in Tamil Nadu
‘Together for Science and Health’ is a global movement convened by WHO to bring together scientists, policymakers, health professionals, communicators, civil society, young people and communities around a shared commitment to science as a foundation for better health, said R. Thara, vice chairperson, SCARF
Together for Science and Health’ is a new movement to strengthen the connection between science, health and society and build trust in evidence-informed decision-making, according to the WHO. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: Getty Images
Advances in science have transformed the understanding of mental health and the way people living with mental health conditions are treated and cared for. On Tuesday (November 10, 2026), the World Health Organisation (WHO) launched ‘Together for Science and Health’, and on the occasion, experts in Chennai touched on various aspects of mental health, be it schizophrenia, dementia, or suicide prevention.
‘Together for Science and Health’ is a new movement to strengthen the connection between science, health and society and build trust in evidence-informed decision-making, according to the WHO.

Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.
The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.
According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.
A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.
Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.
The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.
The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."

  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has denied reports of a heated exchange with US President Donald Trump during a phone conversation over the weekend, which reportedly centred on the possibility of resuming military strikes against Iran.
According to a report by Hebrew-language outlet Ynet, cited by The Times of Israel, Netanyahu's office rejected the allegations, describing them as "Fake news, complete nonsense". The denial came after anonymous sources familiar with the conversation described it as particularly tense, with one source reportedly calling it a "shouting match from hell."
The Times of Israel also reported that a senior Israeli official confirmed the phone call had taken place. However, the official told Ynet that it was “very much not a difficult conversation.”
The denial comes amid reports that Netanyahu has repeatedly pressed Trump in recent days to launch another military offensive against Iran.
According to The Times of Israel, the Israeli Prime Minister has been urging Washington to consider renewed military action even as Trump weighs the possibility of pursuing a diplomatic solution against escalating military tensions.
Earlier in the week, Trump indicated that further military strikes against Iran were not immediately necessary.
However, The Times of Israel noted that Trump said on Thursday that the United States does not “need a deal with Tehran.”
Meanwhile, Defence Minister Israel Katz met today with IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and other senior defence and security officials, asserting that all decisions made during the current transitional period of coalition talks are being handled "responsibly" and in complete coordination with the military.
The Times of Israel reported that Katz's office quoted him as saying, "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, I and the IDF chief of staff see eye to eye on the Iranian issue in all its aspects, and we will continue to work together and do whatever is necessary to ensure the security of the State of Israel and protect its citizens."
The defence minister's office further noted that Katz emphasised during the assessment that "all decisions are made responsibly and in full cooperation between the political and military leadership," underscoring that "Israel’s security is the central consideration," according to The Times of Israel.
The Times of Israel added that these remarks come after Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot—who currently holds the mandate to form a new government—cautioned Netanyahu against deploying security forces in the absence of an immediate threat, following reports that the caretaker prime minister has been pushing for military strikes on Iran over the objections of defence officials.
Meanwhile, citing Hebrew media reports, Times of Israel reported thatPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has begun his security briefing with Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot.
The Prime Minister’s Office does not immediately confirm the reports.
This comes after Israeli media reported that Trump and Netanyahu engaged in a heated telephone conversation over the preceding days, which reportedly deteriorated into an acrimonious exchange amid ongoing disagreements regarding the course of the war with Iran.
According to reports from Israeli news organisations Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, the Israeli leader repeatedly pushed for renewed military action, whereas the American President preferred allowing ongoing peace negotiations with Tehran to continue.
Netanyahu has consistently argued that Washington should resume strikes and actively pursue regime change within the Islamic Republic, while Trump has favoured maintaining economic pressure to secure diplomatic concessions from Tehran. The Israeli Prime Minister's Office rejected claims that the conversation became confrontational, describing the reports as "fake news".
Israeli news outlets Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth reported that Netanyahu repeatedly urged Trump to restart the war during the call. Trump, however, continued to back a diplomatic approach as talks with Iran progressed.
Sources quoted by both outlets described the conversation as having descended into a "shouting match from hell". A senior Israeli official confirmed that the two leaders spoke over the weekend but denied that any confrontation had taken place.
The latest reports emerged days after the Financial Times said Netanyahu had been telephoning Trump daily to persuade him to resume an all-out war. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving Prime Minister, is facing uncertainty over his position after losing seats in the general election held in October.

It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy.
I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing.
What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.
Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this?
I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.
As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week.
Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm.
Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.
Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:
Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.
WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.
Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.
You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.
That’s right. It was really about telling the story.
Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.
Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips.
This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.
It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

Netflix has released a first-look photo (see above) and premiere year for now-titled Planeswalker, its long-in-the-works animated series based on Wizards of the Coast’s Magic: The Gathering. It’s set to launch iin 2027.
Created in partnership with Hasbro Entertainment and Wizards of the Coast, Planeswalker is billed as a fresh adaptation of the massively popular trading card game, created in 1993 by Richard Garfield and published by Hasbro subsidiary Wizards of the Coast. The game has amassed tens of millions of tabletop and digital players across more than 150 countries, according to Hasbro, with annual revenues surpassing $1 billion.
The epic fantasy series from the world of Magic: The Gathering chronicles the fierce clash between formidable mages known as Planeswalkers. At the center of this struggle for power and survival burns Chandra, a volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past. Confronted by an insidious force, Chandra and some of the most legendary Planeswalkers must harness their extraordinary abilities, navigate treacherous alliances, and battle their own inner demons to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence. As the line between victory and annihilation grows thinner, a single spark determines the fate of thousands of worlds.
Watch on Deadline
In Magic: The Gathering universe, a planeswalker is a power mage who has the rare ability to travel across infinite dimensions (called planes) in the multi-verse.
No word yet on the number of episodes for Planeswalker.
Netflix first announced that the project was in development in 2019, in partnership with Joe and Anthony Russo and Wizards of the Coast. It was set to be executive produced by the Russo brothers with head writers Henry Gilroy and Jose Molina. The Russos later exited over creative differences, and Jeff Kline took over in 2021. After a lengthy pause, Netflix restarted development under showrunner Terry Matalas, who now serves as showrunner and executive producer on Planeswalker.
A live-action movie, titled Magic: The Gathering, also is in the works from Legendary Entertainment and Hasbro, with, as we exclusively reported, Maya Hawke set to star.
Cindy Appel serves as co-showrunner and executive produces Planeswalker with Matalas, along with Patrick Osborne. Gabriel Marano will serve as executive producer and Lauren Chavez-Myers will co-executive produce for Hasbro Entertainment. Osborne also serves as supervising director and Daisy West serves as producer. Digic is the animation studio.
Stay tuned for more details.

(Bloomberg) -- When Seema Reddy, 51, moved to the Upper West Side 24 years ago, the fresh-out-of-college art history graduate did what many broke 20-somethings do: She joined a roommate in a railroad apartment best described as a “hovel.”
“I could afford it, but it was awful,” she said, recalling the apartment was burgled while she lived there. Still, she liked the neighborhood and the location was convenient to her first job at Sotheby's Auction House.
In 2002, the median Manhattan rent for a one-bedroom hovered around $2,500, though Reddy paid $1,800 for her portion. Last month, Manhattan’s median rent hit a record $5,000. Across New York City, the rental vacancy rate is just 1.4%, according to the city’s new Fair Housing Growth Strategy report. Five percent is the target vacancy rate, which the city has never reached, according to the report.
Reddy is now married and raising her child on the Upper West Side, in a three-bed townhouse, where the average rent is over $7,500 for a unit that size. Since buying with her husband in 2014, Reddy thinks the UWS is the best neighborhood in the city with easy access to Central Park, museums and arts institutions like Lincoln Center, where she later worked. But she questions whether a recent college graduate can move there today.
The Housing Preservation Department studied what it would take to make housing more affordable, and in a report released Oct. 9 estimated the city needs 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to alleviate its shortage. The proposal, required under a 2023 law, complements Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s $22 billion plan to build or preserve 200,000 affordable homes within a decade.
It also poses an early test of whether Mamdani can deliver on his central campaign promise: make New York more affordable. On Nov. 3, NYC voters passed all of Mamdani’s five ballot proposals intended to fast-track housing, along with expanding outdoor dining and bike lanes, the Associated Press reported. Two of the measures will expedite review for projects on city-owned land and streamline the permitting process. To work, however, the housing plan still has several obstacles to clear, from outdated regulation and classic NIMBY-ism to perhaps the biggest: encouraging capital to enter its dicey market.
Step 1: Make Growth Proportionate
NYC employment hit a record high this year, yet housing production increasingly lags behind job and population growth. That’s squeezing tenants and pushing higher-income apartment-hunters into lower-cost neighborhoods, displacing longtime residents. A wealthier customer base can reshape everything in a neighborhood from rent to the cost of a morning bagel to late-night takeout.
“If you’re looking for an apartment right now, you are radicalized by how few options there are out there and how expensive everything is,” said Annemarie Gray, executive director of the pro-housing group Open New York. “New York City really risks losing its identity as a place that is open and accepting and provides opportunities for people if we don’t turn that around.”
The city’s strategy articulated in its report is to evenly spread housing growth by setting targets for community districts that are partly based on historical housing production and affordability. That means asking some of New York’s lowest-growth neighborhoods to build substantially more.
On the UWS, the report calls for more than 10,700 additional homes over the long term — one of the highest marks in the report — including nearly 3,900 affordable, deeply affordable or supportive units. New units built or preserved since Jan. 1 count toward the total when they receive a certificate of occupancy, while demolished or consolidated units can reduce a district’s total.
Housing Preservation and Development Deputy Commissioner Michael Sandler said the nonbinding strategy is a “shared framework” whose targets will require rezonings, infrastructure investments and other policy changes.
“This is the first step, not the last step,” he said.
The disparity among neighborhoods is stark. From 2010 through 2025, Manhattan’s Chelsea, Hell’s Kitchen and Hudson Yards district added nearly 21,000 units, compared with about 5,800 on the UWS and 1,900 on the Upper East Side, according to a Department of Buildings report. The figures are net units, subtracting demolitions and consolidations from new and renovated buildings.
The shortage is decades in the making. From 2003-2007, drastic rezoning boosted density in previously industrial areas like Williamsburg and Long Island City, while other changes limited growth in established neighborhoods like the UES and UWS to preserve character.
Meanwhile, Manhattan has lost over 100,000 units over the last 70 years as townhouses are combined into mega-mansions and smaller apartments are consolidated into larger homes. Reddy, who leads the local Community Board 7’s land-use committee, worries this is bringing in more ultra-wealthy residents who are less rooted in the local economy and community.
Step 2: Make Room
Sheldon Fine has watched the Upper West Side transform since 1971 from the same West 103rd Street building. When he moved there for his wife, his friends questioned why he would move to such a dangerous block. Fine, a “Bronx boy,” laughed it off. Now, historic demand has made it so there are no bad neighborhoods in New York, according to one developer.
When he moved in, Fine’s two-bedroom cost $215 a month — roughly $1,774 today. More than five decades later, he’s paying $2,225 for the same rent-stabilized apartment.
Fine has spent 41 years on Community Board 7 and runs the West Side Federation for Senior and Supportive Housing, which houses older and vulnerable New Yorkers. Walking the neighborhood with him means regularly stopping to greet someone he knows.
“We’ve had multiple people come to us and say, ‘I grew up here, but I can’t afford to come back,’” Fine said.
He advocates for more affordable housing, but he doubts the UWS has room for almost 11,000 additional homes. That question came to a head when HPD presented the strategy to a Community Board 7 meeting on Sept. 14.
Board members pointed to scarce vacant land, landmark districts and high development costs. One member, Minna Elias, said the lofty, public goal sets the UWS up for failure.
While the question of how the city could set housing targets before determining where the units could go drew the most public feedback according to HPD, the department said those decisions are outside the scope of the report.
“We were not looking at this stage at where there are buildable sites,” said Sarit Platkin, HPD’s executive director of neighborhood planning and equity initiatives. Site-level feasibility would come later, she said.
Not everyone on the board considered the target itself unrealistic. Banker Tibita Kaneene noted District 7 has grown by only about 0.28% annually and said the report’s target of roughly 1.5% yearly growth could be achieved through modest rezonings and policies the board has already endorsed.
“I don’t think that’s ridiculous,” Kaneene said. “I think it’s completely feasible.”
Community Board 7 members also asked what incentives would be available to encourage developers to build in one of the country’s most expensive real estate markets. HPD deferred questions about implementation.
Step 3: Make the Numbers Work
Even if the city creates more places to build, the housing still needs to meet developers’ profitability requirements.
Brooklyn’s Gowanus neighborhood offers a test case. Its 2021 rezoning unlocked thousands of units on formerly industrial land. Charney Companies is working with Tavros Capital Partners to build 1,100 apartments at 175 Third Street, including almost 300 affordable units.
The project was approved under the city’s now-expired rental property-tax incentive. Rosie Tilley, Charney’s head of development, said the same project wouldn’t happen under today’s laws because new affordability and labor requirements add costs that anticipated rents can’t support.
Tax abatements and faster, predictable regulatory approvals are critical to encourage new projects, especially at a time of high borrowing and construction costs, said TJ Edwards, chief production officer of real estate finance at Walker & Dunlop. Lenders must ensure future income can cover debt refinancing if operating costs outpace restricted rents.
“We can’t regulate ourselves to a solution,” Edwards said. “You need equity, debt and policymakers all on the same page working in accord with one another.”
New York may be nearing the limits of property-tax exemptions and traditional affordable-housing subsidies, said Moses Gates, vice president at the Regional Plan Association. With recent zoning reforms already expanding building capacity, policymakers should lower construction costs for developers by addressing outdated building regulations, he said.
Meanwhile, HPD is looking to streamline permitting, interagency coordination and the affordable-housing lottery through its SPEED initiative, which the city says could shorten some publicly sponsored projects by as much as two years.
Gates said these changes need time to work, but reaching 700,000 homes will require getting nearly every piece right at once.
“It’s like you’re running this race and there’s these six to eight hurdles,” he said. “You have to be able to clear all of them consistently.” And even then, “You need to hit a couple of lucky breaks.”
Step 4: Win Over Neighborhoods
Community Board 7 has proposed its own ways to accommodate more housing through “The Manhattan Plan,” including building above city-owned sites like schools, libraries, police precincts and firehouses, increasing density on major streets, expanding Mandatory Inclusionary Housing and reviving Single Room Occupancy units — dormitory-style housing with shared kitchens and bathrooms largely barred in the city.
One of the neighborhood’s last vacant parcels of land, the former ABC campus on 80 West 67th Street, is being redeveloped by Extell Development into what will be the tallest tower on the UWS. The project requires no rezoning, special permits or Community Board 7 approval, and therefore no affordable housing.
Reddy said this project is an example of the importance of community involvement. Extell founder Gary Barnett worked with Community Board 7 to include affordable units to maintain goodwill, even though they weren’t required. Still, board members said they would have liked the city’s help to push for more.
A 171-unit project on West 96th Street also benefitted from local engagement. Fetner Properties CEO Hal Fetner voluntarily engaged neighbors on designs, noise and construction schedules.
“We don’t like to fight,” Fetner said. “Any project I’ve ever done, I’ve actually worked — whether I was obligated to or not — I worked with the community.”
Completed in 2024, it was among the first substantial new rental projects in the neighborhood in more than a decade. While the 96th Street site was previously vacant due to environmental contamination concerns, Fetner said political resistance has prevented housing elsewhere.
“There’s a reason why no one’s built there right now,” Fetner said of some low-growth neighborhoods. “You’ve got city council members saying: ‘I don’t want you here.’”
Step 5: Make Building Easier
Vishaan Chakrabarti, founder of Practice for Architecture and Urbanism, said numerical targets alone are “never gonna win over the hearts and minds of New Yorkers.”
Chakrabarti said it’s possible to add almost 11,000 new homes to the UWS without sacrificing its historic character, but he said officials should emphasize the positives housing can provide for neighborhoods. At its meeting, Community Board 7 members voiced concerns about already crowded schools and public transit, as well as sewer capacity.
The city also has to make it easier to build smaller, mid-rise projects, Chakrabarti said, rather than relying on skinny supertall high-rises.
“We’ve gotta talk about both quality and quantity,” Chakrabarti said. “Having a conversation just about quantity is a losing battle.”
The city’s complicated regulatory system disproportionately benefits large developers with lawyers, lobbyists and consultants capable of navigating it, he said. To succeed, New York has to make it simpler for smaller builders to take on projects.
For Charney Companies’ Tilley, reaching the targets ultimately comes down to whether the city creates the conditions necessary for those homes to be built.
“I love their focus on locating and investing in affordable housing in certain locations which have not realized it,” Tilley said. “But it’s a shame that all of that could come to naught if there’s not the structure to make that happen.”

Why fear questions? Revanth Reddy slams Centre over Norwegian journalist's visa denial
Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng, who drew attention for attempting to question Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a joint media briefing in Norway, claimed that India revoked her visa moments before her scheduled trip to Hyderabad.
Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy on Friday attacked the central government over a Norwegian journalist's claim that her visa to India was revoked at the last minute, months after she drew attention for attempting to question Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a joint media briefing in Norway. Reddy slammed what he called the government's discomfort with questions and warned that the incident raises serious concerns about democratic freedoms.
The Congress leader further alleged asking questions was a fundamental responsibility of journalists and could not be treated as a crime.
"I do not understand why the Modi government is so uncomfortable with questions. A journalist asking the Prime Minister a question is not a crime. It is the responsibility of journalists to ask questions. Whether the Prime Minister chooses to answer or not is his prerogative. But denying entry into India to a journalist merely for asking a question raises serious concerns about democratic freedoms," the Chief Minister said.
Helle Lyng, the Norwegian journalist, claimed that the Indian embassy in Oslo revoked her visa moments before she was scheduled to depart for Hyderabad for an event.
Reddy, reacting to the claim, alleged that there had been instances in which journalists who were granted visas were subsequently denied permission to travel to India by the Ministry of External Affairs and the Ministry of Home Affairs.
The Telangana Chief Minister accused Modi of displaying an authoritarian mindset, claiming that the Prime Minister appeared uncomfortable with being questioned or challenged.
"The impression is that Prime Minister Modi does not like being questioned or challenged. He believes that whatever he knows or says is right. This reflects an authoritarian mindset, which has no place in a democratic country," he said.
Emphasising India's democratic traditions, Reddy said the country had evolved through centuries of debate and discussion, from the time of Gautama Buddha to the present, and that its laws and democratic values had developed through such exchanges.
He also questioned the BJP's criticism of discussions involving international participants, taking a swipe at Union Minister G Kishan Reddy and BJP Telangana president N Ramchander Rao for objecting to the issue. He alleged that the Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) had joined the BJP in criticising the initiative.
"I do not understand why BJP leaders, including Union Minister G Kishan Reddy and BJP Telangana president N Ramchander Rao, are making such a big issue out of this. Even the BRS has joined the BJP in this chorus. Both parties seem to be playing the same tune," he said.
Drawing a comparison with the Centre's flagship international dialogue platform, Reddy asked whether inviting foreign participants for discussions could be considered anti-national.
"If organising discussions and inviting international participants is considered anti-national, then what about the Raisina Dialogue? Several people are invited to participate in such discussions. Does that mean those platforms are also working against the country? Why is the BJP afraid of debate and discussion?" he asked.
He further questioned whether the Prime Minister's electoral prospects could be affected simply because a journalist sought to question him.

Doctors tell the BBC about the targeting of Sudanese hospitals by paramilitary fighters
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."

‘Vehicle overloaded, running at 100 km/h, crossed into wrong lane’: Survivors of deadly bus-truck collision in Assam
The truck's dashcam footage, which has emerged following the accident, has captured the final moments before the collision.
The passengers who survived the deadly bus-truck collision in Assam's Golaghat on Friday claimed that the bus was overcrowded and travelling at a very high speed when the driver lost control and swerved into the wrong lane. The truck driver also alleged that the bus entered his lane, leading to the crash.
“The bus had too many passengers. Around 50 per cent of them were standing, and even the cabin space, which was supposed to be free, was filled with passengers,” said 30-year-old Moksudul Islam, one of the survivors of Friday's deadly road accident near Kaziranga, Assam, alleging that the vehicle was carrying nearly twice its seating capacity when it collided with a goods-carrying truck.
At least 25 people were killed and several were critically injured after a passenger vehicle carrying around 35 people, including school students, collided head-on with a truck in Assam’s Golaghat district on Friday afternoon, police said earlier.
Deep Dive
Also read | At least 26 killed, several injured in road accident in Assam’s Golaghat: Police
The accident took place at around 2.30 pm, when the passenger vehicle, travelling from Bokakhat towards Nagaon, collided with the goods-carrying vehicle, officers said.
Islam, a resident of Golaghat who works for a construction company, was travelling in the bus with four of his co-workers. He said the vehicle, which had a capacity of hardly 30 passengers, was carrying at least 60 persons on Friday.
'Lucky to survive'
“I was sitting at the back, which is why I was lucky to survive. But the bus had too many passengers. Around 50% of them were standing, and even the cabin space, which was supposed to be free, was filled with passengers,” he said.
Also read | ‘Bus was overspeeding, violated restrictions’: Official on Assam accident that killed 26
Islam sustained a head injury in the collision but was discharged by doctors after receiving initial treatment.
Another passenger also alleged that the vehicle was overloaded and travelling at nearly 100 kmph. Recalling the moments before the collision, he said the bus suddenly lost control, crossed into the wrong lane and hit the oncoming truck.
“It was at high speed when it suddenly lost control, crossed into the wrong lane and hit the oncoming truck. I was sitting beside the window and saw it happen. I was so scared that I thought I would die,” he said.
The driver of the goods-carrying truck, who was also injured in the crash, offered a similar account of the collision, claiming that the bus suddenly entered his lane and rammed into the truck while he was driving on his proper side of the road.
Speaking to the media, the driver, whose identity has not yet been confirmed, said he was travelling from Tezpur when the bus approached from the opposite direction.
“I was coming this way from Tezpur and I was driving on the proper side. This bus suddenly came from the opposite direction. On such a wide road, it came directly into our lane and slammed straight into us, a direct head-on collision,” he said.
Describing the speed of the passenger vehicle, he added, “Yes, the bus hit us. It came at such a high speed, it's beyond words.” The driver said he sustained injuries to his hand and other parts of his body.
Dashcam footage emerges
The truck's dashcam footage, which has emerged following the accident, has captured the final moments before the collision.
The footage, authorised by the driver, could provide important clues about how the two vehicles approached each other immediately before the impact.
According to the doctors of the Jorhat Medical College and Hospital (JMCH), where the critical patients were shifted, said that around 12 injured persons are undergoing treatment.
The survivors' accounts have raised questions about the number of passengers travelling in the vehicle and whether overloading and speeding contributed to the crash.
Police said that they are investigating how many passengers were there in the bus and how many survivors are there.
Congress MP Gaurav Gogoi blamed alleged corruption, poor construction quality and a nexus between contractors and politicians for the tragedy, claiming it could have been avoided if highways were properly built and maintained.
Reacting to the accident, Gogoi alleged that national highways across Assam had become a “den of corruption” and questioned the government's collection of tolls despite the alleged poor condition of roads.
Assam Jatiya Parishad (AJP) president Lurinjyoti Gogoi urged the government to ensure advanced medical treatment for those critically injured and take responsibility for the families of those killed.
“Since Jorhat Medical College is there, the necessary medical care required for them must be provided. And for those who have died, the government will have to take responsibility for all their families,” he said.
He also called for stricter implementation of road safety measures and proper maintenance of national highways, saying that people's lives and futures depended on the condition of the roads.
Meanwhile, the All Assam Students' Union (AASU) and Asom Sena have offered to arrange blood donations for the injured.
AASU president Utpal Sarma said members of the organisation are ready to donate blood whenever required.

The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO. Nvidia’s board of directors announced his resignation on Thursday morning and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Jensen Huang is out. What now?
The former Nvidia CEO’s downfall is far bigger than one company.
Huang has been making headlines all week after news broke Friday that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed who the US government alleges was also a Chinese spy.
The revelation Wednesday of a second extramarital affair, this time with an Nvidia employee reporting to Huang directly, added to the pressure, and another affair came to light later on Thursday after Huang’s ouster.
The scandal has implications far beyond one company: Huang’s central role in the AI race can’t be overstated. It was his vision of an AI future that led him to pivot Nvidia from a small company making video game chips into the dominant player in making the chips that serve OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google’s computing needs.
Huang is close friends with President Donald Trump’s and a leading voice in resisting efforts to slow AI progress. And he has pushed for the US to take a less hawkish position toward China’s own AI goals, a stance now called into question by his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Among its other impacts, the news has revived efforts on Capitol Hill to further restrict chip exports to China.
To break down the national security implications of Huang’s departure, how the Trump administration is involved, and what it says about US AI industry writ large, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Garret De Vynck, a technology reporter at the Washington Post.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Nvidia has been called the central bank of AI, which is why it’s so important that we figure out what Jensen Huang may have disclosed to this alleged spy. How long has the president known about this, as far as we know?
As far as we know, the president has known about the fact that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with someone that the US government thought was a spy for about a year. This circulated within the administration, and the decision was made not to tell Jensen.
That doesn’t necessarily mean that it was automatically some kind of corrupt decision of President Trump protecting Jensen Huang. There’s all sorts of reasons why you might not want to tell someone they’re being spied on, the number one being that they might blow up the operation. Maybe you want to learn more. Maybe you suspect that the person themselves knows that they’re being spied on and is willingly sharing information and you need some more time to gather that. It’s unclear why the US government specifically chose not to pull in Jensen Huang.
It’s also a little bit unclear whether he knows he was being spied on, or whether maybe he was told through some kind of back channel. He has said that he did not know that she was a spy and he is admitting to the affair, to the infidelity. He’s admitting to essentially breaking Nvidia’s code of conduct by sleeping with one of its customers, but he is not admitting at all to knowing that she was a spy and definitely not admitting to sharing any information willfully.
It feels like this is the kind of thing that the government would investigate. There’s been reporting that the Commerce Department was involved with some kind of investigation, but that investigation came to an end and no one really knows why.
The context here is that the United States and China are in an AI race. Going back to the first Trump administration, there’s been pretty aggressive export controls saying, “We don’t want China to get our tech so that they can develop AI.” And the Biden administration continued that. He increased the export controls on China. China was complaining very loudly about this. They said, ‘We don’t care. We want to win AI and we need to slow you guys down.’
When Trump came in, he actually lifted his foot off the gas a little bit. They didn’t throw the gates open and say, “You can have whatever you want. All American companies can sell whatever they want to China.” But he said, “Some AI chips that are less powerful than the state of the art. We can send those to Chinese companies.“
The other thing that national security experts have pointed out is that the Trump administration could theoretically have been doing more to stop the smuggling of computer chips to China. And that’s where this story gets so important for national security.
Megaspeed is accused of essentially being a front for Chinese companies to get access to computer chips. Journalists have gone to Megaspeed’s office in Singapore where it’s based, and there were only a couple of people working there. It didn’t really seem like there was a lot going on. Nvidia has said all through this process over the last couple of years that, “No, we’ve checked it out, Megaspeed is a legitimate company and we’re not breaking the law when it comes to this.”
There are a lot of questions and what everyone is focused on finding out, both journalists and I would say congressional Democrats when they come into office in the new year is, is there something more going on here? Is there something where the Chinese either convinced Jensen Huang to sell more chips to them or Jensen Huang himself, who has been advocating for selling more chips to China, essentially did this himself?
“I think there’s this real question of: Do we see a much stronger push to actually ramp up controls on China and how does Trump respond?”
He’s been pressuring the president, he’s been donating to him, he’s been glad-handing with the president and the president has been listening more to this corporate executive who is his friend and who donated him a bunch of money rather than listening to China hawks or national security experts who say we should be limiting what China is able to access.
That’s really where the locus of this investigation is going to be. It’s not so much that Jensen Huang had an affair. It’s more the fact that he himself is someone who has said we need to sell more computer chips to China and he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy, and he’s very close to the president and had influence on the president.
You mentioned the Democrats. Have they said anything? Are they going to call him in front of Congress for an investigation?
Going forward, there are two big things here. One of them is these investigations into Jensen Huang and this whole situation. The company is likely going to continue to investigate. Maybe more information will come out there. Jensen Huang has been called to speak later this month in Congress. And congressional Democrats have also said that when they come into power in January, they will be asking him.
The second big thing that comes out of this is, what does America do when it comes to China and AI? Now that one of the biggest advocates for being a bit more friendly towards China when it comes to selling them things that they need for AI is out of the room and completely discredited, I think that the China hawks, those who say we need to crack down more aggressively, we need to limit China’s access to AI computer chips, they’re really coming into ascendance here and they’re in the Republican Party, they’re in the Democratic Party, some of them, people like Marco Rubio, are even in the Cabinet.
I think there’s this real question of: Do we see a much stronger push to actually ramp up controls on China and how does Trump respond? There’s all sorts of geopolitical things that could sort of spin out of this CEO affair.
I’m old enough to remember when a board tried to get rid of Sam Altman and then he was just back a week later. Elon Musk is already offering Jensen Huang a job. Is there a fair chance that he just goes somewhere that’s not that concerned about espionage affairs or getting with your VP of health or whatever it is? Is he just going to go work for China?
I don’t think he’s going to go work for China. This is definitely the wildest corporate story since Sam Altman was fired as CEO and brought back three or four days later. It’s a very different situation. That was a startup where you essentially have five or six investors who get to make the call about who the CEO is, and the employees at that company overwhelmingly wanted to bring Sam Altman back. I think they wanted more continuity of the company, but they also wanted to make sure that their company didn’t go under and go bankrupt and get disappeared, which was sort of on the table at that point in time.
Nvidia’s not going anywhere. Obviously employees have lost a lot of money in terms of the stock value already coming down due to the situation. So employees are probably shocked. They’re probably upset. Jensen Huang is broadly loved at Nvidia, and so I can definitely see that employees would be doing petitions, asking for him to return.
But this is a giant public company and the board makes a decision here. Jensen Huang was untruthful publicly and I think that also will make other public companies hesitant before rushing to bring him on as CEO.
As we’ve talked about many times in the show, half of our economy is staked on AI at this point. How concerned should we be that one of the most important people in this industry was so easily duped in this honeypot situation? Are these the people we should be trusting with the future of our society?
It’s a really good reminder that people are people. I think that we like to lionize individuals and say that they are the ones who are going to take us into the future and they are inventing the future and it’s so incredible. And I do think Jensen Huang gets a lot of credit for making sure that the companies kept up in AI, but at the end of the day, it was also a lucky break for them that the computer chips they were making just happened to work well for the math that is required by artificial intelligence.
I do think that this speaks to something that a lot of people across the country and maybe even the world really feel. They do not want to sign off the future to a dozen dudes in Silicon Valley and their collaborators in the Trump White House. I think that is a view that a lot of people increasingly have. I think it was one of the factors in the midterms, maybe not the most important one, but people are concerned about concentration of power. They’re concerned about AI and they don’t see it as something that they themselves have control over.
I think that this is just going to be another thing that sort of adds skepticism to the idea that people like Jensen Huang should be the ones making the final decision when it comes to artificial intelligence.

In a significant update to its guidelines for prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society is now recommending that all men get routinely screened for prostate cancer with a PSA test.
Men at average risk should get a PSA test every two years from age 50 to 69, according to the new guidelines released Thursday.
Men considered at high risk due to race and family history should start testing earlier, at 45, and most are recommended to get tested every year. Specifically, yearly testing starting at age 45 is recommended for all Black men, who have higher rates of prostate cancer. Non-Black men should also get yearly testing starting at 45 if a close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or if more than one of their relatives has had prostate cancer. On the other hand, if only one close relative was diagnosed with prostate cancer and it was diagnosed at age 65 or older, non-Black men in this case should start PSA screening at 45, but are recommended to get testing only every two years.
Men ages 70 to 74 should consult their doctor on continuing screening, while those 75 and up are not recommended to get screened.
The new guidance departs from ACS’s previous iteration, published in 2010, which made no universal recommendations for routine screening. Men at age 50 were recommended to use shared-decision making with their doctors on whether or not to get tested. The recommendation was similar to that from the US Preventive Services Task Force, a federal panel that regularly evaluates evidence and makes recommendations on such preventive medical care. (The USPSTF is currently working on an update to its prostate cancer screening recommendation, though it should be noted that the panel has recently been overhauled by anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and new members are reportedly rife with conflicts of interest.)

SpaceX to attempt double catch of huge Starship rocket
- Published
SpaceX will attempt to catch both parts of its huge Starship rocket after it launches on its next test flight on Friday.
Elon Musk's company will use the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower to grab the rocket parts mid-air as they return to Earth.
If successful, this will be the first full recovery of a rocket that's been to space, paving the way for making Starship reusable so it can fly repeatedly.
Nasa will be closely watching the flight: the SpaceX rocket is set to play a vital part in its Artemis programme, which will see astronauts land on the Moon.
The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.
The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society.
"A successful double catch would be visually spectacular, but full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."
- What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next? 
  - Published27 October
- Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test 
  - Published28 September
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.
But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.
Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.
