You can edit Instagram Reels on Mac using Claude AI and the free Instagram Edits app. Install Claude Code, enable the app’s MCP automation server, and connect both. Then use simple text prompts to create projects, arrange clips, add transitions, titles, and effects, and export finished Reels in 4K.
The wait is over. The Instagram Edits app is finally available on desktop, but only on macOS, as of this guide. Instagram Edits is my go-to app not just for editing Instagram Reels, but also a reliable free video editor with all the features and a simple design.
Although the app is designed for creators and competes with CapCut, it has been limited to Android and iOS so far. But a few months ago, Instagram announced a desktop version, and now it is finally here. Right now, the app is only available on macOS, with Windows and other platforms coming in future releases.
I have been using the app for the past couple of days. It is very similar to the mobile app and is also free to use, but it also features an MCP connection, which you can use to connect to any of your AI subscriptions, such as Claude, Codex, and Muse, and let AI edit your videos.
The desktop interface is slightly different and can be complex for beginners. It took me a while to get used to it, but I have created a detailed guide to get started.
I also created a guide on how to connect your MCP, like Claude, to Instagram Edits to edit your videos, and it covers everything about this feature, including common setup errors. This guide is for beginners, so each step is comprehensive and detailed.
Table of Contents
How to Connect Claude AI to Instagram Edits and Edit Reels on Mac
Before connecting your Instagram Edits app to the MCP server, ensure you have the following pre-requirements:
- A Mac with an Apple chip (M1 or newer) on macOS 15.1 or later. Currently, the Instagram Edits desktop app is only available for macOS, with Windows and Linux versions coming soon, but there is no expected release date yet.
- Download and install the Instagram Edits app from here
- A paid AI subscription for any model; you can also use the free AI model.
Part 1: Get Claude Code
Step 1: Open Terminal and type the command: claude –version, and press Return. If you see a version number, it means Claude Code is already installed on your device. You can skip to Part 2 to continue setup.
If you see something like zsh: command not found: claude, it means Claude Code is not installed on your device, or Terminal can not find it yet. Follow the next steps to install Claude Code on your Mac.
Install Claude Code: To install Claude Code, use the official Anthropic installer. To do that, open Terminal on your Mac and paste this command: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Wait a few minutes, and then you will see a ” Claude Code successfully installed message in your terminal.
Check the setup notes below. If you see something like installation exists but ~/.local/bin is not in your PATH, it means the terminal still can’t find Claude Code yet.
Now follow the next two steps. If you don’t see such a note, you can quit the terminal, reopen it, and use this command to confirm that Claude Code has been successfully installed on your device: confirm claude –version. If you see a Claude version, it’s installed on your device. Then continue with part two.
Next, paste this command into the terminal and press Enter: echo ‘export PATH=”$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH”‘ >> ~/.zshrc
Next, paste this: source ~/.zshrc, and press Enter. Now type claude –version and press Enter. You will see the Claude version number. This means Claude Code is successfully installed on your device in the terminal
Part 2: Turn on Claude access in Edits
Next, you need to let Claude access your Instagram edits apps. First, ensure the Instagram edits app is installed on your Mac. If not, you can use the official download link here. Once installed, follow the steps below:
Step 1: Open the app on your Mac and sign in with your account. On the home screen, you will go directly to the Projects tab.
Step 2: Next, you can tap on your profile picture in the top right corner of the screen or click on the edit option in the menu bar at the top of the screen and then click on the settings
Step 3: Next, tap on the automation from the sidebar
Step 4: By default, automation is turned off. Now, from the automation settings, turn on the toggle that says Enable Automation Server.
Step 5: Under the Connect an AI Client section, click the copy icon next to the Claude code. This will copy the connection command with your access token. Remember, don’t share this command with others. In this case, I am using Claude code. If you are using Codex, tap the copy button next to Codex. The same goes for Muse.
You can also connect any AI model. Since it is a standard MCP server, any AI app can connect to the MCP server over HTTPS and can control edits.
Remember to replace <TOKEN> with the Access token from Edits > Settings > Automation, and keep Edits open with the automation server turned on
For Google Gemini CLI:
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For Qwen:
npm install -g @qwen-code/qwen-code
qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp
For DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM, and most others, we can use OpenCode
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
{
“$schema”: “https://opencode.ai/config.json”,
“mcp”: {
“servers”: {
“edits”: {
“type”: “remote”,
“url”: “http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp”,
“oauth”: false,
“headers”: { “Authorization”: “Bearer <TOKEN>” }
}
}
}
}
Part 3: Connect Claude Code to Edits
Next, let’s connect Claude Code (or any AI model) to edits. Remember that you can only do this once.
Step 1: Now, paste the command you copied from the previous section into the terminal. You will see: Added HTTP MCP server metapilot-native
Step 2: Next, for Claude, paste this command: claude mcp get metapilot-native and press Enter. Under status, if you see Connected, it worked. If it says Failed to connect, ensure the edits app is running and follow the previous steps carefully.
For other models, follow these:
| App (models) | Connect command | Check it worked | 
| Claude Code (Claude) | claude mcp add –transport http –scope user metapilot-native http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” | claude mcp get metapilot-native | 
| Gemini CLI (Gemini) | gemini mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | gemini mcp list | 
| Qwen Code (Qwen) | qwen mcp add –transport http –scope user –header “Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN>” edits http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp | qwen mcp list | 
| Codex (OpenAI GPT) | echo ‘export EDITS_TOKEN=”<TOKEN>”‘ >> ~/.zshrc && source ~/.zshrc && codex mcp add edits –url http://127.0.0.1:19501/mcp –bearer-token-env-var EDITS_TOKEN | Run codex, then type /mcp | 
| OpenCode (DeepSeek, Grok, Mistral, Kimi, GLM and more) | No command. Paste the opencode.jsonc block from my last message into the folder you run OpenCode in. | opencode mcp list | 
| LM Studio (local Llama, Gemma, Qwen, DeepSeek R1) | No command. Program tab, then Install, then Edit mcp.json, and paste the JSON block. | Look at the Program tab | 
| Cursor (any model it offers) | No command. Paste the same JSON into ~/.cursor/mcp.json. | Cursor Settings, then MCP | 
Part 4: Start Claude Code
Now go to the folder where the videos are saved to edit them using Instagram edits. I recommend that you store all the videos in the Movies folder so it is easy to access in the future. In this case, I stored all my files in the Movies folder on my Mac. Now, once you have access to the folder, follow the steps below.
Step 1: To use Claude, go to the folder using the CD command. For example: cd ~/Downloads or cd ~/Movies. In my case, cd ~/Movies. Next, once you are in the folder, Type Cluade and press Return.
Step 2: Claude will ask whether you trust the folder you provided. Use the down arrow and select I trust this folder, and press Enter. It asks only once, and once you give permission, you can store all future videos in this folder for edits.
Step 3: To check, you can type /mcp and press Enter. It lists the apps Claude Code is connected to. metapilot-native with a green tick means Claude can control Edits.
Step 4: Go to the metapilot-native option and press Enter to see more details. You can use the down or up arrow to navigate between the options.
Part 5: Make your first Reel with Claude
Now let’s use Claude to create my first reel. In this case, I asked Claude to edit a 50-second coffee reel from five clips. In your case, you can store all the clips in the folder. First, test the connection again. Once done, follow the steps below.
To test the connection, go to your folder and type list my Instagram edits projects and press Enter. You will see metabolist native and the table of all your edit projects.
Step 2 : Now you can ask Claude to make edits for the Instagram reel video. You can manually create a new project, add clips, and point Claude to the project title and edit your videos, or you can ask Claude to create a project, add clips, and edit your first reel. I recommend giving Claude the full location of your clips and the title.
Step 3: That’s it. Claude will now create a new project and add Sunclips. You can open the Instagram Edits app to see the changes.
Step 4: Once you’ve loaded the clips, you can ask Claude to add transitions between them and also add titles, sound effects, and much more. In this case, I’m asking Claude to add the title “Morning Coffee” in big white text for two seconds and then add smooth transitions between the clips.
Step 5: Once you’ve made the edits, you can also ask Claude Core to export the clips in 4K, and it does it for you.
Step 6: Once the video is exported, Claude notifies you of the length, format, and size. You can open the same folder to see the clip. Claude also notifies you where the clip is stored and its title.
Let AI Handle Your Video Editing
This is how to connect Claude code using Instagram Edits MCP. For now, the Instagram Edits app is only available on macOS, and you can connect any AI model to make edits.
Since Claude requires a subscription, you can try a free AI model if you have one. You can also run any free AI model locally and ask it to edit, but the quality may vary and may not be as good as frontend models.
Since this guide focuses entirely on Claude Code, we are also creating a separate guide on how to connect other free AI models, including Google Gemini (which comes with a free Jio AI offer), DeepSeek, and other models.
If you have any issues while connecting Claude Code, let me know. If you prefer a video guide, we have also created one that you can check out above.

Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.
Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.
This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Big Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

Scientists have assembled a cellular atlas of a crucial brain region called the basal ganglia involved in functions such as movement, decision making, emotions and habit formation — an accomplishment that could help guide new treatments for several devastating diseases.
The researchers mapped the cell types and cellular gene activity in the basal ganglia, an interconnected set of structures deep within the brain, in humans as well as in mice and in macaque and marmoset monkeys. Basal ganglia dysfunction is associated with conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, Huntington’s disease, schizophrenia, Tourette’s syndrome, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder and addiction.
“It is important to understand the structure and function of the basal ganglia in order to develop effective treatments of these diseases,” said neuroscientist Hongkui Zeng, director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle and one of the leaders of the research presented in more than two dozen studies published on Thursday in Cell and related journals.
“It is a major milestone in our journey toward a comprehensive, detailed, multimodal, cross-species aligned cell atlas for the entire human brain,” with a target date sometime in 2028, Zeng added.
The research was conducted as part of the BRAIN Initiative, an effort launched in 2014 to advance the understanding of the brain with the support of the US National Institutes of Health. The work presented on Thursday offers the first comprehensive cross-species cellular roadmap for any brain region.
“Until now, there was no reference describing each cell type in the human basal ganglia together with how it regulates its genes,” said Joseph Ecker, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the Salk Institute in La Jolla, California, another of the research leaders.
“In the near term, the atlas is a reference resource for researchers. We are studying a Parkinson’s gene and can now see which cell types turn that gene on, and which DNA switches are active in those cells. Over the longer term, the atlas can help identify cell-type-specific targets for gene therapy and gene editing,” Ecker said. “It also gives a baseline for comparing diseased tissue with healthy tissue.”
Therapies built on the new work are still years away, Ecker said.
Among other findings, researchers identified a new type of brain cell associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, documented genetic changes in specific cell types that could play a role in autism, and discovered changes in gene activity in certain cells associated with aging.
Cross-species comparisons
Using brain tissue from deceased human donors, the researchers examined the role of 21 million cells in the basal ganglia in people, as well as millions more cells in the three other species.
“Understanding the cellular composition of this brain structure across species will allow for comparative analyses of function as well as connectivity patterns and response to pharmacological interventions,” said Salk Institute neuroscientist and biochemist Margarita Behrens, another of the research leaders.
Many studies for ethical reasons cannot be performed using living human brains. Much of what was previously known about the basal ganglia, and most early testing of new treatments, had come from research involving mice and monkeys.
“We rely on animal models to probe the inner workings of brain cells and circuits in generating brain function and mediating disease effects, and to test the efficacies of therapeutic interventions,” Zeng said.
The structures of the basal ganglia include the striatum, globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
“Together they help select and start movements, and they support habit formation, reward learning, motivation and emotion,” Ecker said.
The atlas combines several layers of data. One shows which genes are switched on in each cell. Another involves the epigenome, a collection of chemical compounds and proteins that attach to the DNA and regulate gene activity. A third layer involves spatial maps showing where each cell type sits in the tissue of the basal ganglia.
“Most of the DNA variants linked to brain disorders lie outside the protein-coding parts of genes. Many of them sit in DNA ‘switches’ that control when and where genes turn on, and those switches are often active only in particular cell types,” Ecker said.
The protein-coding parts of genes carry genetic instructions used to build proteins, the complex molecules that perform most of the critical work inside cells.
An atlas like this one helps trace a disease-risk DNA variant to the specific kind of nerve cell or support cell where it acts.
“That is a first step toward understanding how the variant contributes to disease, and eventually toward treating it,” Ecker said.

What Is a Captain’s Day in Fortnite?
On Captain’s Day, a new Captain arrives on the island and takes over a POI on the Fortnite Treasure Hunters Map. The location is transformed and renamed to better reflect the Captain who’s taken over the POI. This stays in place until the end of Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season, which gives you plenty of time to explore all the locations.
They are also featured on the map as Bosses in Fortnite Hunters, whom you can challenge to a fight. Defeating them grants you rare Sprites and Exotic Fortnite weapons, which are otherwise hard to obtain via regular means.
Each week, depending on the Captain that’s in charge on the island, Treasure Hunt Chest rewards vary. The only constant is the Fortnite Pirate Shop Access Token, which remains in play regardless of which Captain is in charge on whatever day.

As telescopes go, few if any are more famous than the Hubble Space Telescope. Over 30 years of operations, the telescope has been essential to groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally transformed humanity’s view of the universe. But like all satellites in low Earth orbit, it’s been gradually descending.
This happens because of atmospheric drag, and the Hubble Space Telescope is not equipped with a propulsion system to adjust its own orbit. According to NASA’s analysis, if left unchecked, the telescope will likely re-enter Earth’s atmosphere in 2033 or 2034, eventually crashing back onto the planet.
Hoping to delay this conclusion, NASA has issued a formal Request for Information seeking proposals from the private sector for “in-space servicing” of the famous telescope. This would likely involve raising Hubble’s altitude to extend its operational lifespan, but the agency is also open to industry’s suggestions for managing a safe and controlled reentry or disposal of the telescope while still in orbit. Space companies can also propose upgrades to enhance the telescope’s functionality in its remaining years.
“Hubble is a national icon,” Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a statement. “Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated reentry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”
The telescope was designed with the expectation that astronauts would perform repairs and upgrades in orbit. Since it was launched in 1990, a total of five service missions have been carried out. The last of these missions was canceled after the space shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003. But NASA later determined that the benefits of servicing Hubble outweighed the risks of a final mission, and in 2009 a crew took measures, such as replacing the battery, to extend the telescope’s lifespan.
This is also not the first time NASA has considered private-sector resources for raising the Hubble Space Telescope’s orbit. In September 2022, NASA entered into a nonfunding partnership agreement with SpaceX to investigate the possibility of using the company’s Dragon spacecraft to move Hubble into a more stable orbit. However, according to NASA’s announcement at the time, the agency had no plans to conduct or fund the service mission itself; the study was intended solely to assess commercial feasibility.
Meanwhile, NASA commissioned the private company Katalyst Space Technologies in September 2025 to perform an orbital raise for the Swift Observatory, which was experiencing faster-than-expected orbital decay. However, the company’s spacecraft, launched in July 2026, suffered an attitude control malfunction, forcing the mission to be abandoned. On November 4, Swift reentered the atmosphere over Indonesia.
The problems facing the Hubble Space Telescope are not limited to its drop in altitude. The spacecraft itself is also experiencing malfunctions. In June 2024, NASA announced that it would transition the Hubble Space Telescope to a new operating mode using only one of the six gyros on board to assess the telescope’s orientation. After more than three decades in space, only three of the gyros were operational, and one of those was starting to return abnormal readings. The other remaining functional gyro is now being kept in a ready state for future use.
NASA estimates that a mission to raise the telescope’s orbit will need to be carried out by 2032. In an announcement made in 2022, NASA also explained that if the Hubble Space Telescope could be raised to a higher, more stable orbit, it could continue to observe the cosmos for several more years.
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already in orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen. These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.
With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.
Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Online travel aggregator (OTA) Yatra swung to the red and reported a consolidated net loss of ₹78.4 Lakhs in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27). In contrast, the travel tech platform has reported a net profit of ₹14.3 Cr in Q2 FY26 and ₹33.9 Lakhs in Q1 FY27. The losses came despite the company raking in ₹1.7 Cr in one-time deferred tax benefits during the quarter. The bottom line was primarily impacted as the company’s revenue from operations tanked 39.1% to ₹213.6 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹350.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, on a sequential basis, Yatra’s top line rose 13.7% from ₹187.9 Cr in the preceding quarter. The OTA attributed the losses to the “challenging operating environment”, lower MICE (meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions) volumes, and the reorientation of the MICE vertical towards smaller corporate group programmes. “... Our year-on-year profitability was impacted primarily by MICE, which faced an exceptionally strong comparable quarter last year and a tactical shift towards smaller corporate group programmes amid prevailing uncertainty…,” said Yatra CEO Siddhartha Gupta. Including other income of ₹4.4 Cr, Yatra’s total income stood at ₹218 Cr in Q2 FY27. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter under review declined 35% to ₹219.9 Cr compared to ₹339 Cr in Q2 FY26. The company also incurred an additional tax expense of ₹59.3 Lakh during the quarter. Revenue less service cost (RLSC), which is essentially the gross margin, declined 0.2% to ₹125.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. As a result, EBITDA declined 47% YoY to ₹13.2 Cr, while EBITDA margin stood at 10.48%during the quarter under review. In a statement, the company’s gross bookings grew 6% YoY and 3% QoQ to ₹2,165.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. During the quarter, Yatra said that it added 54 new corporate customers with an estimated annual revenue potential of ₹203.5 Cr. “We continue to make progress on our strategic priorities, including expanding into the SME and mid-market segments through Travel Pro, strengthening our expense management offering through RECAP, expanding hotel supply and leveraging AI-led automation. These initiatives are helping us broaden our addressable market and build a more scalable business, positioning us for sustainable growth and improved profitability over the medium term,” added Gupta. Yatra’s US Entity On Nasdaq’s Radar Separately, the travel tech platform’s US-listed entity, Yatra Online Inc, said that it has received a letter from Nasdaq after its shares traded below the exchange’s minimum $1 closing bid price for more than a month. This has effectively put the travel tech company on a compliance watch. The company said that the notice does not immediately delist the company’s shares from the Nasdaq Capital Market. However, the OTA said that it has been given a timeline of 180 days, until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance. To do so, its shares must close at $1 or higher for at least 10 consecutive business days, even though Nasdaq may require up to 20 consecutive days in certain cases. If Yatra fails to meet the requirement by May next year, it may qualify for an additional 180-day compliance period. This would require the company to meet Nasdaq’s other continued-listing thresholds and formally notify the exchange of its intention to cure the deficiency. A reverse stock split is among the options available to lift the share price. Yatra said it may consider such a move if necessary, but cautioned that there is no assurance it will regain compliance. Nevertheless, Yatra said it intends to closely monitor its closing bid price and may evaluate available options to restore compliance. The notice highlights the pressure facing the travel-tech company’s US-listed shares. As of 1:13 AM IST, shares of Yatra Online Inc were trading at $0.77, down 18% in the past six months and nearly 57% lower on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. This comes as the US-listed Yatra Online Inc has been reporting increased net losses, compressed margins and falling revenues. Slowing growth in core verticals, market volatility and rising short-term trade-related borrowings have further led to the sell-off in the stock. But a sustained share price below $1 can further reduce liquidity, deter institutional investors and complicate future fundraising. Meanwhile, shares of India-listed Yatra closed Thursday’s trading session 0.94% lower at ₹81.03 on the BSE.

Failed health check, elevated load, server restart: What led to the Microsoft outage
Automated server shutdowns created an infrastructure bottleneck, even as engineers deploy alternatives, while an initial fix attempt don’t seem to be delivering results
Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365 for Business and Enterprise, as well as consumer products such as Microsoft Teams, Outlook, OneDrive, and Office on the web, continue to experience what the tech company described as a “service degradation” following a major global outage that has stretched across several hours.
Microsoft has yet to confirm why the services went offline in the early hours of Friday, but it attributes the outage to several servers unexpectedly becoming unavailable after failing automated health checks, which placed elevated strain on the remaining infrastructure worldwide.
The Microsoft Service Health Status currently lists all customer services as “operational”, but Microsoft’s update on X indicated there were issues to resolve.
Deep Dive
“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected. We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances,” said Microsoft 365 Status account on X.
Why the services went offline
By all accounts, the outage was caused by a cascading infrastructure failure.
It began with automated health checks across its server infrastructure, which failed on certain servers and caused them to shut down. This increased the load on the remaining online servers, causing a cascading effect. Microsoft engineers have attempted to restart these servers, and Microsoft 365 Status does indicate that a portion of the affected servers has been restarted and remains stable.
Restarting a server requires as long as 30 minutes, depending on hardware and workload. After an unexpected crash or hard reboot, the server may run a disk check process, which can take a long time on large drives. There is no guarantee that the issue which caused the server to shut down or become unresponsive will be fixed by a restart.
“We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that’s causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” Microsoft said before it started deploying certain fixes. That attempt hasn’t delivered results so far.
Microsoft said the disruption wasn’t driven by a spike in user traffic or a cyberattack. Instead, a core process on affected servers became overwhelmed, causing capacity loss when servers failed automated health checks and dropped offline. As a result, services became unavailable and unstable.

How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.
In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.
As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.
You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?
Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.
There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.
One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.
We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.
We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.
You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?
Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.
One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.
Can you give an example?
One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.
There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.
The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?
When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.
The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.
So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.
What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?
This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.
Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.
If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?
I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.
I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

Would you cancel a trip because it falls on Friday the 13th? For some people, the date brings more than a passing worry. It can trigger intense fear even when there is no clear danger. That fear has a name that may be harder to face than the calendar itself. It is called paraskevidekatriaphobia. The word comes from three Greek terms. Paraskevi means Friday, dekatria means thirteen, and phobia means fear. Another name for the same fear is friggatriskaidekaphobia. The fear of the number 13 alone is called triskaidekaphobia. Say it slowly as par-uh-SKEE-vuh-dek-uh-TRY-uh-foh-bee-uh. Psychotherapist Donald Dossey helped popularise the term. He joked that once you could pronounce it, you were cured. Getting the syllables right may earn a laugh. For someone whose fear disrupts daily life, treatment can help. A person may feel anxious just thinking about the date. Even seeing the date on a calendar can bring on symptoms. Others may panic as the day approaches. Their heart may race, and they may sweat or feel sick. Some people may also feel dizzy or struggle to catch their breath. Fear can influence ordinary decisions, too. Someone might postpone a journey, put off signing a contract or cancel dinner plans. Some people arrange their work around the date to avoid meetings or important decisions altogether. Others might stay home to avoid anything they believe could bring bad luck. How much this fear disrupts daily life matters more than any one symptom. A doctor or mental health professional can assess persistent fear and its effects. The exact origin remains uncertain. One Christian tradition connects the number 13 with the Last Supper. It identifies Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus Christ, as the 13th guest. Friday also carries its own associations, including the crucifixion of Jesus. Another story links the date to the arrest of the Knights Templar. The arrests began in France on Friday, October 13, 1307. The link to today's superstition remains uncertain. Research generally finds Friday the 13th is about as unlucky as any other day. Friday the 13th occurs three times in 2026. The first two fell in February and March. November 13 is the last one this year. If the fear regularly changes your plans, a mental health professional can help. One common treatment for specific phobias is exposure therapy. It involves gradually facing what you fear with guidance. The aim is to reduce the fear and help you return to your usual activities. The AI agent can schedule appointments, make reservations and wait on hold for you.
Meta's Muse just got another ability that could make the AI agent feel a little bit more like an actual personal assistant. Muse is now able to place phone calls on your behalf, if you have a paid subscription.
With the change, Muse is able to call businesses to help with tasks like making reservations, scheduling appointments and other "calls you don't want to make," Meta's Chief AI officer Alexandr Wang said in an update. The feature is available to those who have paid for a separate Muse subscription, which comes with additional tokens and some extra features.
Some users who have had access to the feature already have reported that Muse has been able to handle phone-related tasks with relative ease. Moltbook creator and Meta Superintelligence employee Matt Schlicht shared a recreation of a phone conversation his agent had with a Volvo dealership last month, noting that it was able to wait on hold in order to get the info he needed.
My muse called Volvo for me to see when the next available appointment is.
You can listen to the phone call here.
I have it do multiple calls like this every day (I'm still trying to get better and better at leveraging muse).
My muse called, waited on the line for 15 minutes,... pic.twitter.com/bosH1tyW1R
— Matt Schlicht (@MattPRD) October 9, 2026
Interestingly, in the call shared by Schlicht, Muse doesn't explicitly identify itself as an AI agent though it notes it's calling his behalf and that it's transcribing the call. That may be enough for some straightforward tasks, but there's always a chance these types of calls could go off the rails or the person on the other end hangs up when they realize they're speaking with an AI.
Meta has been steadily churning out new features for Muse, which has already drawn more than 10 million users, according to the company. People can also now assign a dedicated email address to their agent in order to loop it into important emails without giving wholesale access to their inbox.
The company isn't the first to experiment with phone-calling abilities for AI. Google has introduced a number of similar features over the years, including "Call For Me" for Pixel phones and Instinct recently introduced a "Concierge" feature for its agent that's meant to handle more complex calls.

Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
- Published
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.

In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.

The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI has introduced local inference and data processing for its APIs in India, adding to its efforts to expand the commercialisation of ChatGPT in its largest market. For context, local data inferencing allows businesses to ensure that both API requests and the computing required to generate responses take place within India for supported workloads. It is initially available for the GPT-6 Luna model and extends OpenAI's existing data residency options in the country. OpenAI's India enterprise head Nitin Bawankule pointed out that local inference gives businesses greater control over where their data is processed and could help more organisations move from experimenting with AI to deploying it in their day-to-day operations. "Some Indian businesses have not fully deployed AI for important work because they need the information involved to be processed within the country," Bawankule said. To use the new offering, customers need to create a new API project, select India as the location for both data storage and processing, and use the corresponding India regional endpoint. With the launch, India joins Australia and Japan as the latest markets where OpenAI has introduced API inference residency. Global AI Giants Push For Data Localisation In India Data localisation has emerged as an important consideration in enterprise AI adoption. While global AI models offer advanced capabilities, businesses handling sensitive information require a greater understanding of where their data is going. Storage and processing of data before model deployment is something that cannot be compromised from a security perspective for banks, financial institutions and government agencies. For these clients, data residency and infrastructure requirements can limit the use of international frontier AI models in production environments. OpenAI is not the first international AI company looking to address India's data localisation requirements. In August, Anthropic announced plans to bring in-country inference for its Claude AI models to India through Amazon Bedrock, AWS' managed service for building generative AI applications. The move was aimed at addressing data residency and infrastructure requirements that have kept banks, financial institutions and government agencies from deploying international AI models in production. Anthropic has since made similar data residency capabilities available for certain models on AWS Bedrock. For Indian AI startups such as Sarvam AI, locally hosted inference has also been an important differentiator when competing with global AI players. However, the entry of OpenAI and Anthropic into this segment could narrow that advantage as international companies begin offering similar capabilities in the country. For OpenAI, data inferencing is another piece of its India revenue. The AI giant has established a strong hold on the Indian market, where more than 10 Cr people interact with ChatGPT on a weekly basis. The company is looking to monetise its India holding. OpenAI Expands Its Business Offering On ChatGPT In a bid to deepen its engagement with businesses, OpenAI introduced Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta offering that allows businesses to claim and manage their profiles through a new Business Hub. Companies can update their information, add product feeds and access aggregated insights into how users discover and engage with them on ChatGPT. These insights include business mentions, website clicks and discovery topics across conversations where their websites are cited. OpenAI has also introduced Business Agents, which allow customers to interact with businesses, explore their offerings and ask product-related questions directly within ChatGPT. However, the feature is initially available only to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the US. Businesses in markets where ChatGPT is available, including India, can claim their profiles through Business Hub, subject to eligibility and verification requirements. OpenAI's broader efforts to expand its presence in India include investments and partnerships to develop domestic AI infrastructure. Earlier this year, the company partnered with Tata Group to develop domestic AI data centre capacity. It has also extended data residency capabilities for certain models through AWS Bedrock. Gold smuggled from war zones entered the UAE despite new regulations, report says
A new report says that the United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from conflict zones despite new regulations on the trade
CAIRO -- The United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from war zones despite new regulations on the trade imposed by the government after facing international pressure, a new report says.
Many gold refiners and traders in the UAE are not following the rules and enforcement is lax, according to the report by Swissaid, a Switzerland-based aid and development group. The report recommended that the UAE be added to an international watchlist for possible financial wrongdoing.
The Emirates, which refines and processes the precious metal to send to major markets like Switzerland, India and China, was the second-biggest gold exporter in the world after Switzerland in 2024, a year after the new rules took effect. Smuggled gold from Russia, Yemen and Sudan continues to flow into the UAE, the report says.
The UAE introduced the new guidelines to regulate the gold trade, including responsible sourcing and vetting supply chains, after a global anti-money laundering body raised concerns that the UAE was not doing enough to stop criminals and militants from hiding wealth there.
Despite the new rules, the UAE imported at least 591 tons of illicit gold, valued at $74 billion, the report says. Gold smuggled out of conflict zones, Russia or African countries accounted for 42% of the UAE's total imports of the precious metal in 2024, the report says.
Imports of the precious metal mined and smuggled out of Africa made up nearly half the gold coming into the UAE from the continent, the report said. Some of that gold entered the UAE officially, through third countries. That trade showed a slight increase in 2024, according to the report.
“The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa. And it continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions,” the report said.
The UAE did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report’s findings.
Swissaid said most of the smuggled gold in 2024 — some 453 tons valued at over $56 billion — reached Dubai refineries from African gold-producing countries, including Guinea, Mali and Sudan, a country that faces international sanctions. Nearly 29 tons of gold originated in Sudan, according to Swissaid, whose findings were based on data from the U.N., official trade statistics and civil and international organizations. Authors of the report said 2025 data was incomplete, but partial recent data showed the rising trend continuing.
“We had hoped that with the new regulations, conflict gold from countries subject to international sanctions would be stopped,” Marc Ummel at Swissaid told The Associated Press.
The illicit gold trade has been a key component of Sudan's war between the country's military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Since the war began in 2023, large quantities of gold have been smuggled out of Sudan to finance the RSF, who control gold-producing areas in Darfur and Kordofan regions, according to U.N. experts.
The RSF carried out mass killings, sexual violence and destruction in northern Darfur, in a “campaign of destruction” that U.N. experts said bears the “hallmarks of genocide.”
“From our point of view, since April 2023, all gold from (Sudan) should be considered as conflict gold,” Ummel said.
The Swissaid report found that in 2024 an additional 137.7 tons, valued at nearly $17 billion, were imported into the UAE from Russia and Yemen, which are also subjected to international sanctions.
Despite the risks associated with sourcing gold from the UAE, Switzerland was the top importer of gold from the UAE. The report said gold imports from the UAE increased drastically between 2024 and 2025 — going from 155 tons to 420 tons.
The Swiss government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report’s authors recommended that the UAE again be placed on the “gray list” of the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force, an international body that combats money laundering and terrorist financing. The gray list calls for increased monitoring, while its “black list” recommends countermeasures against countries with the most serious deficiencies.
The FATF placed the UAE in 2022 on the gray list. It removed it in 2024 after the new gold supply chain regulations.

Eurovision is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up to take the stage
- Published
On Saturday, the biggest and longest-running international song contest will make a leap into unknown territory.
Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.
And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.
It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.
Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).
Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.
"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.
"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.
"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."
Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.
This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.
Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.
Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.
There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.
A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.
Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.
The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.
Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.
The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".
In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.
Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.
For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.
"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."
The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format – no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music.
This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience – think Poland's My Słowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry.
There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh – where same-sex activity is illegal – and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year.
Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers.
Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer Tóc Tiên's song Em Tiên ("Fairy Maiden").
It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time.
The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music.
The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth.
"I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us.
"The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are."
Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.
Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.
Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.
Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water.
If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.

The world is no longer safe for frozen H2O.
New research published in Science on Thursday shows that the conditions that have kept ice, frozen soil, and snow stable are slipping away due to the burning of fossil fuels—and the implications are grave for the entire globe.
The climate of the past 12,000 or so years has been remarkably steady. That’s allowed for all kinds of wonderful things to happen, like human civilization flourishing. But rising temperatures are pushing the climate outside that envelope, and the new research looks at what the team behind the new findings has called the “safe operating space” for the icy, snowy landscape known as the cryosphere.
The scientists looked at changes to polar sea and land ice, mountain glaciers, permafrost, and snow cover over the past 12 millennia to analyze conditions that have allowed both civilization and other ecosystems to thrive. They then identified boundaries on those conditions that, if crossed, would upend the stability and safety humans have enjoyed for millennia.
The results show an “accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity.” Arctic and Antarctic sea ice have both fallen outside the safe operating threshold, as have snow cover and the area of permafrost—frozen soil laden with carbon. While land ice hasn’t yet fallen out of its safe space, it’s on the brink. And because of warming that’s already been locked into the climate system, it’s likely to also fall outside the threshold in the coming centuries.
While it may feel like the Antarctic ice sheet or permafrost covering Alaska are distant concerns, they’re anything but. The West Antarctic Ice Sheet, which a growing body of evidence shows is nearing the brink of irreversible decline, has enough ice to raise sea levels by 11 feet (3 meters). Permafrost, meanwhile, holds trillions of tons of carbon dioxide. Any degradation means that CO2, as well as even more potent methane, could end up in the atmosphere, accelerating global warming even further. Other examples of major risks abound, including how melting Greenland land ice could slow down or even collapse the ocean conveyor belt that helps keep Europe temperate.
“The consequences of a changing cryosphere extend beyond regions where ice and snow are disappearing,” says Albert Noström, a climate researcher at the Stockholm Resilience Center who co-authored the new paper.
Dipping outside the safe operating space doesn’t mean that the world will see 11 feet of sea level rise in the next year, a trillion-ton CO2 eruption, or a Day After Tomorrow scenario. But it does mean that the odds of crossing dangerous tipping points are rising.
“As we scratch 1.5 [degrees Celsius] and go above it, we are just really gambling with potentially triggering some of these Earth system tipping points,” Noström says. The safe operating space framework also “takes a broader perspective” that assesses slower changes over time and “how far, in this case, the cryosphere is moving away from the conditions that have supported a relatively stable Earth system,” he adds.
Cutting emissions is the most obvious and straightforward way to stop the cryosphere from sliding further outside our comfort zone. But there are a growing number of proposals to pursue more radical interventions that could protect the world’s ice. Scientists have already draped glaciers in the Alps in blankets during the summer to prevent melting. Other researchers have explored techniques to pump cold sea water to the surface to help thicken ice and modeled whether a manmade barrier could stabilize the West Antarctic Ice Sheet.
These geoengineering approaches have the potential to be costly, and there’s no guarantee they would work. They’d also do nothing to stop the root cause of warming: burning fossil fuels. Noström says emissions cuts are the most urgent way to protect ice and snow (and ourselves), but with the cryosphere sliding into a more dangerous space, “in principle, we shouldn't put the lid on” research for more far-flung interventions.
“The safe operating space is a precautionary framework,” he says. “It ensures that we try to stay as far downstream from the point where these really potentially existential or huge consequences and risks can happen.”

How to keep your anger in check: 3 tips from experts
From adjusting your expectations of others to rehearsing calmer responses, psychologists explain how small changes can help prevent heated exchanges.
Stopping yourself before you erupt in anger takes practise, and it starts with recognising patterns. The most obvious is that we are more likely to lose control when we are tired or stressed. “We all have less bandwidth when we are overwhelmed,” said Chris Huffine, a psychologist in Portland, Oregon, and the executive director of Allies in Change, a counselling nonprofit that promotes healthy relationships.
Fortunately, there are things you can do to release some pressure. Here’s what experts have to say.
DON'T EXPECT PEOPLE TO CHANGE
Anger often bubbles up from wanting someone to simply be different. Or, let’s face it, more like you. “Expect people to be who they are, not who you want them to be,” Dr Huffine said.
This does not mean you let a loved one off the hook. Accepting that you have different standards – whether about how to do the laundry or how often you see your in-laws – can help keep you from becoming exasperated. “Then you have a communal problem instead of an oppositional one”, and you can more calmly talk about a solution, said Denise Solomon, a professor of communication at Pennsylvania State University who focuses on interpersonal communication and conflict.
ANTICIPATE THE SAME ARGUMENTS
Because people are who they are, you will probably fight about the same things repeatedly. “The people in your life who trigger your anger are pretty reliable,” said Raymond DiGiuseppe, a professor of psychology at St John’s University. You’ve reacted the same way a thousand times. If you want to respond differently, you have to practise.
“Imagine them doing whatever it is that makes you mad, and imagine yourself having a new response,” he said. That might mean leaving the room for five minutes or asking yourself what’s actually going on. “But if you don’t practise, you won’t do it in the moment,” he added.
HAVE A CATCHPHRASE
The easiest thing to practise? Repeating a single phrase that can stem your rising anger. It can be absurd, like saying, “I will not strangle this person,” Dr Huffine joked. “Humour helps.”
Your mantra could simply be “I will not yell”. Or maybe “I shall not yelleth” in a funny accent. Dr Solomon said that when her children were teenagers and lobbed mean insults her way, she would respond, “I’m sorry, I’ll try to do better tomorrow,” which took the wind out of their sails and avoided a fight.

Japanese tech investor SoftBank yesterday offloaded 7.6 Cr shares of listed ecommerce giant Meesho in a block deal worth ₹1,885.2 Cr. Fidelity, through multiple affiliates and funds, picked up the biggest chunk of the shares for ₹573.1 Cr. The Youth Olympic Games in Dakar earned high marks from the International Olympic Committee on Thursday, a day before the closing ceremony, but the event’s future remains unclear.
Senegal is the first African country to host an Olympic sporting event, with the Youth Games involving almost 2,700 young athletes from 204 national Olympic committees. Africa has never hosted an Olympics Games.
“Everyone came here with certain expectations and those expectations have been far exceeded,” IOC President Kirsty Coventry, the Zimbabwean former Olympic swimming champion, told a press conference.
“It has been an magnificent journey. It has been extremely magical.”
Coventry said the IOC, which this year paused the process for awarding the hosting of the 2030 Youth Games, was still analysing all aspects before a decision is taken.
“We took a pause..and we are analysing and that’s where we are. We are still analysing. The data we will collect from Dakar will be added,” she said.
“As we move forward the way we want to engage with young people is extremely important. We have to analyse what will be the best way for the movement to continue in the future.”
She did not say when a decision was likely on the future of the event.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.
