Surfing speedster Beardman gives a glimpse of Ashes future
- Published
How would you celebrate after posting record bowling figures on a debut aged just 21?
If you're Mahli Beardman, now the most exciting fast bowler in Australian cricket, it's easy: "Try and get down to the beach!"
In his maiden one-day international, which was also his first match for Australia on home soil, Beardman took 6-24 - the best figures by an Australian on a one-day debut.
In doing so, the man who loves surfing swept aside England and set up a crushing victory in Perth.
"I would love to live my life like him - pretty carefree, loves the ocean and loves to learn about fast bowling," beamed proud captain and fellow Western Australian Mitchell Marsh.
With the nonchalance of youth and a flash of the future, Beardman was the perfect antidote during this moment of crisis for Australia.
To him, sandpaper is merely used to clean up his surfboard.
However, he has been made to wait for this moment and has had his troubles.
Two years ago, and with only one professional match to his name, he toured England with Australia's white-ball teams after an impressive Under-19 World Cup.
He did not play but bowling spells during intervals - his blond hair billowing behind him - felt like a glimpse into Australia and England's Ashes future.
Watching Mitchell Johnson tear apart England in the 2013-14 Ashes inspired Beardman to take up cricket, while he has worked with Dennis Lillee, another Australian Ashes legend, since his teenage years.
Add in accuracy, zip and effortless pace, and all of the ingredients appear to be there.
But in 2025 he suffered the first of two stress injuries in his back – the scourge of the young fast bowler.
The second of those came after his one previous Australia appearance to date – a T20 in Pakistan in January, in which he returned figures of 2-33.
Two weeks earlier he had dismissed and unsettled Australia great Steve Smith in a Big Bash play-off match which had built momentum further.
"There is always doubt," he said after his match-winning performance on Friday.
"I don't think I ever lost my love for the game, it was more 'Will I come back and be able to bowl the same and will the air speed be there?'"
After a carefully managed return, those questions were emphatically answered in Perth – where he has played all of his domestic cricket to date.
Across 7.4 overs, Beardman averaged 86.5 mph – his quickest match on record. His fastest delivery was clocked at 90.6mph, again his best effort on record.
Most impressive was his control of line and length, however. Rarely was there a ball there for England to hit.
He moved the ball in and out, not a lot but enough – enough to find Harry Brook's outside edge for his first ODI wicket at the start of his second over.
"After I got the first wicket, Zamps [spinner Adam Zampa] ran up, tapped me on the back and said 'keep a level head, mate'," Beardman said.
"That helped calm the adrenaline a little bit."
After that, Joe Root edged a drive and Jordan Cox tentatively nicked off. A bouncer to Sam Curran, which the England all-rounder hooked to fine leg, showed Beardman has the skills to unsettle a batter too.
"He bowled lively, got it to swing both ways, and his control was immaculate," former Australia all-rounder Tom Moody told BBC Test Match Special. "I don't think his heart rate went up much."
It points to Beardman's inexperience that Friday's ODI was the first time Moody – as astute an operator as there is in franchise cricket – had watched the young quick in the flesh.
This international was his 12th professional 50-over game to go along with 14 T20s. His first-class debut remains much anticipated.
"I've seen him in the Big Bash and he just has that persona," said former England captain Michael Vaughan.
"Sometimes you look at sportspeople and say 'yes, they have got it'.
"It's hard to explain what they have got. It's the way he strolls around. He is playing the game like it's his club side.
"If he stays fit, he has an incredible career ahead of him."
Australia are not afraid of accelerating the progression of young quicks – Glenn McGrath famously played only eight first-class matches before his Test bow – but his injuries mean Beardman's immediate future is in white-ball cricket.
"It's just a game-by-game thing at the moment," he said earlier this year on the prospect of a red-ball debut for Western Australia. "There hasn't been a set date."
Talk is now inevitable after this breakout showing.
Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc have been brought into the centre of the sandpaper storm by Usman Khawaja's book but debate over who will replace Australia's trio of Ashes and World Cup winners has been going on far longer.
Starc is 37, Hazlewood 35 and Cummins 33, while their current back-up Scott Boland turns 38 in April.
"He offers something quite different to those guys, slightly wider on the crease," former England bowler Steven Finn said on TNT Sports.
"He gets similar movement to Cummins, where he angles the ball into the right-handers, forces them to play and at the last second gets it to zip away.
"That's what the best bowlers in the world do."
In giving England another pounding in Perth, Beardman has moved himself towards the front of a queue of Australia's quicks in waiting.
The line also includes 20-year-old left-armer Harry Hoekstra, who has taken 20 wickets in his past three matches in his debut domestic season, and Lance Morris - once dubbed The Wild Thing and who caught the eye of England coach Brendon McCullum last week.
"We've been crying out to see what the next generation looks like. Ladies and gentlemen, this is what it looks like," Moody said.
Australia needed something to be excited about, even if the man himself, the surfer, speedster and star of the future, is treating it as another day on the beach.

Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats
Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!
Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!
It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."
So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.
Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.
Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri, a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.
"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.
"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."
"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."
And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.
Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?
Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.
Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.
"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."
One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.
The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."
Don't talk yourself out of it
It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.
Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.
"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.
The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.
"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."
In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.
"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.
"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.
Nature or nurture?
And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?
Jeff R. Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.
"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."
Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.
A ripple effect
And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.
In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.
"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."
"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."
When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.
"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."
So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.
It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.

Jensen Huang’s Leather Jacket Comes Back to Bite Him
The Nvidia founder’s signature look branded him as a maverick. Does that image read differently now?
Just before Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday from Nvidia, the Silicon Valley chip juggernaut he founded three decades ago, an uncanny photo of him made the internet rounds: Huang, in what appeared to be a haute-punk Saint Laurent jacket.
It wasn’t strange to see Huang in a leather jacket. After all, rare is the public appearance where Huang doesn’t wear one. He wore one on the cover of Time in 2021 and at Nvidia’s keynote in March. In a 2016 Reddit AMA, he described himself as “the guy in the leather jacket.” (A flat descriptor that sounds as if it could be applied to a video game avatar or a cartoon character.)
But this one was well beyond his typical style: drenched in studs, with fat flapped lapels. It was also, to fashion collectors, a coveted jewel, stemming from Hedi Slimane’s tenure at the French luxury house.
Alas, it was an artifact of A.I. fakery. (Nvidia confirmed that the photo had been doctored.)
To the many gawkers who followed the chronicle of his affairs this week, the executive’s more over-the-top Billy Idol-esque leather simmered with midlife crisis energy — the clothing equivalent of a new Porsche. The studded jacket in the A.I.-generated image seemed to declare “you can’t tame me!” as his company’s stock price, and reputation, crumbled. People ate it up, even as it was debunked.
Still, the photo brought into focus how perhaps even Huang’s leather jackets — the real ones — were an indication of a man branding himself as too much of a renegade.

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

It was far more effective than the bogey-free round of Nelly Korda, the No. 1 player who could only laugh at her clean card because it was cleaner than she would have preferred - 15 straight pars, one birdie, two closing pars for a 69.
That left Korda four shots behind going into the weekend at Pelican Golf Club, where a victory would make the 28-year-old American eligible for the LPGA Hall of Fame.
"I had a lot of chances," said Korda, competing for the first time in two months. "But you can just tell that from yesterday morning to today afternoon with the wind, that's what the defence of this golf course is. It's as fast as Bermuda as I've putted on throughout my career."
It wasn't a problem for Solheim Cup star Carlota Ciganda, who birdied her last four holes for a 63 to join Choi and Lindy Duncan (66) atop the leaderboard at 12-under 128.
The Japanese duo of Mao Saigo (65) and Minami Katsu (69) were two shots behind.
Choi has been an LPGA member for five years and it has been a curious chase for that first LPGA victory, particularly since she was 17 when she had a late lead in the 2017 US Women's Open and wound up as a runner-up.
She also had two good chances at winning during the recent Asia swing, where she was runner-up in Shanghai and South Korea.
Choi was playing in the group with Korda for the opening two rounds, which she believes has tested her enough to calm her nerves on the weekend. She wasn't rattled by the bogey-bogey start, or the bogey on the par-five 14th, her fifth hole of the round.
She pieced together enough birdies to regain some momentum, then hit an approach that got a nice kick around the green and rolled out to just under 15 feet for eagle on the par-five seventh.
"I have two rounds left, but I have recently played in a champion group on the tournament before, so I have that experience and I'm going just try my best and concentrate on my game," Choi said.
Scoring was low enough in the opening round that one-under 139 made the cut. This is the final regular-season event of the year, and the top 60 in the Race to CME Globe advance to the finale next week in Naples, where the winner gets $2 million.
Julia Lopez Ramirez of Spain, who defeated Yealimi Noh in a crucial singles match in her Solheim Cup debut, was among those at nine-under 131. That was important for the Spaniard, who came into the week at No. 66 in the Race to the CME Globe.
Duncan, the 35-year-old Floridian, has yet to win on the LPGA Tour and this was the first time she had at least a share of the lead through 36 holes. She went 2-1 in her Solheim Cup debut.
"The week has gone by really fast, which is sometimes a good thing," Duncan said. "Because if you're playing a lot and you get some momentum going, that's kind of a nice way to play. So it's just been kind of rolling with it."
Charley Hull was five shots off the leaders on seven-under after shooting 67 on Friday. England's Lottie Woad finished the second round level with Hull on seven-under.

President, PM condole Assam accident; Modi announces ₹2 lakh ex-gratia for each deceased
At least 26 people died, including women and minors, and 20 others were injured in the accident near Kaziranga National Park in Assam on Friday.
President Droupadi Murmu, Vice President C P Radhakrishnan and Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday condoled the tragic road accident in Assam that left at least 26 dead and 20 others injured.
Modi also announced an ex-gratia of ₹2 lakh each to the families of each deceased and ₹50,000 to the injured in the accident involving a head-on collision between a minibus and a container truck.
At least 26 people died, including women and minors, and 20 others were injured in the accident near Kaziranga National Park in Assam on Friday.
Deep Dive
"The news of the deaths in a road accident in Kaziranga, Assam, is deeply saddening. I express my heartfelt condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones in this accident and wish a speedy recovery to those who were injured," Murmu said in a social media post.
Responding to this on X, the Assam Chief Minister's Office said the state government is engaged in relief efforts and will provide every possible assistance to the families of the deceased during this difficult time.
Vice President C P Radhakrishnan said, "Deeply saddened and pained by the tragic loss of precious lives in the road accident in Kaziranga. My heartfelt condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones in this unfortunate tragedy."
"My thoughts and prayers are with them during this difficult time. I also pray for the swift and complete recovery of all those injured," he added.
Modi expressed deep anguish over the loss of lives in the accident in Golaghat district of Assam.
"I extend my condolences to the bereaved families in this hour of grief. Praying for the speedy recovery of the injured," the Prime Minister's Office said.
"An ex-gratia of ₹2 lakh from PMNRF would be given to the next of kin of each of those who lost their lives. The injured would be given ₹50,000: PM @narendramodi," it added.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah also said he is deeply saddened by the tragic road accident in Kaziranga that took away precious lives.
"My thoughts are with the families who have lost their loved ones. Praying for the speedy recovery of those injured," he added.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital.
Fact: The video is clipped out of context. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat was recounting an incident from the 1930s where a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS against an attempt to ban it. While making this argument, Ibrahim had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Bhagwat was quoting Ibrahim’s statement, not remarking himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post (archived) by The Economic Times, dated 09 November 2026, featuring a longer version of the same video. Upon reviewing the video, we found that Mohan Bhagwat was not making the statement himself but was quoting a person named Ibrahim. Referring to an incident from the 1930s, Bhagwat said that when the Central Provinces Assembly first attempted to ban the RSS, there were no volunteers or supporters of the RSS’s ideology to defend it. In this context, he recounted that a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS by saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Ibrahim further stated that he knew Dr Hedgewar, that he was not insane but a good man, and therefore, the RSS could not be communal.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) covering the statement made by Mohan Bhagwat on 09 November 2026, while inaugurating the newly constructed auditorium at the renovated headquarters of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited in Nagpur.
We also found a video of the event, which was livestreamed on 09 November 2026 on the Facebook account of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Ltd. In the approximately 1-hour-and-36-minute-long video, we found the segment corresponding to the viral clip at around 1:16:00.
During this segment, Mohan Bhagwat said, “The RSS, which was formed 100 years ago, is being discussed everywhere. That’s why so many books are being published now. I held an intellectual class here in Nagpur, where I explained that when the first attempt to ban the RSS was made in the Central Provinces Assembly in the 1930s, none of the RSS volunteers came forward to defend the RSS or support its ideology.”
He further said, “There was a Mr Ibrahim who spoke in favour of the RSS. He said that the RSS should not be banned and that it was not communal. But how did he make this argument? He said that those who say India is a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. This is my opinion, and I know Dr Hedgewar. He is not insane; he is a good man, and therefore, the RSS cannot be communal. So, that was in the 1930s. Five or seven years had passed since the RSS was founded. Everyone knew about the RSS, but Dr Hedgewar knew“
We also found that Jagran reported that a book on the lives of former RSS pracharaks was released during the event. Bhagwat discussed the lives of former RSS pracharaks and recounted an incident from the 1930s in this context. This confirms that the viral clip presents Bhagwat’s statement without the necessary context. In the original video, Bhagwat was quoting a person named Ibrahim, who had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. The remark was made by Ibrahim, not Bhagwat.
To sum up, this video shows Mohan Bhagwat quoting Ibrahim’s remark about sending those who call India a Hindu nation to a mental asylum.

Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
- Published
Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.
Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues first began, as Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress" and email queues were nearing normal levels.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said the problem was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.
By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
- Why is Microsoft's outage lasting so long and will emails be lost? 
  - Published2 hours ago
- Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world 
  - Published3 hours ago
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".
His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".
Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.
"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.
"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.
'Encouraging recovery signals'
Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
- Published
Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.
Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.
Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.
And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.
With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.
Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.
Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.
The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.
Salah and Hakimi shine
Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.
The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.
The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.
Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.
Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.
In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.
But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.
However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.
Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.
Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.
The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.
Tunisia downed as McCarthy frustrates Bafana
Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.
The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.
Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.
Libya, who last played at an Afcon in 2012, climb to second in the table and go level on points with Uganda.
South Africa are a point clear of Guinea at the top of Group D after a 2-2 draw against Benni McCarthy's Kenya in Johannesburg.
Amos Wanjala's own goal gifted the hosts an early lead before Michael Olunga levelled from the penalty spot just before half-time.
Relebohile Mofokeng restored Bafana Bafana's advantage with 13 minutes remaining, but Kenya claimed a point when Ryan Ogam's low shot from 20 yards crept inside the left-hand upright in the 90th minute.
Elsewhere, Burkina Faso joined Benin on seven points at the top of Group F thanks to Elohim Kabore's 94th-minute winner against Mauritania in Ouagadougou.
Ethiopia upset Mozambique
Mali extended their winning start to go top of Group K after Mamadou Camara completed a 3-2 comeback win at home against Rwanda, who had led twice in Bamako.
Rwanda had won their first two fixtures and are three points ahead of Cape Verde, who registered their first points with a 4-2 victory over Liberia in Praia.
Ethiopia registered their first win to upset Mozambique in Maputo, with Kenean Markneh scoring the only goal in the 87th minute after Mambas keeper Ernan spilled a low shot from Carlos Damtew.
The East Africans move on to three points but remain bottom of Group J, behind Sudan on head-to-head record, while Mozambique are on four points and three behind leaders Senegal.
Zambia moved level on four points with Group I leaders Algeria after a 1-1 draw at home to Burundi. The North Africans have the chance to open up a three-point gap when they host Togo on Saturday.
In Group G, Comoros were held to a goalless draw by Congo-Brazzaville in Moroni. Cameroon lead the section on seven points, with Comoros on four, Namibia on three and the Congolese bottom on two points.

Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia,
NEW DELHI: India may not yet be fully secure in meeting its food requirements, with heavy dependence on imports for essential commodities such as edible oils and pulses, NITI Aayog vice-chairman Ashok Kumar Lahiri said on Friday.Speaking at an event in Delhi, Lahiri said India imports more than half of its edible oil requirements and relies on other countries for several pulses.He questioned whether the country was sufficiently prepared to deal with disruptions in global supplies and sudden price increases."We are talking about Viksit Krishi in Viksit Bharat in 2047. As we move towards Viksit Bharat at 2047, are we secure regarding our food supply across the various products? Perhaps not as yet," he said.Lahiri said he was surprised to learn that chana (gram) consumed in India comes from Australia, while masoor dal is imported from Australia and Canada. Some pulses also come from Myanmar, African countries and Russia, according to news agency PTI."Now you can ask what is wrong with India importing edible oils or oil seeds from Indonesia, Malaysia, Argentina, Brazil, Russia, and Ukraine, and pulses from Australia, Canada, Myanmar, Africa, and Russia," Lahiri said.
"The problem is, first, the issue of vulnerability to global supply disruptions or price shocks," he added.India meets more than half of its edible oil demand through imports. These imports are estimated at 17 million metric tonnes, worth around $20 billion, Lahiri said.India is also the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses, accounting for nearly a fourth of global consumption. The country consumes around 25-27 million tonnes of pulses every year."For our dal-chawal or dal-roti, we require pulses and edible oils. Any disruption of supply of these essential commodities or price shock can assume the gravity of a strategic disaster," he said.Lahiri said reducing dependence on imports would require greater focus on domestic production of pulses and edible oils. He pointed to the need to diversify crops and reduce the dominance of wheat and paddy in Indian agriculture.
Since pulses and oilseed crops generally require less water, he said, promoting their cultivation could also help address agricultural challenges.The NITI Aayog vice-chairman also stressed the need to reduce and eliminate waste in Indian agriculture.

From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis
- Published
When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.
Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.
Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.
One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.
During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.
Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.
For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.
I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.
When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.
We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.
Sacked on the drive up for pre-season
When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.
One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.
During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.
When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!
Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.
My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.
I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.
I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.
Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.
I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.
That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.
'Every manager needs to think about their cardboard box'
I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.
Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.
We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.
"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."
That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!
It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.
I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.
It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.
I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.
It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.
Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.
Finishing as friends
I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.
When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.
I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.
Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.
I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.
After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.
Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.
After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.
My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.
I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.
My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”
Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.
This is only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.
Unfortunately for travelers, based on what is known so far, this is likely to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines have already canceled flights scheduled to leave later Friday, and American Airlines warned that disruptions are expected for the rest of the day. “This is going to take some time,” Mullin said. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”

FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which is currently under investigation, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a "temporary telecommunications outage."
"Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the post reads.
The outage hasn't been linked to a threat or attack, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
"There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin told reporters at the White House. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."
The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.
That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.
The telecommunication issue doesn't extend to the entire U.S., Mullin said. Without naming the regions in question, he stated, "there's two areas inside the United States that are still able to communicate just fine."
Mullin also said that other countries' aviation systems don't seem to be affected by the FAA outage.
The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.
"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
Passengers stranded
The nationwide ground stop has caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancelations during the holiday season.
At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.
"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said.
Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she's thinking about how soon she can make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.
"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.
This is a developing story.
Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

Eight Army personnel were injured after a military truck carrying 14 jawans overturned after hitting a roadside tree in Telangana’s Rangareddy district on Friday morning, police said.
The incident happened at Allawada village in Chevella mandal, about 50 km from Hyderabad, at around 8 am.
“The military truck carrying 14 jawans from the Golconda Army camp left for Shabad at around 6.30 am, as part of an army training exercise. A trainee driver, who was driving the vehicle, lost control over the steering and hit the median. The truck later rammed into a roadside tree and overturned,” Chevella assistant commissioner of police B Kishan told reporters.
On receiving the information, the Chevella police rushed to the spot and launched rescue operations. “Eight Army personnel were injured and the others managed to escape,” the ACP said, adding that the injured jawans were taken to the Army hospital in Golconda.
He said no complaint had been received from the Army authorities so far and, hence, no case had been registered yet.
Further details regarding the circumstances leading to the accident were not available.

EXCLUSIVE: Watch out Oscar. Spider-Man is aiming to get your attention.
Sony Pictures and Marvel‘s Spider-Man: Brand New Day is about to launch an all-out campaign to land a spot in the Best Picture race at the 99th annual Academy Awards. Can the highest-grossing movie of not just this year but all time at the domestic box office (now just shy of $41 million to become the first billion-dollar grossing movie domestically), land a place among the coveted 10 the Academy names as Best Picture nominees? Tom Rothman, chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group, thinks so and has decided to put the full weight of the studio behind the effort.
“The Academy is meant to recognize greatness. So, to be honest, I think it’s greatness. I think it’s received wisdom. If there aren’t people thinking about it, we’re gonna do what we can just to make people think about it,” Rothman told me this week. “I think it’s also incumbent upon studios who make these kinds of quality commercial films to get people to think about it, and here’s what I ask people when I walk around: ‘Are you telling me that there are 10 films this year that are better than this film?’ ”
Watch on Deadline
Spider-Man: Brand New Day, , the fourth entry into the MCU Tom Holland era of Spidey movies at Sony, is at 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, nearly as critically acclaimed there as perceived large-scale Oscar contenders The Odyssey and Project Hail Mary which are also in the 90s ( and even some of the more arthouse-style contenders). Both of those, along with the upcoming unseen Dune: Part Three, are in Gold Derby’s projection of the current top 10 movies with best chances to land a Best Picture nomination. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is listed way down at No. 36, with a 0.46% chance of making the cut, well below The Sheep Detectives and a few notches above I Love Boosters. Pundits are basically ignoring the year’s biggest film, so we have to ask why.
Of the previous eight live-action Spider-Man films Sony has released since 2002, the only Oscar nominations they have received have been in the Visual Effects and Sound categories, the most recent nom for Visual Effects for 2001’s No Way Home. 2004’s Spider-Man 2 is the only one to actually win an Oscar, that one also for Visual Effects. On the animated front, 2018’s Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse won for Best Animated Feature, and its 2023 sequel was also nominated.
Not one of these 10 films has cracked the Best Picture race. Rothman feels Brand New Day can, and deserves to be the breakthrough.
“I think to be honest, it’s because there are things like Gold Derby, you know, whatever that is, that just tend to think only about the art film world, and look, I’m an art film guy. I made my bones in the art film world, I’m Mr. Searchlight, right? You know, my whole career, I love art films. But I’m a traditionalist, and I was never for expanding the number of Best Pictures from five to 10. Okay, I liked it the old way, but I believe that the very reason it was extended from five to 10 was so that the Academy would have room to recognize really quality commercial filmmaking,” he said pointing (correctly) to Christopher Nolan’s Best Picture-snubbed superhero movie The Dark Knight as the key reason.
“I think wise heads know that quality commercial filmmaking is extremely difficult, and to make a movie like this, never mind the fact that it’s the highest-grossing movie in history of America, forget that. It’s in the 90s on Rotten Tomatoes for critics, it’s in the 90s on audiences on Rotten Tomatoes. Here’s the thing: the movie’s great. I’m a biased witness, but that’s not me, that’s objective. You don’t have the results that you have, where we had people seeing the movie two and three times. You don’t do close to a billion dollars in America. But are there 10 films that are better than this film, just in pure quality? I think when you see movies like F1 and Barbie and Wicked and Bohemian Rhapsody, whatever, getting nominated, well that is the very reason that that the Academy changed to 10.”
So Sony has hired awards consultants and is making big plans. The studio plans a “robust” screening strategy starting just before Thanksgiving, including multiple FYC Q&As with filmmakers and department heads. Stars Tom Holland and Zendaya are also involved in campaigns for other 2026 contenders like The Odyssey and Dune 3 and Holland is in pre-production on a new film, so their availability going forward is not known. Rothman himself plans to host screenings and tastemaker events on both coasts.
In addition to Los Angeles and New York, there will be special screenings in London, Paris, Madrid, Copenhagen, Sydney, Rome, Mexico City, Berlin and Tokyo. And, as Deadline teased in September, the studio plans to do a big rerelease of the movie before year’s end — possibly as Deadline intimated with some unseen footage — that will also bring new attention to the film and hopefully inspire those Academy voters who have not seen the movie (and based on my conversations there are many) to see it in a theater.
“I think Academy members would be interested in this because it’s very significant from a storytelling movie. This is really the first of these kind of movies that I can think of that does not climax in a giant battle. In this movie there is no giant action sequence at the end. The climax of this movie are two young people sitting on the edge of a bed, talking to each other, and sharing their their deepest pain. This movie is melancholy in that way and beautiful,” he said. “I think people might take Spider-Man for granted, and not only that, I think they make assumptions about it. When you see the movie those assumptions are undone. It’s a very moving, quite personal film. Destin (Daniel Cretton) is a really personal filmmaker. This is the guy who made Short Term 12. That’s what I say when I encourage people to see it, you know, people of my generation. I say you may take it for granted, you may think it’s just another, but it isn’t. It’s really the first, when I think about it. I think it’s the first superhero movie that’s really a super person movie.”
To date, the only movies even remotely in the “superhero” universe to crack the Best Picture race have been 2018’s Black Panther, and 2019’s Joker, though the latter is really a drama far removed from what is expected in the genre.
So the biggest question is can Sony change the trajectory of the franchise in terms of Oscar and get the point across that the record-shattering success of this movie is for a reason? Rothman compares it to the Lord of the Rings franchise in hoping there can be recognition for a movie that has taken a known brand to, yes, a brand new day.
“The Academy members are really, really smart, and they know filmmaking,” he said. “And if they see the movie, which maybe they wouldn’t necessarily do, if they see the movie, I think they’ll recognize how extremely skillful it is, because they’ll know how hard it is to tell an intimate emotional story in that arena. But more than that, I think it’s this specific movie. It’s the work that Destin did, as I said, a true humanist director who put character and emotion first.”
Andreas Wiseman contributed to this story.

Youth dies after assault over firecracker dispute in Pune’s Viman Nagar: Police

Journalist’s Arrest Adds to Fears Israeli Security Agency Is Being Politicized
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was detained without being charged with a crime, raising concerns that the domestic security service is overstepping its authority.
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a 38-year-old journalist and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, said he was putting on his pajamas on the evening of Nov. 3 when police officers and intelligence agents burst into his family’s third-floor apartment in Jaffa.
They strip-searched him, confiscated his phone, allowed him to dress and then whisked him away, he said in an interview at a restaurant in the city.
Five days later, after interrogations by Israel’s domestic security agency, the Shin Bet, Mr. Abu Shehadeh, who lives with his wife and two young children, was let go.
A former elected member of the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Council, Mr. Abu Shehadeh has not been charged with a crime. The Israeli authorities have not publicly offered a reason for his arrest, though court records reviewed by The New York Times show that he was accused of being in contact with an unnamed “foreign agent.”
His highly publicized arrest — a week after Israel’s national elections — came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have claimed that foreign actors illegally funneled large amounts of money to bribe Arab citizens to vote for Arab political parties.
Critics say that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the record gains by Arab parties in the Parliament, or the Knesset, by contending without basis that Arab voters stole the election.

The three-member Commission of Inquiry, set up by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to probe the 2023 Manipur ethnic violence, was given a sixth extension on Friday.
The Ministry notified that the commission, which was constituted on June 4, 2023, “shall submit its report to the Central government as soon as possible but not later than May 20, 2027”.
More than 300 people have been killed in the ethnic violence that erupted between the Kuki-Zo and Meitei people on May 3, 2023. Around 60,000 people have been displaced from their homes.
The probe panel’s report is awaited even as the ethnic conflict has now spread to the Kuki and Naga communities. Since February this year, more than 60 people have been killed in Naga-Kuki clashes.
The commission is now headed by former Supreme Court judge Balbir Singh Chauhan, after Ajai Lamba, the former Chief Justice of the Gauhati High Court, resigned as the chairperson of the panel in February this year. The panel is yet to finalise its report.
Justice (retd.) Chauhan is also heading the judicial inquiry into an incident of violence that occurred in Ladakh’s Leh city on September 24, 2025 where four civilians, including a Kargil war veteran, were killed in police firing. The Ladakh report is yet to be submitted to the government.
11,000 affdavits
Manipur’s Commission of Inquiry has received around 11,000 affidavits.
President’s rule was imposed in the State on February 13, 2025 and on February 4 this year, a new Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh took oath, ending Central rule.
The inquiry commission is mandated to probe the causes, extent of violence and riots targeting members of different communities, the sequence of events, and whether there were any lapses or dereliction of duty on the part of any of the responsible authorities and individuals.

Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
The hard-line position of Russian officials in closed-door negotiations about ending the war thrusts European security into the heart of the talks.
Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands, including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.
Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.
Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.
The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.
Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.
The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. To critics, the United States risks enabling Mr. Putin’s long-running attempt to reassert a Soviet-era sphere of influence as far away as Central Asia.

Former Indian cricketer Sachin Tendulkar has joined the cap table of Hyderabad-based cleantech startup Recykal. The startup did not disclose the size of the investment. In a statement, Recykal said that Tendulkar infused the capital during the extension of the startup’s recently closed $23 Mn bridge round. Back in June, the clean tech startup had raised $17.6 Mn in equity funding. The round also comprised an additional secondary component worth $5.4 Mn, which saw participation from existing backers and family offices. “What drew me to Recykal was seeing how technology was being used to solve an everyday problem. Recykal’s mission to use technology to drive behavioural change across 1 Bn people is what really connected with me, and I hope together we can encourage more people to make responsible choices every day,” said Tendulkar in a statement. Founded in 2016 by Abhay Deshpande, Abhishek Deshpande, Ekta Narain, Vikram Prabakar and Anirudha Jalan, Recykal operates a B2B marketplace for recyclable materials. It also provides software solutions to help brands track plastic and e-waste recycling to meet compliance mandates. The startup also recently launched a deposit return system (DRS), a reverse vending machine service for recovering consumer packaging. Under DRS, consumers pay a refundable deposit on containers at purchase and get it back when they return the container to a collection point. Backed by the likes of Morgan Stanley, 360 ONE, Circulate Capital and the Murugappa Group, the startup has raised more than $60 Mn in funding to date. Recykal claims to operate a network of more than 5,000 waste aggregators and recyclers and claims to cater to 650 enterprise brands, including the likes of Hindustan Unilever, Samsung and BMW. In June this year, the startup had told Inc42 that it closed FY26 with a gross revenue of ₹1,498 Cr, up 53.2% from ₹978 Cr in the year ago fiscal. However, losses jumped 7% to ₹60 Cr compared to ₹56 Cr in FY25. Interestingly, Tendulkar’s investment in Recykal comes almost two weeks after he backed gaming startup Metasports Interactive, the company behind mobile cricket strategy game Hitwicket. Besides, the retired cricket icon has also invested in a range of other startups such as used car marketplace Spinny, listed fintech startup Kissht, and former Swiggy Instamart leader Karthik Gurumurthy’s activewear brand Ten X You.

The nine newly included schemes under the Prime Minister’s Awards for Excellence in Public Administration (PMA) 2026 are Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban), Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), Gyan Bharatam, PM Matsya Sampada Yojana, TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, Crop Diversification under three components, PM SHRI, Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen), National Mission on Natural Farming and Capacity Building under iGOT (Integrated Government Online Training), the statement said.
Three schemes from PMA 2025 have been retained for 2026 -- Har Ghar Jal Yojana, PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana and Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, it added.
The schemes approved under PMA 2026 will also continue for the 2027 awards, the statement said.
Districts with Aspirational Blocks will participate in the Aspirational Blocks Programme category, which covers 513 blocks across 331 districts in the country, it said.
The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) launched the portal (https://pmawards.gov.in/) for the PMA 2026 on November 13 to begin the registration process.
The launch ceremony was held through video conferencing and attended by officials from various Union ministries and departments, principal secretaries (administrative reforms) of states and Union territories, and district collectors and district magistrates.
More than 2,000 officers from 750 locations across the country attended the session, the statement said.
The ministries were requested to submit quantitative, qualitative and governance parameters to DARPG by November 17 to facilitate the formulation and uploading of the application form on the awards portal for submission by districts, it added.
The PMA 2026 will comprise a trophy, a scroll and an incentive of Rs 20 lakh for each awarded district or organisation. The amount is to be utilised for implementing a project or programme or bridging resource gaps in any area of public welfare.
The awards are presented on Civil Services Day, observed on April 21.
