Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

New Delhi, The NHRC has issued a notice to the education ministry over a complaint alleging that adequate awareness and educational activities concerning the Veer Baal Diwas on December 26 have not received "commensurate attention".

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

Microsoft services are returning after an outage took down Outlook, Teams and more
Health care providers, schools and governmental bodies are among those affected.
Microsoft services that went down amid a widespread outage are gradually coming back online, the company said. An issue that impacted Microsoft 365 on Thursday afternoon took out services such as Outlook, Teams and Copilot 365, disrupting businesses and organizations around the world.
The company toiled overnight to restore service. Around 10PM ET on Thursday, it said some attempts to "improve serviceability" didn't work as hoped. By 2:45AM the following morning, though, it was "seeing positive results for service stability and increased capacity as a result of our latest traffic optimization actions."
Around 8:30AM, the company reported "continued recovery progress across affected regions, with broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific." In an update 45 minutes later, Microsoft said that while some people might be experiencing delayed email deliveries in Outlook or spotty connectivity, it was seeing "sustained improvements" in availability of affected services.
"We're seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure," the company said in an update at 10:39AM. "We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us."
The company later said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused you and your business." The outage was not the result of a cyberattack or AI agents causing havoc. "The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change," according to Microsoft, which has "addressed the underlying issue."
It added that it was "seeing broad recovery and stability across our services," which it restored gradually. A high level of demand meant it needed to validate system stability at each stage of the process. "While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," it said. "We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete."
The day-long outage underscored how important it is for people and organizations to have redundancies in place. It had a widespread impact across the globe, affecting calls to emergency services, governments, the House of Representatives, court systems, schools and other organizations.
The UK's National Pharmacy Association said the email issues could cause "delays to some prescriptions." In Japan, where the majority of businesses and institutions are said to use Microsoft services, some companies seemingly went back to using fax machines on a temporary basis.
Given that the outage prevented them from doing their jobs properly, some workers in Australia and the UK used it as an excuse to clock off early on Friday and go to the pub. However, the inevitable return to normality weighed on some people's minds. "I thought it was heaven because I wasn't getting any emails at all, but this is just a Microsoft outage, so I'm actually just waiting in line at the gates of hell," the Japan Times quoted one person as saying.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.
I’ve tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.
For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.

Best Open Earbuds Overall
Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Battery life | 8 hours, 32 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP57 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones I would recommend to anyone looking for great open earbuds. They are exceedingly comfortable and easy to use all day, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them.
They’re clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don’t expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.
There are other open earbuds that are nearly as good as these, and some surpass them in areas like sound quality. But it’s a combination of small details that puts the AeroClip 2 at the top. The physical button controls on each earbud are much easier to use than touch-sensitive alternatives, especially when running or exercising outdoors. The charging case is surprisingly small, smaller than most other options on this list. And, importantly, the call quality is great. These buds use the same AI-powered chip as the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro, and while they don’t sound quite as good, they are noticeably better than other open earbuds, especially in noisy environments.
The best part? They cost less than many similar competitors I tested.
Runner-Up
Shokz OpenDots 2 Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.1 | 
| Battery life | 10 hours, 40 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IP57 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
My former top pick, and still a great option, especially if you value battery life. These earbuds do most of what the Soundcore AeroClip 2 does, just a little larger and a little pricier. The buds are exceedingly comfortable and stable for all-day wear, even during outdoor workouts.
What sets them apart from the AeroClip 2 is battery life. They are best in class—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and water-resistance rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I’ve worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.
They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.
Best Premium Open Earbuds
Bose Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen) Specs
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Battery life | 6 hours, 24 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IPX4 | 
| Wireless charging | Yes | 
The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds were a big deal when they launched in 2024—a brand-new design from Bose and one of the biggest swings from a major brand in clip-on open earbuds. Two years later, the brand launched the second-generation version, and they are a solid, if expensive, option. That’s mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds sound clearer and more defined than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.
Like the Soundcore and Shokz earbuds, they are very comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I am wearing them. This gen-two version has a more distinct, two-tone material design that is certainly eye-catching, especially in the white colorway. They also now support wireless charging, a big omission in the first generation. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.
Best Cheap Open Earbuds
Soundpeats PearlClip Pro Specs

| Battery life | 7.5 hours, 30 with case | 
| Water/dust resistance | IPX5 | 
| Wireless charging | No | 
It can be a little nerve-wracking to spend big bucks on a concept (open earbuds) you aren’t totally convinced by. That’s one reason I love this $50 option—the PearClip Pros aren’t super pricey and are a great way to find out if you even like open earbuds in the first place, especially the kind that clip onto the outside of your ear.
They are far less refined than Shokz or Soundcore. Things like the app and touch controls can be a little finicky. But that’s common at this super-low price point, and you can always upgrade to a more premium earbud if you fall in love with the clip-on form factor.
Best Open Ear Headphones

| Wireless charging | No | 
The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more like headphones than earbuds—with a wraparound headband, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver clearer sound than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.
I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I’m currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and I’m hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.
Honorable Mentions
Apple AirPods 5 With Wireless Charging Case for $149: Apple AirPods 5 are semi-open earbuds—they still go in your ears, but don’t have rubber eartips that block outside noise, meaning you can still hear the world around you pretty clearly. Because they go in your ear somewhat, they have better sound quality and automated noise-canceling than nearly all of my top picks. Fit, however, is a big issue. While nearly all of my top picks are excellent workout companions, the AirPods 5 are quite the opposite—they can fall out often during exercise and are tricky to control mid-run.
Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn’t clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that’s forgivable.
CMF Clip Pro for $99: If you want something a little nicer and a little more comfortable than our budget pick (the Soundpeats PearClip Pro), these CMF open earbuds are a solid option. Sure, they’re a big step up in price, but for under $100, I found them more comfortable and easier to use thanks to the physical button control on each earbud (similar to my top picks).
JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn’t very detailed and is generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Former WIRED reviewer Waniata found the overall package punches above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, a comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multi-device Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, often sells for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don’t dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don’t, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it’s not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life and come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of total battery life. There’s nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don’t see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retails for the same amount and offers more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: it's built for athletes and syncs with Suunto fitness watches, but the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2 outclasses it in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery).
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn’t as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically lack noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple’s AirPods, sit inside the ear but don’t have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they’re usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I don’t expect them to cancel any noise, so I don’t test them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren’t really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

They say we are what our fathers leave behind. The latest Tamil film John Doe revolves around fathers of all kinds — one who fed shame and toxicity to his child, one who failed to stand by his daughter, and one who looks after a childlike wife. Even when they are absent, or through that very absence, some of these fathers keep shaping their children’s lives.
Which is why, even though John Doe revolves around the mysterious murder of an eight-year-old boy, director Madhumita begins her story elsewhere — with another boy child in another period who grows up listening to his terrorising, toxic police officer father humiliate him daily. The child can’t eat as much as he wants to, can’t score anything less than first rank, and isn’t even allowed to cry at his mother’s funeral.
As fate would have it, Chandru (Arjun Das) becomes a police officer, a Kerala Police Sub-Inspector in Kadampuzha. He has achieved what his father said he couldn’t, and yet Chandru’s father (Badava Gopi is a great casting choice; his voice becomes a character), even posthumously, has his clutches firmly on his son’s psyche, constantly chiding and shaming him, especially when he feels low or makes mistakes. Credit to Madhumita for how John Doe becomes the story of Chandru proving his father wrong by becoming a good police officer.
It is also about figuring out who he is. He knows he isn’t the person the voice in his head keeps portraying him to be; if so, who is he? In fact, even the film’s title alludes to this. ‘John Doe’ — as a coroner explains — is a term used in American law enforcement to refer to an unidentified male body or patient (‘Jane Doe’ is for a female). By attempting to identify and seek justice for this young John Doe, who was killed by drowning in a lake in Kadampuzha, Chandru is also identifying who he himself is and seeking justice for the child in him who was slowly killed.
Simultaneously, we follow a new family arriving in Kurinjimedu, Tamil Nadu: Darshana (Srishti Y), a widow, her eight-year-old son Hriday (Nirav S), and teenage daughter Lakshmi, a.k.a. Lucky (Zaara Vineet Chandhokhe). One evening, Hriday goes missing, after which Inspector of Police A Rao (Sanchana Natarajan) begins a missing-person investigation. By initially showing the drowned corpse of a boy who resembles Hriday in Kadampuzha, Madhumita ensures that every additional shot of Hriday, a normal child who just wanted a dog in his new, spacious house, disturbs you. The rest of the film shuttles between Kurinjimedu and Kadampuzha, and these worlds collide when Chandru unearths disturbing details.
First and foremost, if you believe the sole worth of a whodunit or investigative thriller lies in how cleverly it executes its climactic twist or reveals the killer’s identity, John Doe may compel you to rethink. A genre fan would see the pre-intermission twist coming from afar, and the film hardly tries to hide its killer. Though it mostly gets its casting right, in a whodunit, when you see a familiar face amidst a group of non-actors, you tend to look closer, which spoils the fun. A more experienced genre filmmaker could have done it differently to drive home the fact that anyone can commit crimes.
Such predictability aside, John Doe would compel your attention and keep you hooked throughout its runtime. Madhumita excels in the little moments between the dramatic spikes in the narrative. The nuances and the sensitive writing are what you might take home with you. Watch how a couple takes the news of the death of their child. Their son had gone missing five years ago, and Madhumita tells you what the psyche of such parents would be like — they don’t scream and wail as you might expect; the mother, who had held on to hope, struggles far more than the father, who had long accepted grief. Similarly, you will see a child suffering from trauma wanting a family member to accompany him into a psychologist’s room — because, to him, the doctor too is a stranger, and he doesn’t wish to go anywhere alone with him after what has happened to him. Now, also see how sensibly the psychologist (Karthik Kumar) behaves, in contrast to the hot-blooded cops. We wish more filmmakers had this emotional aptitude.
‘John Doe’ (Tamil)
The film’s genre pleasures include how Chandru and A Rao, a unique buddy-cop duo, also become metaphorical parental figures to the children of this world. Chandru is so attached to the case that he puts his career in jeopardy; even if she appears stoic, Rao, too, takes this quite personally. Just as you begin to wonder if this is the typical good-cop-bad-cop routine — where the good cop is usually more intelligent and the bad cop more brawny — a superb action scene set in a lodge tells you these two truly complete each other. One follows ‘instincts’, while the other packs a punch — you can never settle on who is who. It also helps that these two actors look the part; Arjun moves like a cop finding his footing, while Sanchana, despite some occasional theatricality, shows immense potential.
Of course, the film takes some liberties with that idea in the second half that don’t work. More subtlety could have helped the film in general, like when it keeps underlining Lucky’s bratty, hormonal teenage personality (here, a line about the goth subculture feels stereotypical, given that the subculture is now far beyond its conventional association with darkness and death).
You are also asked to extend some cinematic liberties for a few nitty-gritty details — like how you don’t understand how the car plunged into the lake in Kadampuzha at that speed, or how Chandru failed to notice the culprit. Also, this could have been a far more atmospheric thriller, had the film taken these characters through these hillside towns more often instead of the few locations the plot circles (cutting between two similar-looking police stations also disturbs the immersion at times).
Now, if this film still manages to steer through all these flaws, it is because of how resolute the writing feels in giving its viewers an engaging experience. Which is why, when I realised that John Doe might have a sequel, I wasn’t all that sceptical (given it is a trend to end films with a hint at a sequel to aid potential franchising). It seems like Chandru and Rao are just starting, and Madhumita is testing the waters in a genre she is not too used to making films in.
In cinema, it is unfair how filmmakers are often weighed against their last film. But I must confess that having two Madhumita directorials released in the same month meant that I still carried the aftertaste of Love Always before entering John Doe. You might too, if you watched that JioHotstar series. However, all works of art deserve an objective, discerning audience, and this John Doe deserves its attention.
Contrary to its title, this film isn’t suffering from an identity crisis. It knows what it wants to be, and it puts in the effort to become that. Such cinema is worth rooting for any day.

NEW DELHI: A global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted operations across offices as Outlook email, Teams calendars and the tools that connect ChatGPT and Claude to Microsoft's workplace services remained paralysed.
The problem, which started late Thursday (India time), was partially restored on Friday evening though intermittent issues persisted. By late evening in India, Microsoft said mailbox access was improving, and delayed emails were being processed, while stating that it had found no indication of a cyberattack. This was the second disruption since Oct 2025 when MS Azure services faced an eight-hour-long global outage.
Companies that rely on MS services were forced to opt for other alternatives such as Slack, Webex and Zoom to keep their operations going. 
Tata Motors
 Passenger Vehicles cited the outage in a stock exchange filing and shifted its quarterly results webcast with Jaguar Land Rover executives to StreamCart. IBM reportedly moved workplace communication to Slack during the disruption. HDFC Bank told customers on X that its banking services remained available.
Airlines and airport operators said operations continued while email communication with passengers was disrupted. Travellers who bought or changed tickets during the outage had to download them from the airline's website or app if their confirmation email did not arrive. Airport operators said they were unable to send emails. Air India rerouted incoming messages, IndiGo directed passengers needing urgent help to its 6E Skai chatbot, and Akasa Air asked customers to call or use social media.
Overseas, Australia's sanctions office directed urgent enquiries to the phone. In UK, National Pharmacy Association warned that disruption to NHS email could delay prescriptions. On Thursday, Microsoft first flagged trouble accessing work mailboxes in the Americas. In India, complaints picked up mainly as offices opened on Friday.
Microsoft starts reversing recent network change
Outage tracker Downdetector logged around 3,800 Outlook complaints at 10.12am, close to the overnight peak.
“We regret the disruption today’s outage has caused for many of our customers,” Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia, wrote on LinkedIn. “Our global teams continue to work with urgency to resolve the issue.”
The problem centred on Exchange Online, the service that runs workplace email and calendars. Some servers unexpectedly went offline, leaving fewer machines to handle the same workload. 
Some stopped responding again when users reconnected.
Microsoft began reversing a recent network change that coincided with the start of the disruption and was investigating whether it triggered the outage. Teams chats and calls could still work even when calendars and meeting invites failed.
Anthropic said most email, calendar and search requests through Claude’s Microsoft 365 connector were failing. Some users could not open Claude for Outlook, while others had trouble performing mail and calendar tasks. OpenAI said ChatGPT users could have trouble setting up new connections to Microsoft services and that some existing connections were also failing.
Anthropic separately investigated sign-in errors affecting Claude.ai, Claude Code and its developer platform. It began investigating at 3.28pm IST and said at 4.35pm that it had deployed a fix and was monitoring recovery.

The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas. Do parallel universes exist? What would it look like if a pandemic wiped out life as we know it? Is time travel possible?
How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction
The author of Station Eleven talks science, fiction, and doppelgängers.
I host the science podcast Unexplainable, where we often speak to scientists about their attempts to puzzle through life’s greatest mysteries, but academic researchers aren’t the only people wrestling with these concepts.
On the latest episode of the show, I spoke with Emily St. John Mandel, the award-winning author of Station Eleven, about her new book, Exit Party, which grapples with the question of the multiverse. We talked about how she approaches science in her fiction, and how, even if we never get clear answers to some of these strange ideas, they can still help us think deeply about ourselves and our world.
Below is an excerpt from our conversation, edited for clarity and length. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts and Spotify, or watch us on Netflix.
Emily, you are often writing about really interesting scientific ideas. Why do you put these scientific concepts at the heart of the books that you write?
Because they’re so interesting. I don’t have an educational background in science. I didn’t study it in school. I did work in a cancer research lab for years, so I’ve definitely hung out with scientists. I was great with grant budgets. But I could not actually tell you the mechanisms by which microRNA 335 impacts breast cancer metastasis,
Neither can I.
But you know what? Science is interesting to me. I like reading about ideas in the fringes of science. But my understanding is that physicists are more or less evenly split on the question of whether we’re living in a multiverse.
Where do you start with exploring these concepts?
It’s really book by book. Sea of Tranquility was the first book I wrote that had more of a hard sci-fi component, because I do have a time-traveling detective in that book.
And what that came out of was it was the spring of 2020. The pandemic hit. I was promoting The Glass Hotel on Zoom, and I thought that for my own sanity, it might be nice to be immersed in the grand project of a book. That can be good for you sometimes when everything is chaos, like in the early days of a pandemic.
I’ve always loved time travel novels as a reader and a fan. The problem with the time travel narrative, though, is that it falls apart instantly.
What do you mean?
If you think about it for a second, it’s like, if I walk out of this podcast studio and I’m transported back to 1812, was I not always going to walk out of the studio and be transported back to 1812? And doesn’t reality break upon my arrival? That raises other questions like immortality — am I always going round and round in time? The causation gets really complicated and weird.
But I felt like, you know what? I’m going to write whatever I want. So I start writing about my time-traveling detective, and then I run into the time travel narrative problem, the loops and the paradoxes and all the rest of it.
And my solve for that, I thought, “What if I added a whole other layer of science fictional weirdness to try to make that work?” Enter the simulation hypothesis, which is the hypothesis that all of our reality is a simulation. And something I love about that is you can find really smart people convincingly arguing either side.
I thought it was a cool idea, and I realized that I could use that to make time travel work. And so that’s what got me into that little branch of science for Sea of Tranquility.
And then Exit Party, I had an idea about writing about doppelgängers. I’d been thinking about it for years — the idea of a counter life.
Counter life?
The life you did not live, where you moved to a different city or took a different job or married a different person — any of those inflection points. I wondered if doppelgängers could be thought of as a sort of embodiment of a counter life. It’s another you who has lived a different life in a different version of reality. That’s what got me to the multiverse idea. But then I was also thinking, “Okay, well, I’ve thought about the counter life of the individual. What is the counter life of the state?”
And that can be a really interesting thought experiment. There are some very obvious inflection points in our recent history, but every country has them. You know, the election that went a different way or the decision made to go to war or not. A policy that was enacted or not enacted and the fallout from that, and any of those inflection points create a somewhat different country. It was thinking about counter lives and doubling, and that’s what got me to this idea of the multiverse.
You’re talking about these ideas almost like, “It’s a fix to this problem that I created.”
It often is. Exit Party opens with a woman going to a party, two doppelgängers show up, and somebody else disappears. I realized pretty early on, wait a minute, at some point I am going to have to account for where the doppelgängers came from, so in that case, it was definitely a fix. But it was also thinking about the double life of a state — the state that you could live in if things had gone a different direction at some inflection point.
Something that interested me as a thought experiment in writing this book is: How might the tropes of science fiction map onto actual lives? Doppelgängers are very science fictional. But we all have counter lives, so imagine those as the embodiment of the counter life. Or later in the novel, there’s a conversation about time travel. And the character says something to the effect of, “I think if you live long enough, you become a time traveler. It’s like you’re a migrant from another timeline.”
“I want to focus on how people respond in these interesting scenarios I’m putting them in.”
There’s nothing more science fictional than a time traveler. That is the definition of a trope, basically. But that is how adulthood works, or how time works. You learn to navigate the world as an adult, and then you look up one day and realize that world is long gone.
If you’re lucky enough to get to live for a while, if you live into your 80s or potentially even older, that world that you learned is really gone.
You get to a certain point in your life, you look back, and you realize you’re not really looking back at a life singular. It’s really one life after another, isn’t it?
I wanted to express that. You were a different person 10 years ago and living a different life, and I wanted to follow a character, Ari in this case, from one life into another.
I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say, you drop us into a fairly dystopian world.
I mean, I collapse the United States in the first sentence…
I was almost expecting that we were going to enter into another world where we made different choices and everything worked out so wonderfully.
I mean, my wife wishes I would write a utopia.
No, it’s true. I do then present an equally dark vision. I think the key, though, and where I find hope personally in my life, but also in this book, is in transience — this idea that nothing lasts forever and everything ends.
There’s such obvious grief and loss attached to that idea, but I think there’s also a lot of hope. Because if I look at it through the lens of my personal life, the worst moments of my life did not last forever. You move through them, and there’s something else after that. Or if you look at it at a larger scale, the worst moments in your country’s life don’t last forever either.
In the second universe of the book, the authoritarian state, I was thinking in terms of modern-day surveillance states, but I was also thinking about East Germany and the Stasi system of citizen informants.
And you know, here’s where transience and hope intersect. A lot of what I know about them I learned in the DDR Museum in Berlin, because the Stasi are gone. We make museums about them. They’re both fairly dark visions, but in both sides of the book, we are moving through them toward something else.
You won’t always be in a terrible situation. You also won’t always be in a good situation. That’s where the loss comes in.
How did you go about trying to think through what the fractal parallel universes would look like?
I was thinking about that with the character Ari. She’s got this character defect. She’s pulled toward criminality. It’s this deep, fundamental proclivity that she has, and there’s a world where somebody like that just goes toward criminality and becomes a criminal, as she did in a previous part of her life.
But what if that same person were growing up in a much more repressive state where the consequences were much worse for breaking the rules? Maybe that interest in criminality pulls a person toward law enforcement, and it was interesting to think of that as almost two sides of the same coin.
When you’re borrowing these scientific concepts, do you feel trapped by the science of it all? Do you feel like you have to stay within certain boundaries?
I don’t, which may annoy some readers of sci-fi, but I think there’s a really interesting choice that you have to make if you’re writing speculative fiction, and that’s how accurate do you want to be, or how deep into the weeds do you want to go with your science fictional technology?
On one end of the spectrum, you’ve got an author like Cixin Liu, who wrote The Three-Body Problem. I really love his work. He gets so granular about those technologies. When I first started working on Sea of Tranquility, I thought, “I want to figure out how the time machine works.” I guess it was a bit of insecurity on my part. So I spent some time reading about current ideas and technologies that I imagine eventually evolving into time traveling. I was reading about the quantum blockchain, and then after I’d spent a bit of time in that rabbit hole, I realized I don’t actually care.
I had this realization: If I’m not describing how a car engine works in the 2020 section, why do I care about the mechanics of the time machine? It’s literally just transport.
And that was kind of liberating, realizing that I care more about the characters. I want to focus on how people respond in these interesting scenarios I’m putting them in. So honestly, the level of scientific detail I’m aiming for is “plausible within the context of a literary novel,” which is a low bar.
For this parallel universe stuff, did you look into some of the physics debates about this?
A little bit. Like the simulation hypothesis, you can find smart people on either side. I feel very unqualified to participate in the debates.
But as a novelist, I’m like, This is interesting. I can work with this.

A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.
The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.
To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.
Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.
The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.
Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.
While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.

A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the company failed overnight to resolve an issue that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools. The services did seem to be on a slow path to recovery by midmorning on Friday.
“We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft said in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning. The company had said on Thursday evening that its initial attempts to fix the problem were “not taking as expected.”
The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge.
Microsoft has not said yet what caused the outage but has hinted that it was related to cascading server failures inside multiple data centers around the world that shifted too much load onto remaining operational machines.
“We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company wrote in Microsoft 365 Status update on Thursday afternoon. “We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” the company added a few minutes later.
An additional update a few minutes after that noted, “We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”
Microsoft emphasized repeatedly in statements that there was no indication of the outage being caused by a cyberattack.
“This is absolutely going to go down as one of the big ones, up there with the Facebook outage of October 2021,” says Doug Madory, director of internet analysis at monitoring firm Kentik. “We don't know the root cause yet, but it is interesting to break down the traffic by source data center. The recovery came in fits and starts and varied greatly by source, probably due to Microsoft's efforts to bring the service back online.”
A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older company that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.
“What makes this particularly significant is the criticality of the services affected, especially email and communication systems relied upon by government and other essential organisations,” says Swapneel Patnekar, the CEO of Indian web security firm Shreshta IT Technologies. “The impact goes well beyond the inconvenience of a typical service disruption.”
Many observers pointed out on Thursday and Friday that Microsoft has recently shed staff through attrition, layoffs, and buyout offers. The company’s annual filings say it had 223,000 full-time employees on June 30, down from 228,000 at the same time in 2025. Then in July, the company eliminated 9,000 jobs globally, of which 3,200 were cuts related to an overhaul of its Xbox teams. In October, the company reportedly made buyout offers to 60,000 employees, though apparently this was intended to speed attrition, not cull all of those roles.
Then there’s the AI factor. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in April that as much as 30 percent of the code the company is generating is now written using AI in automated tools.
“Satya's recent comments have a much different look today than they did even a week ago,” says Jake Williams, a faculty member at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy. “I don't think we'll ever be able to say that the staff reductions caused this outage, but you'll never convince me that all the tribal knowledge that walked out the door wouldn't have been invaluable in resolving it.”
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Reports of widespread disruption from the Microsoft outage started appearing during the working day on Friday in countries in Asia and Australasia, spreading across the world as more people logged on.
Schools, retail stores, courts, and medical organizations across Australia said everything from exams to health care appointments were disrupted. “Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax,” one person told Australian media. Officials in Japan’s government said its own platforms had been disrupted, and staff were using phones and chat tools as they couldn’t access Outlook.
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.
Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.
Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.
“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”
During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.
Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.
Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president António Costa said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”
The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.
Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.
But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.
Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.
The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.
Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.
The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”
The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.
At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.
Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.
Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday, November 9, 2026.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labelling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.

News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley—including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation, after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned.
As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave.
Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing.
“In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure.
Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol.
The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company.
That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report.
Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate.
Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman.
On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.”
Huang’s resignation left them in shock.
The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure.
The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says.
Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week.
Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision.
Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer.
