And what of Putin?
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
You can see why.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

The incorrectly attributed quote as written above spread online in November. In the real video clip, which was from December 2025, Kirk said, "What I miss the most, what really just hits me hard, is when I'm in the grocery store and I see his hot sauce. I want to buy it." Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot in September 2025, did have a hot sauce company.
In November, social media users claimed that while appearing as a guest on Fox News, Turning Point USA CEO Erika Kirk attempted to promote her late husband's hot sauce brand, purportedly saying, "It's the little things. I miss Charlie when I see his hot sauce on the shelf, which is now available at grocery stores everywhere."
Conservative commentator Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at a Utah Valley University event in what authorities characterized as a targeted attack.
The above quote spread on multiple platforms (archived). Some posts were accompanied by a video clip of Erika Kirk speaking on Fox News. Others featured only an image of her appearing on the Fox News segment.
We found that Kirk never said the quote spreading online in November. Therefore we've rated that the remark was incorrectly attributed to her.
However, Kirk did say something similar on Fox News in December 2025, three months after her husband's death.
While promoting Charlie Kirk's posthumous book, "Stop, in the Name of God," on "Fox & Friends" on Dec. 9, she said (at 7:13):
It's interesting. What I miss the most, what really just hits me hard, is when I'm in the grocery store and I see his hot sauce. I want to buy it. Or — it's the little things. You know, his clothes everywhere.
Charlie Kirk did indeed have a small-batch hot sauce company called Kirk's Hot Sauce, which sold for $8.99 a bottle, according to an archived version of the site, which appeared to be down for maintenance as of this writing.
Some social media users pointed out it was unlikely Erika Kirk would casually see his hot sauce at the grocery store, since it appeared to be sold only in one Florida location.
We called Seed to Table Market, the grocery store in Naples, Florida, that the archived hot sauce website listed as its retailer, and a representative said they were still selling Kirk's Hot Sauce. They could not confirm whether they were the sole retailer.
We reached out to Turning Point USA seeking information about other potential retailers of the hot sauce and will update this story if we receive a response.

Under cofounder Jensen Huang, Nvidia has become the engine for the AI boom — and one of the tech industry’s biggest environmental liabilities. Its sought-after chips have triggered a new wave of water- and chemical-intensive factories, drained power grids from inside massive data centers, and set the stage for a looming e-waste problem.
Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
Nvidia’s environmental footprint extends way beyond its own offices.
Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia clashed with environmental groups seeking to hold the company accountable for its so-called “hidden” emissions. Huang has talked up the idea of using AI to fight climate change while his company’s supply chain emissions ballooned. Nvidia’s investments, meanwhile, have supported the buildout of data centers that have sparked intense backlash for both their local and global impact. Now, after the CEO’s shocking resignation amid a sprawling sex-and-espionage scandal, advocates are urging Nvidia to turn the page.
He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”
“Jensen Huang has failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy, to slow down the unchecked expansion of data centres or to prevent its chips from being deployed in unethical applications like automated warfare,” Avex Li, Greenpeace East Asia’s project lead for AI supply chain campaign, said in a press release Thursday. The organization is now pushing interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing by investing in renewable energy, as well as ensuring its technology is used in a way that “respects human rights.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge.
Huang has projected optimism about how AI can boost the adoption of renewable energy, even as the planet-heating emissions of tech companies — including his own — have grown in the generative AI era. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into A.I. It is the best opportunity we have to get there,” Huang said in a September episode of The Ezra Klein Show, arguing that electricity demand for AI is leading companies to buy more sustainable energy.
In the same interview, however, he admitted data centers will rely on more fossil fuels in the near term, and that building up the infrastructure for AI will likely result in “an enormous amount of pain and suffering.” He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”
Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. It’s an increase of about 9.4 million metric tons of planet-heating pollution, roughly equivalent to the emissions from nearly 25 gas plants over a year. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report.
Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi.
Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture. Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases.
Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. When Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang’s speech at Nvidia GTC in Berlin last month, he responded onstage by saying, “I’ll talk to you guys later … All important issues, but let me get through my keynote.” In the Thursday press release, Greenpeace says Nvidia has yet to meet with Greenpeace despite the organization’s attempts to “seek dialogue” with the company over the past two years.
“One of Huang’s defining legacies is inflating a speculative AI bubble, pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure with little regard for the real-world consequences inflicted on local communities and the climate,” Katrin Wu, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in an email to The Verge. “Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”
“Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”
Beyond Nvidia’s day-to-day operations, Huang threw his weight around as the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies — chumming it up with President Donald Trump and lobbying for the US to allow sales of its powerful chips to China. The company’s influence on the global economy extended beyond chips as it invested in data centers stocking its GPUs.
And with electricity supply often the thorniest bottleneck to building more and bigger data centers, Nvidia’s long tendrils reached into the energy sector as well. NVentures, the company’s venture capital arm, has funded battery recycling company Redwood Materials and startups developing AI tools to optimize power grids and make data centers more responsive to fluctuations in energy demand.
Nvidia joined one of those startups, Emerald AI, along with Google to cofound the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) in September. The alliance advocates for strategies that tech companies promote as ways to keep data centers from overwhelming power grids or raising utility bills for other customers, including generating power on-site and making “flexible” facilities that can pause operations during times of peak energy demand. Notably, some environmental groups argue that those measures might just help data centers come online faster without fully insulating households from the impact that rising electricity demand has on their air quality or utility bills.
Whether Nvidia’s environmental footprint shrinks or expands from here will depend on whoever steps in to fill Huang’s shoes. Over the years, Greenpeace and other environmental groups have pointed out that despite having an outsize impact on the environment, Nvidia doesn’t necessarily come under the same public scrutiny as more consumer-facing brands like Apple or Google. Huang’s exploits have thrust the company into a new kind of spotlight, however, just as data centers increasingly face backlash from nearby communities. Nvidia won’t be able to hide from the glare.

Karnataka’s Health Department is developing a mobile application to track the collection, sale and reuse of used cooking oil, with the objective of preventing its re-entry into the food chain, Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday (November 12).
The application, which is expected to be developed within three months, will create a digital trail from the point at which cooking oil is purchased by hotels and other food business operators to its eventual disposal or transfer to authorised agencies for industrial use, Mr. Khader said.
The initiative is aimed at addressing the illegal diversion of used cooking oil, which is sometimes collected for industrial purposes such as soap manufacturing and biodiesel production but allegedly finds its way back to small hotels and eateries for reuse in cooking.
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Mr. Khader said the Food Safety and Drugs Administration Department would manage the application. All manufacturers and food business operators would be required to register on the platform. The department would initially conduct a trial run in Bengaluru, Mysuru, Mangaluru and Hubballi.
Proposed mechanism
Explaining the proposed mechanism, he said hotels and other establishments would have to enter details of the quantity of fresh cooking oil purchased, its source, and the quantity of used oil generated. They would have to record the identity of the person or agency to whom the used oil was handed over.
The collectors, in turn, would have to upload details of whom they sold the oil to, the quantity transferred, and the amount paid.
“If a hotel uses 500 litres of oil in a month, it must account for the 50 to 75 litres of used oil generated, assuming a 10% to 15% recovery. It must submit details of whom it handed over the used oil to. The person who collects it must record whom they sold it to. The entire chain has to be tracked,” he said.
No reliable data
The Minister said the system was necessary because the department currently lacked reliable data on the movement of used cooking oil and its eventual destination.
Under the proposed arrangement, used oil collected from food establishments would have to be channelled towards authorised industrial uses rather than being sold back to food businesses.
Illegal diversion
Mr. Khader said some agencies authorised to collect used cooking oil for industrial purposes were diverting a portion of it to small hotels.
Explaining the economics behind the diversion, he said collectors could receive around ₹80 for a litre of used oil intended for industrial purposes, while small hotels were willing to pay ₹120 to ₹125 a litre.
“Why would someone sell it for ₹80 when they can get ₹120 by supplying it to a small hotel?”
He pointed out that used cooking oil had several legitimate industrial applications, including the manufacture of soap, biodiesel and aviation fuel. However, the absence of an effective tracking mechanism made it difficult to ensure that oil collected for these purposes did not return to the food market.
The Minister said the Karnataka government would write to the Centre seeking greater flexibility in the regulations governing the reuse and export of used cooking oil, particularly given the demand for it in the aviation fuel sector.
He said the department would eventually explore a system to collect used cooking oil from households as well. “Just as we have a system to segregate and collect wet and dry waste from households, we can eventually establish a mechanism for households to store used cooking oil in cans and hand it over for collection. But this will be a step-by-step process,” he said.

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 50 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, official data showed.
The level of PM2.5 (a major pollutant) in Akshardham was 760.99 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data. This is about 50.73 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic meter for a 24-hour period.
Deepavali 2026: All you need to know about Supreme Court-permitted time slots, green crackers and other directives
PM2.5 (Particulate Matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
The level of PM2.5 in Anand Vihar was 767 micrograms per cubic meter at 11 p.m. on Sunday (November 8, 2026), as per DPCC data — This is about 51.13 times the WHO permissible limit.
The level of PM2.5 in Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium was 702 micrograms per cubic meter, as per DPCC data, which is about 46.8 times the WHO permissible limit.
The overall air quality of Delhi continued to be in the “very poor” category while many parts of the city continued to reel under “severe” air quality.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

India skipper Shreyas Iyer on Friday blamed the change in the pitch conditions for its massive 244-run defeat to New Zealand in the fourth ODI on Friday.
Shreyas admitted the loss was a tough one to take, but vowed to take inspiration from the first two ODIs into the final match of the white-ball leg on Sunday.
New Zealand posted 333 after being put in by stand-in captain Iyer, but India’s batting line-up suffered a spectacular collapse, being bundled out for 89 in 26.4 overs. Pacer Matt Henry ripped through the top order to finish with figures of 6/27.
Shreyas admitted the loss was a tough one to take, but vowed to take inspiration from the first two ODIs into the final match of the white-ball leg on Sunday.
“There was a huge difference between the wickets between innings,” Iyer, who is captaining India in ODIs for the first time, said during the post-match presentation.
“But also credit where it’s due, the way Henry bowled in the right areas right from ball one. I think that was sensational. We tried almost everything in the first innings, the way they were playing on the rise. And we thought that the wicket was better to bat on considering they got 330 after that. Obviously a couple of dropped catches, but that definitely happens in a game.
“But yeah, when we got into the dressing room, we thought that we would be cruising through the chase as well. But the way the ball was seaming in and out, you couldn’t basically decide from inside that this is how I’m going to play. Or even if you saw the wickets, no one threw the wicket away. It was good deliveries.”
The win kept New Zealand’s hopes of levelling the series alive.
“It’s important to forget about this one, obviously, analyze what went wrong in terms of bowling and batting. But at the back of the mind it’s important that we have also won two games. So a lot of inspiration from that one and see to it that we come with a fresh set of mind,” Iyer said.
ALSO READ | New Zealand vs India 4th ODI: Matt Henry’s six-wicket haul powers 244-run win after Will Young’s century
New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner was pleased with his team’s effort, though he felt it had initially fallen short of a competitive total by around 20 runs. The bowlers, led by Henry, made up for it by chipping away with wickets.
“Pretty happy. Didn’t get to bowl again, so pretty happy. Young did his thing and we got a good score despite leaving a few out there. I think we were thinking 360, the intent was great. Maybe if we got 20 more each partnership, we could’ve gotten there but they chipped away with wickets,” he said.
“Henry wanted to play today. With the new ball with a wicket that offers a bit, he’s the best. Will chill tomorrow. Pacers will, I’ll have to come and bowl. Then see what Sunday offers from a pitch and conditions point of view and take it from there.”
Returning to the squad after recovering from a concussion, Henry said he had focused on hitting the right areas and hoped New Zealand could level the series in the fifth ODI.
“Great to be back. Obviously it’s been a funny odd year. So, good to be back here with some one-day cricket,”
On the collision with Devon Conway during training, Henry said: “I think I take a bit of responsibility on that one too. So, not ideal, but it just pushed things back a little bit. But thankfully we’re doing alright now.
Henry struck three times in the opening over, dismissing Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and captain Shreyas Iyer for ducks to leave India reeling at 0 for 3.
“Yeah, it’s quite funny, isn’t it? The wind was so strong and it was keeping things pretty simple, and it’s funny when you’re actually trying to have a simple game plan. A bit of luck as well. One shot a little bit low there too, so maybe the wind pushed me a bit sideways,” Henry said.
“With the way the wind was going, I wasn’t too worried about the swing. So from ball one it was just about trying to have the strengths and bring the stumps in play, really. We knew that there was a small window there with the new ball that you could put the batters under pressure.
“So just trying to be as simple as possible, obviously, and when it moves sharply like that in the first over, when people are facing first ball, it’s pretty tough.”
Henry, however, said he doesn’t want to read too much into his performance as he is aware India remains a formidable side.
“I don’t want to get too carried away. No, they’re a world-class outfit, and I think that’s the message that we were saying right through. They can bat deep, and yeah, look, it’s one game and we’ve got another one coming up soon that hopefully we can level the series.”

Millions of Ebola dollars missing with staff unpaid while virus spreads, charity says
- Published
Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.
A report from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.
It added that in some cases ambulances had run out of fuel.
More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.
MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.
This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.
At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.
The Congolese health minister echoed these concerns, saying that aid agencies were required to provide details of their work so the ministry could provide oversight but that only 22% had done so.
"Our requirement is clear: transparency must be total. The response relies on a single plan, a single budget, and a single coordination," Health Minister Samuel-Roger Kamba said on X., external
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
In its report, external, the charity said: "Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to contain the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets."
It also mentioned Ebola monitoring "surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground".
"Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunctions they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable," said MSF president Javid Abdelmoneim.
One important way of stopping Ebola from spreading is contact tracing - finding all those people who had come into contact with an infected person and putting them into isolation.
"Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic," MSF said, adding that two-thirds of deaths were occurring in communities not treatment centres.
According to British epidemiologist Neil Ferguson, more than half of the cases are going undetected, meaning the outbreak is likely to last another year, reports the Reuters news agency.
MSF also raised concerns over "excessive concentration" of efforts in certain areas at the expense of other areas where needs were more urgent.
It said the response was "too slow" in North Kivu province while Haut-Uélé remained "dramatically overlooked".
In both provinces, MSF observed that teams were "inadequately resourced to respond effectively" with health facilities lacking essential items such as water, chlorine or triage systems.
"This has turned some facilities into new centres of transmission, rather than places of care that contribute to containing the disease," MSF said.
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.
There are very few good roads in the area, making it very hard to travel around.
On Thursday, the UN and government warned that the areas worst affected by Ebola were also suffering from a severe food crisis, with almost 10 million in the region in dire need.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.
On Wednesday, the last person infected with Ebola in Kenya was discharged, marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation.
The Bundibugyo species is relatively rare and has no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel, instead limiting the probe to crimes committed by the Taliban, according to court filings released Friday.
The ruling comes as the court and 13 current and former staff members are under sanctions by the Trump administration, which is opposed to any investigation into American citizens or U.S. allies, such as Israel.
The decision, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence” in the case. It does not elaborate.
The court's prosecutor's office told The Associated Press it has already appealed the decision.
It is not clear if the decision will mitigate Washington's attacks on the court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to “dismantle the ICC — brick by brick, if necessary." The United States is not a member of the court and does not recognize its jurisdiction.
But the U.S. has also taken issue with the ICC's investigation into Israeli officials. The court has outstanding arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as well as his former defense minister, over allegations of crimes against humanity in Gaza. They have strongly rejected the accusations. Judges at the global court authorized an investigation in 2020 covering offenses allegedly committed by Afghan government forces, the Taliban, American troops and U.S. foreign intelligence operatives dating back to 2002. Two years later, then-chief prosecutor Karim Khan chose to “deprioritize” aspects of the investigation that could have involved Americans, citing challenges in obtaining evidence. Khan was ousted over sexual misconduct allegations earlier this year.
The part of the investigation involving the Taliban will be split off into a separate inquiry.
Last month, the court unsealed arrest warrants against four senior Taliban leaders, accusing them of the crime against humanity of gender persecution against women, girls and members of the LGBTQI+ community in Afghanistan since the Taliban seized power in 2021.

Fallout from the Nvidia scandal may dampen the exuberance around the AI boom
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation has sent ripples throughout the global technology industry, with competitors itching to take advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the chip giant

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation has sent ripples through the global technology industry, with rival chipmakers itching to take advantage of the uncertainty and others wondering if the downfall of one of AI's biggest cheerleaders will dampen the mood around the civilization-altering technology.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, was the very public face of a company that dominates the market for computer chips used to train and run AI models. In March, Huang predicted Nvidia will be grappling with a $1 trillion backlog in orders for its chips by the end of the year, doubling his estimate from a year earlier.
A linchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street's most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms.
Some of Nvidia's biggest rivals, such as Broadcom, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, saw their shares advance Thursday following Huang's departure as investors predicted that its customers will look to diversify their suppliers. In the end, analysts say, this might not be a bad thing.
“This could turn what has effectively been a monopoly into a horse race again, as competitors rush to meet growing demand,” said Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at the global consultancy West Monroe. “Nvidia did not create that demand, and a shift in this part of the market could ultimately diversify the supply chain, create more choice for customers and strengthen the broader AI industry in the years ahead.”
Competitor chipmakers and designers see opportunity
Nvidia carved out an early lead in tailoring its chipsets known as graphics processing units, or GPUs, from use in powering video games to helping to train powerful AI systems. Demand soared as tech companies scrambled for more chips to build and run AI systems.
In annual filings, Nvidia has identified competitors including Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, Intel, Broadcom and cloud services companies like Google, Amazon and Microsoft. While these other players are established and respected within the industry for their chips, they have been trying to catch up to Nvidia.
Nvidia has had an advantage from the start and as soon as a competitor releases something just as good, Nvidia has put out the next better chip, said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer of International Services Inc. “Nobody’s just sitting still,” he said.
While some competitors saw bumps to their share prices Thursday, “their gains are going to be smaller than Nvidia’s losses,” said Chester Spatt, a finance professor at Carnegie Mellon University. But Spatt said he also anticipates chip purchasers could also become “much more reluctant to concentrate their purchases with a single source.”
The incident is also sure to prompt elected officials to seek stronger export controls on American-made chips, but that could be a boon for Chinese chipmaker Huawei, another Nvidia competitor. Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, said she suspects Chinese AI firms could accelerate efforts to secure overseas computing capacity ahead of tighter controls.
“Chinese chipmakers have already rallied on Nvidia’s troubles, but China’s AI developers depend heavily on Nvidia’s ecosystem,” she said. “This could be both an opportunity and a headache for China.”
Huang has had an outsized role as AI evangelist
While Huang is not the only face of AI — OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google's Demis Hassabis and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton are among the others — he's been an influential one. A celebrity-level industry evangelist with President Donald Trump's ear and support, he has advocated for a light touch on AI regulation and has been bullish about AI’s potential to transform society, creating faster economic growth and more scientific breakthroughs.
“Jensen Huang’s resignation is a watershed moment for Nvidia, which now has to prove it can maintain its AI dominance without the leader largely responsible for building it,” said Asa Hiken, a senior analyst for research firm eMarketer. “And given the broader AI industry’s heavy dependence on Nvidia’s chips, Huang’s departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself.”
Lee, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said the resignation fallout will ripple across the AI ecosystem.
“Obviously Nvidia’s technological leadership won’t disappear, but Huang had played an outsized role as its chief strategist, dealmaker and — very importantly — political advocate, with close access to both Washington and Beijing,” she said. “This happens at a critical juncture when markets are already questioning the sustainability of massive AI spending.”
Nvidia’s ‘circular financing’ deals spread the risk
Huang’s relationships across the tech landscape translated into Nvidia’s numerous partnerships and investments into companies that purchase its chips. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO turned interim CEO, has been a key force behind that strategy, but that approach is under closer scrutiny as the scandal and resignation have rattled the market.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, closed down almost 7% on Thursday. Nvidia holds a nearly 13% stake in the company.
Leadership within companies across the tech sector likely spent much of Thursday in meetings aiming to figure out a “backup plan” for some of their financing, Aldebert said. He described the circular financing practice as “incestuous.”
Many experts will be keeping a keen eye on what Huang’s departure and its fallout mean for pending public debuts of AI companies like Anthropic’s pending IPO, valued at $1.3 trillion.
It also comes in the wake of midterm elections marked by hostility toward data centers, ushering in many Democrats promising aggressive stances on AI regulation.
“This is all very interconnected and I think that we’re going to see a lot interesting dynamics happening the next month as it plays out,” said Greenstein, of West Monroe.

GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.
In a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That’s around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.
Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.
Modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common among those using compounded versions of GLP-1 medications. Among all GLP-1 users, at least 23 percent used a compounded version; an additional 9 percent said they didn’t know whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

Only between a quarter and a third of people currently diagnosed with obesity should be considered as in poor health, according to a new study that joins calls to overhaul how the condition is diagnosed.
The study, published in Nature on Wednesday, follows a proposal last year from experts and medical organisations to move obesity diagnosis beyond just body mass index (BMI), based on a person’s weight and height, to include body fat and broader health.
The study attempts to show what this new definition could mean for diagnosis levels, prevalence, and ultimately, treatment, for a condition the World Health Organization currently estimates affects more than one billion people globally.
Obesity can be a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease and cancer. The study suggests defining it as pre-clinical, when the condition is largely a risk factor, and clinical, when it is causing ill health.
Waist circumference should be part of diagnosis, study says
Using data from almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the study estimates that under the new framework, 1% to 3% of those defined as obese using BMI alone would not be, while another 5% to 9%, with higher body fat for example, would be diagnosed with the condition. Across a population, this could affect tens of millions of people.
The study’s senior author Francesco Rubino, professor and chair of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London, said the inaccuracy of BMI measurements was well-known.
“But we haven’t so far got a better system,” he said. That is what the new framework aims to do, he added, saying it could “provide a meaningful clinical characterisation of obesity that can inform care and policy.”
The new framework proposes measuring body fat, including by waist circumference, as well as BMI, and considering if a patient has any organ dysfunction linked to weight, like heart or liver problems, before making a diagnosis.
This means some people with high BMI alone would not be classed as having obesity. Those who have high body fat and high BMI would be diagnosed with “pre-clinical obesity”, and those who also have organ dysfunction would have “clinical obesity” – considered an active disease that would usually require more urgent treatment.
Under these criteria, only on average roughly 27% of people with obesity across the four studied countries have clinical obesity, the study estimated – representing around 8.5% of all adults.
The majority of those with “pre-clinical obesity” – around 82% on average across the four countries studied – did not progress to clinical obesity, although progression rates were higher in China and Spain, the study found.

Saud Shakeel missed out on a century for the second successive time but his gritty 97 foiled Sri Lanka's push for a win on the fifth and final day in the drawn first cricket test against Pakistan on Friday.

Shakeel, who made 93 in Pakistan's first innings of 434-9 declared, dug in for almost entire final day before he was bowled by Lahiru Kumara after facing 210 balls late on the fifth and final day.
By that time, the home team had reached 284-8 for an overall lead of 272 as the players shook hands and the match was called off.
Sri Lanka's pace bowlers had rattled the top order under overcast conditions in the first session by reducing Pakistan to 125-5, but Shakeel showed lot of temperament and shared a match-saving 92-run stand with Ghazi Ghori, who made 35, to deny Sri Lanka unlikely win.
Milan Rathnayake (3-47), Asitha Fernando (2-35) and Kumara (2-65) had given Sri Lanka a sniff before Shakeel stood firm and saved Pakistan from going down in the two-test series.
The second test will be played at the same Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium from next Tuesday after it was relocated to Rawalpindi due to increase in the smog level at Lahore.
Steely Shakeel stands firmPakistan's batters had stumbled against Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis' innovative field setting in the first session which was disrupted by 20-minute stoppage of play due to bad light.
Skipper Babar Azam scored 34 and Salman Ali Agha made 13 before both fell into Mendis' fielding trap and offered catches at short backward square leg on a second successive overcast morning at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium, where 117 overs were lost due to bad light and rain during the first four days.

Babar added 50 runs with the defiant Shakeel and struck six boundaries with his trademark cover drives and straight drives but yet again couldn't convert a good start into big innings as his century drought in test matches was extended to 42 innings.
Babar also survived two chances. Kamindu Mendis grassed a regulation chance in the second slip when Babar was on 22 and then had a close lbw call go in his favor on an umpire's call before he fell into Mendis' trap and gave a simple catch to Lahiru Udara.

Swabbing public transport to identify urban microbiomes, a city’s microbial signature
A recent study in the Chennai Metro Rail showed a wide range of microbes found on high-touch surfaces, though researchers said there was no cause for fear and no immediate reason to act
A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters. Photograph used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: JOTHI RAMALINGAM B
From waste-water surveillance to public transport surfaces, mankind is constantly on the lookout for diverse microbial sources to test, to understand anti-microbial resistance patterns in a particular society. The latest in the urban transport systems sweep, performed at Chennai Metro Rail stations, showed that Chennai had a distinctive ‘transit biome’ - influenced by the city’s coastal climate, humidity, urban density and relatively nearby agricultural activity.
A team of researchers from IIT Madras swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains on Chennai Metro’s Blue and Green Lines in December 2021 and January 2022, targeting four high-touch surfaces: station handrails (bannisters), ticket-vending kiosks, train handrails (rods), and ticket counters. The team swabbed 96 samples from 12 stations and trains and after quality control, 47 samples were sequenced using whole-genome metagenomic sequencing. Metagenomics is defined as the direct genetic analysis of genomes contained with an environmental sample.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths in 2021, highlighting the need for coordinated action across human, animal, and environmental health sectors, experts said at the sixth Global Media Forum on AMR.
Speaking ahead of World AMR Awareness Week (November 18-24), Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, Director ai-AMR Department, World Health Organization (WHO), and Director, Quadripartite Joint Secretariat on AMR, said gaps in financing, surveillance, and coordination continued to hamper global efforts. “Behind these numbers are patients, families, farmers, and communities,” he said, stressing that global commitments should translate into results on the ground.
The updated Global Action Plan on AMR for 2026-2036 seeks to strengthen prevention, surveillance, responsible antimicrobial use and sustainable financing. World leaders have committed to reducing bacterial AMR-associated deaths by 10% by 2030.
Junxia Song, deputy chief veterinarian and chief of the One Health and Disease Control Branch, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), said antibiotic use in livestock could increase by nearly 30% by 2040 without intervention. Better animal health and farm management practices could reduce use by up to 57%.
Aitziber Echeverria, AMR coordinator, Chemicals and Health Branch, United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), called for action against environmental pollution, including antimicrobial residues in wastewater.
Kefas Samson, senior technical officer and lead of multisectoral coordination, AMR Department, WHO headquarters, highlighted gaps in diagnostics, surveillance and access to quality-assured antimicrobials. Jane Lwoyero, programme officer, World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), stressed the importance of vaccination and farm biosecurity.
Shobha Shukla, chairperson, Global AMR Media Alliance (GAMA), and host of the forum, called for a person-centred, rights-based and gender-transformative approach to tackling AMR.
The forum also recognised 56 journalists and media professionals as Global AMR Media Awardees 2026 for their contributions to reporting on antimicrobial resistance.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Samsung’s latest Galaxy Z Fold 8 ad mocks Apple’s iPhone Duo at a difficult time. Reports of cracked displays, long delivery delays, and missing features have raised concerns about Apple’s first foldable. With its reputation for hardware excellence at stake, Apple needs more than silence to restore confidence.
Believe it or not, Samsung might finally have landed an ad glove on Apple. While the two brands have been taking digs at each other for years, Apple has kept things subtle, while Samsung has never been shy about being more direct. So when Apple finally decided to join the foldable race with the iPhone Duo, it was hardly surprising to see Samsung going all out against its rival – from Apple’s late arrival to the foldable party, the Duo name, the features, the price, you name it, and Samsung probably has tried to make fun of it. But as in the past, these attempts seemed just that… attempts to ruffle a leading brand on a perceived weakness, and to reassure their own fanbase. But very recently, we think Samsung struck a bit of a serious nerve in the Apple nervous system.
The Samsung Z Fold 8 slices up an apple (no, really!)
Samsung released a 32-second video on Instagram that shows an apple (duh) with a “new” sticker on the open screen of the Galaxy Z Fold8. The phone folds, and the apple gets sliced. This slice rolls down the floor, through all the old versions of the Z Fold in the past to show how many foldables Samsung launched before Apple made its first.
The video also boasts about the Z Fold 8 being thinner and lighter than the iPhone Duo, all while comparing it to a slice of apple. This is not the most clever or cinematic Apple attack we have ever seen, but it is entertaining and thankfully is not over the top (unlike some others). What it also is, is a direct jab at something that Apple rarely has had to face – a perceived hardware problem with the iPhone.
iPhone Duo: from potential elixir to possible albatross
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, we thought it would be just the thing the foldables needed. Foldables have been a regular part of tech news and product portfolios since pre-COVID times (the first Galaxy Z Fold came in 2019), but even after years of iterations and multiple devices from multiple brands, the foldable segment was actually running out of steam.
So, when Apple launched the iPhone Duo, we thought that foldables would finally get some serious momentum. After all, once Apple launches something (even if it has been in the market for some time), it usually becomes more desirable and eminently “inspirational” for the competition: we have seen new features, specs, and design get picked up by the competition from Apple products, and become mainstream. From accepting touch to rejecting 3.5 mm audio jacks, it has all happened. So you could hardly blame many for thinking that Apple would launch a foldable phone, and voila! All foldable phones would start selling like hotcakes.
That scenario, however, does not seem to be playing out.
When Apple launched the iPhone Duo, the tech world went abuzz, which is business as usual when a new iPhone launches. But when the iPhone Duo became available for purchase, all the news that came in was not good. In many markets, due to supply and production issues, consumers had to wait for two months or more to get a device even after paying an advance. The brand’s decision to limit sales to two devices per person was also not well-received in some markets. It would have been understandable in the case of a new brand launching its first product, but from the first trillion-dollar company in the world, it just seemed unusually odd. The fact that it came with a super premium price tag did not help matters.
All those who have got their hands on Apple’s first foldable phone have not been thoroughly impressed with it either. There has been talk of users missing the speed and convenience of Face ID, the lack of app optimization, the new placement of the status bar, and more. And as if that were not enough, there was news that landed Apple in perhaps the hottest soup it has been in a very long time – reports have started coming in of the internal display cracking at the hinge, and a line of dead pixels appearing on it.
Often coming late to the party and rocking it…but perhaps not this time!
Once again, such problems from a new brand’s first product might have been treated with more patience. But imagine spending Rs. 2,99,900 and getting a device whose display has hardware issues. Imagine also being a person who has booked the device and is waiting for their unit, which is two months away. While Apple has acknowledged the issue, insisted that the issues exist in a small number of devices, and has assured users that all devices facing the issue will be replaced, a lot of damage has been done.
Apple’s reputation has, in some ways, worked against it. With Apple, the tech world has become accustomed to waiting for features, functions, and form factors that were seen on other devices. Android users have mocked Apple fans for getting the features that were on Android after years. But while Apple has delayed the addition of a feature or an entry into a segment, it has generally delivered an excellent performance. And that has been the defense of many Apple fans – Apple might not be the first to make a certain kind of device or bring a certain feature, but its implementation (whether it was capacitive touchscreens, Touch ID, App Store, and more) has been excellent and often an industry benchmark.
With Duo, that belief is being rocked. The brand has stepped into the foldable zone almost seven years after others, and launched a device with what seems to be a hardware flaw– not a software bug that can be fixed with an update, but a problem that can only be fixed with replacement.
Is silence golden for the communication wizard?
Apple’s handling of the issue so far has been a little unusual. The brand has found itself in trouble in the past as well with issues such as Antennagate and Bendgate, both of which generated a storm of criticism. But Apple officially addressed those issues publicly – Steve Jobs himself came out with an explanation in the case of the iPhone 4 when its stainless steel band interfered with the phone’s cellular performance, and the company also issued a very detailed statement on BendGate, famously pointing out that the issue had occurred with only nine users.
While there has not been radio silence from Apple with regard to Duo’s screen, no major management figure has come out to explain the issue or build back confidence – even in his first earnings call, new Apple CEO John Ternus limited himself to saying that while the issue existed, it affected a very small percentage of units. This relative silence could be (mis)interpreted by many in the public. To many, it does not seem as if the brand is working out solutions, as it has actually been launching devices left, right, and center since the Duo was launched.
To see management showcasing new products and talking of record earnings, even while complaints trickle in about a high-profile flagship does not make for great optics. We hope that changes soon, or alternatively, Apple comes out with a strong defense of its first foldable – it needs it. The longer it keeps silent, the more space it gives to its competitors to score points off its perceived weakness. And Apple cannot really afford to let cracks develop not just on the Duo, but in its own reputation for hardware excellence. As Samsung has shown, its competitors will not hang back in taking potshots at it. And unless credibly explained, these shots will start to hurt.
Given its potential and the hype around it, the Duo could still prove to be the elixir the foldable sector needs, but Apple needs to address the issues around it swiftly and effectively. This is a challenge unlike any other the brand has faced in recent times. Even the relative failure of the Vision Pro was more about a product being too futuristic (almost a prototype of sorts for an elite audience). The Duo, however, is supposed to redefine how we use foldables in particular and even smartphones in general. Many have even called it Apple’s most radical iPhone since the OG iPhone. How John Ternus tackles the issues surrounding the Duo could well define the tone of his tenure.

As Yellowjackets reaches its final destination after four seasons, many fans are still curious about an episode that never made it to air.
While discussing Season 4 of the supernatural survival thriller, which premieres Nov. 20, co-creators Bart Nickerson and Ashley Lyle shed some light on the unreleased bonus episode for Deadline after it was intended to air following Season 2.
“I mean, ultimately, the canon of the show is sort of what’s aired, and for us, the fourth season is like the final installment of a complete story,” explained Nickerson. “And so, along the way of the making of it, there were lots of paths considered and things like that were explored, but I think ultimately, the final version of the show is what it was supposed to be.”
Lyle first confirmed the bonus episode’s existence on social media in June 2023, days after the Season 2 finale, responding to a fan’s post stating they’re “staying up a couple hours late” in the off chance the then-rumored episode would make a surprise midnight drop.
Watch on Deadline
“Noooo. Go to bed! Get some rest!” wrote Lyle on X at the time. “There will be a bonus episode between seasons, but I love you guys and I don’t want y’all to lose sleep thinking it’s tonight.”
Although photos circulated on social media of series star Melanie Lynskey’s husband Jason Ritter filming on set for Season 2 after his casting was announced, the episode never aired, leaving the season with only nine episodes instead of the 10 every other season has received.
Behind-the-scenes images of Ritter led fans to believe his character would be the mysterious “Cabin Guy,” whose skeleton the team discovers in the cabin, along with his plane in the woods. Liverpool and Van Dijk have a decision to make
- Published
After Liverpool beat Brighton in October, Virgil van Dijk went upstairs to the Boardroom at Anfield and met up with Alan Hansen.
It was Van Dijk who, at the end of the 2024-25 season, asked the former Liverpool and Scotland defender to present him with the Premier League trophy and this time they posed for a picture that inevitably did the rounds on social media.
Whenever the time comes for Van Dijk to move on from Liverpool, he will go down as arguably their greatest centre-half, alongside Hansen. The question now is whether he will finish his career at Anfield like Hansen did in 1991.
Van Dijk's contract expires next summer and, even if the 35-year-old insisted this week that he was in no panic, it is a topic that will be a source of debate until a decision is made.
"Let's see what the season brings. I've had an amazing time already so far. If that will be extended, that's the case. If not, then I will go somewhere else," the Liverpool captain told reporters at Selhurst Park.
Two seasons ago, with Van Dijk in a similar situation, there was a similar sense of calm and come April 2025 he signed a two-year-deal.
Judging by Van Dijk's comments there is a feeling of him wanting to stay, but both he and Liverpool have an important decision to make.
Liverpool keen to avoid Salah repeat
Aside from a poor error against Villarreal in the Champions League, Van Dijk has shown this season that his standards haven't dropped.
His partnership with Jeremy Jacquet, who joined in the summer, is going from strength to strength and Van Dijk has played every minute in the Premier League since the start of last season.
A "little niggle" has affected him in recent weeks and this is the first international window he has missed with the Netherlands since Euro 2020, but it isn't a major cause for concern.
Liverpool have lost a number of senior figures in recent years but Van Dijk remains a leader in every form, and that was evidenced by his suggestion to Andoni Iraola that the squad should visit the museum at Anfield to learn more about the club's history.
At Crystal Palace on Sunday, it spoke volumes of Van Dijk's character that he came over to a group of reporters and asked if they wanted to speak to him, rather than the other way around. He regularly fronts up, regardless of the result.
Van Dijk is certainly not the force he was under Jurgen Klopp but he remains an elite centre-half and the stats justify that.
Per 90 minutes this season in the Premier League, he averages 60.7 successful passes per game, wins possession 3.5 times and makes 7.1 clearances. He has a 75% success in duels and 79% when it comes to aerial duels.
In his first full season at the club, in 2019-20, he averaged 72.4 successful passes per game, won possession 5.1 times and made 5.3 clearances. He had a 76% success in duels and 75% when it came to aerial duels.
That said, the Liverpool hierarchy will have seen the way the situation with Mohamed Salah unfolded last year and will be keen to avoid a repeat. After a stellar season in 2024-25, Salah's numbers plummeted in 2025-26.
Liverpool have a number of young centre-backs within their ranks, from Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni to the likes of Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye, but letting Van Dijk go would be a risk and leave a gaping hole.
He didn't take a pay cut in 2025 and continues to earn a salary understood to be in the region of £400,000 a week.
Joe Gomez, 29, is also out of contract this summer and Liverpool do have an option to buy Ronald Araujo, 27, at the end of the season from Barcelona but there would be a clear loss of experience and leadership if Van Dijk leaves.
For sporting director Julian Ward, the future of the Dutchman will be a priority over the coming months.
No resolution to contract talks expected soon
Providing he is fit, Van Dijk will make his 390th appearance for Liverpool when they take on Manchester United after the international break.
And given his consistency, he is likely to reach 400 appearances by the end of the year. He would become only the 28th Liverpool player to do so.
The 36 goals he has scored for Liverpool is the most for a defender at the club.
In terms of a resolution with his contract, this is likely to be one where both parties bide their time and, given that the existing relationships are strong and there's a mutual respect, it would not be a surprise to see negotiations go into 2027.
Come January, Van Dijk will be able to sign a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club and as such, AC Milan and Juventus are monitoring the situation.
Sources in Turkey are also hopeful that they could tempt him to make the same move as Salah if an extension isn't agreed at Liverpool but, as it stands, it would be quite a surprise if Van Dijk moved on this summer.

The investigation started with a tip from a British couple.
After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “three-parent IVF,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person.
In the U.K., MRT is allowed at only one academic medical center, and only for the purposes of lowering the risk of passing on mitochondrial disease. But according to IFG, the procedure could also help older women overcome issues that make the odds of IVF go down significantly after the age of 40. Despite being a doctor herself, the woman in the couple had been taken in by the hope of a miracle.
Her husband reached out to me concerned the claims were unfounded, and hoping STAT could look into it.
Over the past eight months, my reporting took me inside an emerging international MRT tourism industry. It led me to IFG’s headquarters in an office park outside of Chicago and to one of its partners in Albania, an upscale fertility clinic where a Turkish embryologist living in Slovakia would fly in monthly to perform the procedure on IFG clients’ eggs or embryos. With the help of an Albanian journalist, Inva Hasanaliaj, we dug into corporate registration and medical licensing records. Freelance science reporter Edward Chen helped us to gather the stories of current and former IFG clients and interview scientists, including the world’s top MRT researchers.
All of this reporting was undertaken in an effort to understand what is driving demand for this unproven procedure, what risks women are taking to seek it out, and how commercial claims stack up against the science. Here’s what we found.
Evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking
Currently, there are no peer-reviewed studies in humans supporting the idea that MRT can overcome infertility issues caused by aging, especially in women 35 years and older. A pilot study from a fertility clinic in Greece, published in 2023, reported that MRT could improve live birth rates for women under the age of 40, but the biggest improvements occurred among the youngest patients. For the 12 patients who were 39 at the time of MRT, the live birth rate was less than 10%.
Researchers affiliated with IFG did present some data in a conference abstract for a 2025 European scientific meeting, claiming that among 66 patients with a mean age of 39, live birth rates following MRT reached rates of 40% or higher. But scientists told STAT the abstract lacked key information required to support that claim, and a conference organizer questioned whether it should have been accepted.
The most compelling evidence it might work in older women comes from a single lab study in mice. But even the underlying hypothesis that mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to age-related infertility is supported by very little direct evidence, experts told STAT.
And, in fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age
Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv was poised to become the MRT capital of the world. Women traveled from Europe, Israel, and the U.S. to at least three clinics there offering it as an infertility treatment. Unpublished data from the Nadiya Clinic — the most advanced operation in Kyiv — shows that a form of MRT called pronuclear transfer did not improve the odds of IVF for older women. Among 19 patients aged 36 to 44, only one gave birth to a baby following pronuclear transfer.
In contrast, among 10 infertile patients under the age of 35, MRT resulted in nine live births.
That hasn’t stopped reproductive tourism agencies and fertility clinics overseas from marketing MRT to older women
For the past few years, International Fertility Group has advertised its MRT program as “a groundbreaking fertility treatment that offers renewed hope to women with advanced maternal age or a history of failed cycles.” The company’s social media posts about MRT frequently targeted women over the age of 35, and its own internal data showed its clients were skewing older. According to an IFG webinar from February, the average age of a patient in the company’s MRT program was 39.2 years old in 2022; last year it was 45.6 years old.
After STAT contacted IFG about these materials, which several experts described as “misleading” and “unethical,” the company removed them. In a statement, IFG acknowledged that the evidence for MRT remains limited and emphasized that its role is to provide nonmedical support to patients. “IFG does not characterize innovative treatment as guaranteed, routine, or risk-free,” the statement said. “Patients are not promised a pregnancy, a live birth, or any particular outcome.”
The company’s MRT program is currently on pause. Last week, hours after STAT’s investigation was published, Birol Aydin, the Turkish embryologist who performed the procedure for IFG clients in Albania, announced on LinkedIn that he was stepping back from clinical work to focus on research.
Clinics unaffiliated with IFG operating in Mexico and the Bahamas are continuing to market MRT as a fertility treatment to women 40 and older as a way to combat age-related declines in egg quality. Neither has published any outcome data.
Bioethicists worry about patients being misled and possible health risks for resulting children
The concerns are twofold. First, that companies are profiting from selling false hope to people with a strong desire to try everything possible to have genetically related children. And second, that children born through commercial MRT won’t be monitored for any adverse health effects that might emerge later in their lives.
Scientists still see promise that it could work better than conventional IVF for some forms of infertility in younger women
Data from the Nadiya Clinic underscore similar results from that 2023 pilot study in Greece, showing that a different form of MRT, called maternal spindle transfer, could help women under the age of 35 with a history of severe infertility get pregnant and have children.
Researchers at Ghent University are currently launching a small study of MRT for addressing these types of fertility failures, which collectively are called OZEMA (for oocyte, zygote, and embryo maturation arrest). Initial results are expected sometime next year. Positive outcomes would add to the increasing pressure to ease restrictions on human trials of MRT for infertility in countries where such studies are currently banned, including the U.S., so that people don’t have to go abroad.
