The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 combines a stylish translucent design with smooth linear switches, a compact 75% layout, multi-device connectivity, and excellent battery life. It’s great for everyday typing, but limited customization, closely packed keys, and a premium price may put some buyers off.
ASUS has a wide range of product categories, and its mechanical keyboards are quite popular among gamers.
ASUS also offers standard mechanical keyboards for regular users. The company recently sent us its recently announced Jelly75 keyboard for review. It features a 75% layout, a unique translucent design, and multi-device connectivity. The keyboard also comes with a slightly higher price tag of Rs 7,999 (US $129.99)
I have been using this keyboard for the past several days, and in this review, you will learn everything about the keyboard, including the good and the bad things, and also learn if this Jelly75 keyboard is worth the price for what it offers.
Table of Contents
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review: Design, Typing Experience, and Everyday Use
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Unboxing
You get a fairly simple package when you unbox the ASUS Jelly75 KD201. Inside, you find the keyboard, a USB-A to USB-C cable, a 2.4GHz wireless receiver, a quick start guide, and warranty documentation.
However, ASUS doesn’t provide a keycap puller or even a switch puller out of the box.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Design and Build Quality
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard is available in two colors: Volt Green and Orange Meadow. I received the Volt Green variant of the Jelly75, which comes with a translucent chassis and a combination of white, black, and mint green keys. This color combination makes it very attractive for a vibrant and unique desktop setup.
If you don’t like contrasting looks, the Orange Meadow color variant, which offers muted colors and a retro-looking design, is the best choice, which I personally prefer.
But the Volt Green variant also looks good in person and stands out more than the regular black-and-white finishes on most mechanical keyboards.
The standout feature on both variants is the translucent design, so you can see parts of the internal keyboard structure through the casing.
However, the body and keys are made of polycarbonate, but it’s solidly built, and the weight adds extra rigidity.
The steel plate inside the keyboard adds to its weight, bringing it to about 1.19 kg.
While the weight helps the keyboard stay stable during typing, it can be inconvenient if you plan to carry it often.
Since the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard uses a 75% layout, it measures about 326.2 x 142.1 x 39.5 mm, which takes up less space than traditional full-size keypads but more than smaller percentage keypads.
If you are not familiar with keyboard percentages, here is a detailed visual guide we created to help you understand different keyboard layouts.
The keys are densely packed together, and there is not much space between them; also, there is no gap between functional keys and the regular keys, especially around the arrow key cluster, where, until you get used to this layout, there is a high chance that you can accidentally mispress the other keys.
Also, the keyboard doesn’t have any knobs, which would have been a nice addition for direct volume control. Additionally, the Caps Lock key doesn’t come with any light indication to show it’s active.
The rubber pads on the bottom help it stay stable and in place without sliding on a smooth desk surface.
The keyboard also comes with adjustable kickstands that let you set three typing-angle positions.
While the design is attractive, the translucent, lighter-colored keycaps make dirt more visible. It also supports a wireless receiver, but the keypad doesn’t have a dedicated compartment to store it, which is inconvenient, especially if you plan to carry it between workspaces. It won’t be much of a concern if you plan to connect it via Bluetooth, but it’s something you should know.
Continuing with the design, you will find the ASUS logo on the bottom right, a toggle to switch between connection types on the top, and a USB-C charging port on the top left.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Keyboard Layout and Ergonomics
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 uses a 75% keyboard layout, which is a sweet spot between portability and functionality.
Unlike smaller 60% or 65% layouts, it includes a function row at the top and navigation keys on the right.
However, it doesn’t include a separate number pad, which full-size keyboards often have.
This compact layout has all essential keys and doesn’t miss anything, especially if you are coming from notebooks or a Mac.
This layout works for writing, programming, office work, and even standard gaming.
Although you get a dedicated number row below the function keys, a dedicated number pad is still more convenient, especially if your work involves entering numbers regularly.
However, the keys are densely packed, with negligible gaps between them.
ASUS has also included a dedicated Copilot key near the arrow key cluster, which could accidentally launch Windows Copilot, especially until you get used to this densely packed layout.
In terms of key design, ASUS used tall, squarish-rounded keycaps instead of the flatter options found on many keyboards.
While this makes them look unique, it may take time to get used to, especially if you are switching from a MacBook or another low-profile keyboard.
Since these keys are taller, I recommend a separate wrist rest, especially if you plan to use the keyboard lying flat.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Switches, Keycaps and Typing Experience
Typing experience is one of the most important things to consider when buying a mechanical keyboard, since you spend several hours every day writing, coding, or working on documents.
The ASUS Jelly75 comes with linear mechanical switches that offer 4mm of total key travel.
However, you won’t get tactile feedback when you press the keys. Unlike tactile switches, which have a noticeable bump when pressed, the Jelly75’s linear mechanism presses the keys gently, creating a smooth typing experience.
I personally prefer tactile feedback because I am used to my MacBook keyboard, but many also prefer smooth switches for longer typing sessions.
ASUS also rates the switches at 50 million keystrokes, which should last longer with regular use.
The keyboard also offers a gasket-mounted structure. ASUS calls it Uni-cushion technology, where it uses cushioning between the internal keyboard layout assembly and the outer body to help absorb vibrations.
This is especially useful if you press the keys harder, as the chassis absorbs vibration and stays steady overall.
The keycaps have a rigid feel. You won’t get rattling, wobbling, or uneven keypresses even on the larger keys like the spacebar.
As a mechanical keyboard, the ASUS Jelly75 offers hot-swappable switches, so you can remove and replace individual switches without soldering.
If you prefer tactile switches, you can also replace linear switches with tactile options.
However, ASUS doesn’t include a switch puller in the box, so you will need to buy it separately if you plan to swap the keys.
The ASUS Jelly75 keyboard comes with a white backlight instead of RGB backlighting. It keeps the keyboard looking cleaner.
You can adjust the white backlighting to four brightness levels using the dedicated keys on your keyboard, including Fn + F9 shortcuts.
You can also turn off the backlight completely, which can help extend battery life further.
However, the backlight illuminates the area around the keys and doesn’t illuminate the letters and symbols printed on the keys; instead, it glows around them.
This won’t be an issue if you are already used to this keyboard layout and type without looking at the keyboard, but if you look at the keys while typing, the lighting may not be as helpful in low light.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Connectivity and Multi-Device Switching
Another big advantage of the ASUS Jelly75 KD201 keyboard is its connectivity. If you use multiple devices, such as a Windows PC, MacBook, or iPad, you can connect this keyboard to all of them wirelessly and switch between them easily.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports three connectivity options: Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, and a wired USB connection, and it can connect up to five devices using all three connection types.
The Jelly75 keyboard supports Bluetooth 3.0 and 5.0, and it can remember up to three Bluetooth devices.
To pair your devices, switch the keyboard to Bluetooth mode and hold Fn + 1, 2, or 3 for more than three seconds.
Once paired, you can easily switch between devices using the corresponding shortcuts.
You can pair up to three devices via Bluetooth. It also supports a 2.4 GHz wireless connection using the included USB receiver. ASUS says the wireless range is about 10 meters.
You can also connect the keyboard using the USB cable provided in the box.
The USB cable is long and suitable for any desktop layout, and its braided design lets you fold it easily and keeps it tngle-free.
However, as I said before, the main limitation is that it lacks a dedicated compartment for storing the 2.4GHz receiver if you plan to carry the keyboard between workplaces.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Customization
You won’t get much customization on the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard. Instead, ASUS kept it simple with a plug-and-play design.
It supports dedicated shortcuts to switch between Windows and MacBook layouts and offers several function-key shortcuts.
You can use Fn + F1, F2, and F3 to mute or adjust the volume, and F6-F8 to control music playback. It also includes shortcuts for switching between applications, searching, and launching Launchpad on macOS and Windows Search and Spotlight on macOS.
The keyboard also includes a dedicated Microsoft Copilot key, which lets you launch Copilot directly from your keyboard.
However, one noticeable downside is that, unlike other mechanical keyboards, it doesn’t include dedicated software for advanced key-mapping customization, so you can’t set custom shortcuts.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201: Battery Life
The ASUS Jelly75 KD201 has a 4000mAh rechargeable battery. ASUS rates the keyboard as lasting up to 8500 hours on a single charge with the backlight off, which translates to roughly 354 days.
It can last days without needing to charge. I used this keyboard with the backlight on throughout the entire two-week review period. I didn’t have to charge it once.
Regarding charging, the Jelly75 uses a USB-C port and includes a USB-A to USB-C cable in the box. It supports up to 5W charging. You can also charge the keyboard by connecting it directly to your device. It also includes a useful wired USB mode, which can be convenient if you suddenly run out of battery.
The keyboard uses battery light indicators to show the remaining battery. When the battery level drops to 20%, the status light slowly flashes red and reminds you to charge it. While charging, the indicator flashes, and when it’s fully charged, the light turns solid white. You can also check the remaining battery life in the Bluetooth settings for the connected device.
Asus MD105 Wireless Mouse Review
Along with the Jelly75 keyboard, ASUS also sent the MD105 wireless mouse, which pairs well with it. Interestingly, it comes in two color variants: Volt Green, which perfectly matches your keyboard if you picked up the Volt Green variant, and Milky White, which suits the Orange variant.
In terms of design, the MD105 mouse looks like a conventional mouse with a slightly wider body, and it comes with a dedicated thumb rest designed for right-hand users that offers great support, especially if you are a creator and plan to use the mouse for several hours a day.
It feels very light and weighs just 66 grams without a battery, and although it’s slightly wider, it isn’t as travel-friendly as other compact mice.
One feature I particularly like is the silent-click mechanism, which reduces clicking noise. This can be especially useful in shared offices and libraries, or when you’re working late at night.
The MD105 uses an optical sensor with three adjustable DPI settings, including 1200, 1600, and 2400. You can switch between them using the DPI button. Lower DPI settings offer more controlled cursor movement, while higher settings let you move the cursor faster.
For my big hands, the mouse feels perfectly compact, and my right finger rests comfortably on the support, making it comfortable to use.
Since it is lightweight, it is also quickly responsive and easy to move. For connectivity, the MD105 supports Bluetooth 5.0 and also offers 2.4 GHz wireless through the included USB receiver.
You can pair up to three devices: two via Bluetooth and one via the wireless receiver.
It also offers a wireless compartment in the mouse. If you are planning to use it with Bluetooth, you can safely store the wireless receiver in the compartment.
Since it supports multiple devices like the ASUS Jelly75 keyboard, it is also useful for switching between Windows and Mac computers.
A few months ago, I switched to a mouse with a built-in battery, but the MD105 comes with a single AA battery included in the box.
You need to replace it whenever you want, without waiting for the mouse to recharge. However, I prefer a rechargeable mouse, as mine also comes with a battery level indicator, so I can charge it.
If you can, this MD105 mouse suggests you need to keep an AA battery on hand in case it suddenly runs out of battery
The ASUS MD105 mouse is priced at Rs 1,699, which is a good value considering the ergonomics, comfort, and portability it offers.
It also has dedicated left-side switches for extra shortcuts, and its quiet operation, adjustable sensitivity, and multi-device connectivity make it a great buy if you are planning to get it alongside the Jelly75 keyboard.
ASUS Jelly75 KD201 Review Verdict
At Rs 8,999 (US$129.99), ASUS faces stiff competition from brands like AULA, Royal Kludge, and Keychron, which offer feature-packed mechanical keyboards with hot-swappable switches, RGB lighting, and dedicated volume knobs.
Some keyboards, like Royal Kludge, also offer a small dedicated display that shows useful information such as battery status and connection mode.
However, ASUS Jelly75 bets on its design, with colorful, translucent, rounded keycaps that make it one of the most distinctive-looking keyboards.
The gasket-mounted construction, linear switches, and multi-device connectivity also make it a great everyday companion with a simple plug-and-play device for a productive and attractive-looking desktop setup. However, if you want a fully customizable keyboard experience with a dedicated knob and customizable software, this might be a limitation.

- Comfortable typing experience
- Hot-swappable switches
- Multi-device connectivity
- Excellent battery life
- Keys are tightly packed
- No storage for the USB receiver
- Compact but heavy

- No Caps Lock indicator

As Delhiites burst firecrackers well past the 10 p.m. deadline set by the Supreme Court for Deepavali night, air pollution shot up to over 150-200 times World Health Organisation (WHO) limits in parts of the city, but fell through the early morning hours of Monday (November 9, 2026) due to better weather conditions, show official data.
At the peak of pollution, following the bursting of firecrackers on Sunday night, crucial air quality data were missing from several monitoring stations managed by government authorities. Experts say missing data on peak values of air pollution will artificially show better air quality than the reality.
Though the Supreme Court allowed only green firecrackers during fixed windows on November 7 and 8, traditional firecrackers, which are more polluting, were also available in the markets of Delhi.
As per the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) data, the level of PM2.5 (a major pollution) in Patparganj of East Delhi was 2,597 micrograms per cubic metre at 1 a.m. on Monday — about 173.13 times the WHO permissible limit of 15 micrograms per cubic metre for a 24-hour period.
Similarly, the level of PM2.5 in NSUT West Campus was 3,008.4 micrograms per cubic metre at 5 a.m. on Monday — about 200.5 times the WHO permissible limit. PM2.5 (Particulate matter 2.5) are fine inhalable particles, which can get into lungs and bloodstream and lead to a range of respiratory and other diseases.
Favourable wind
Gufran Beig, chair professor, National Institute of Advanced Studies, said though the air pollution spiked around 12 midnight on Sunday to 5 a.m. on Monday due to bursting of firecrackers on Deepavali, both wind direction and speed were very favourable for faster dispersion of air pollution.
“The wind direction was earlier north westerly, originating from stubble burning areas in Punjab and Haryana. But around Sunday afternoon, it changed to easterly and south easterly and also picked up speed by Sunday evening. The reversal of wind direction led to almost negligible effect of stubble burning in Delhi,” said Mr. Beig, who is also the founder-director of the Central government’s SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting Research).
The 24-hour average overall Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 344 (“very poor”) at 4 p.m. on Monday, lower than 376 (“very poor”) a day earlier, according to the CPCB’s daily bulletin, which is considered the day’s AQI. A higher AQI means worsening of air quality. The overall AQI of Delhi which stood at 370 (very poor) at 9 a.m. on Monday, improved through the day to reach 344 by 4 p.m.
Meanwhile, both the AAP and the Congress attacked the BJP government over the missing data, with the former alleging that it was “data fraud”. Hitting back, Delhi Labour Minister Kapil Mishra alleged there was a “conspiracy” by AAP-governed Punjab to set stubble on fire on Sunday evening.
Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.
Stubble burning in Punjab
Meanwhile, Punjab recorded 1,152 stubble burning incidents on Sunday — the highest this paddy harvest season, according to the Indian Agricultural Research Institute’s (IARI) daily bulletin. But it dropped to 198 on Monday, taking the total this harvest season to 4,657, the second lowest since 2020 (till November 9), the data show.
The contribution of stubble burning in neighbouring States to PM2.5 (a chief pollutant) in Delhi on Sunday was 5.1%, according to the Union Ministry of Earth Sciences data.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme, external.
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.
In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, accoprding to US media.

Meta Platforms Inc.-owned Instagram and Alphabet Inc.-owned YouTube have rolled out built-in artificial intelligence (AI) dubbing and translation tools to help regional content creators reach audiences beyond their home markets. The expansion, however, raises two questions: will additional viewership translate into meaningful engagement and higher earnings, and can dubbed videos retain the cultural nuances and natural delivery that make original content resonate?
On 16 January, Instagram expanded its Reels translation feature to Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Marathi, in addition to four existing languages: English, Hindi, Spanish and Portuguese. On 4 February, YouTube opened its auto-dubbing feature to all creators and expanded support to 27 languages.
Instagram and YouTube did not respond to Mint’s queries by press time.
Meta said during its first-quarter earnings call in April that more than 500 million users each on Instagram and Facebook watched AI-translated videos every week. However, wider distribution has not necessarily translated into higher earnings for creators.
“AI dubbing could potentially open up additional distribution opportunities and make regional content accessible to a wider audience. However, the commercial upside will depend on whether that expanded reach translates into meaningful engagement and conversions,” said Shubh Dutt, co-founder of influencer marketing firm Ringlight Media.
Reach beyond home
Ipsita Moitra, a Bengali-language creator in the beauty and lifestyle space, said AI dubbing had helped her reach audiences beyond West Bengal, which earlier accounted for around 65% of her audience. Her working comparison suggests that the share of viewers outside the state has increased from approximately 35% to 45-50% through multilingual distribution. Her regular Reels typically receive 50,000 to 1 lakh views.
“In my initial AI dubbing experiments, I have been using a benchmark of approximately 50,000 views for an original Reel against a potential 60,000–65,000 views for its multilingual version. This represents an increase of around 20–30%,” Moitra said.
Kannada-language finance creator Rajeev KS said most of his core audience still came from Karnataka, but AI-dubbed videos had helped his content reach 20-30% more viewers. The tools had also reduced the time and cost involved in producing multilingual videos.
“Traditionally, manual translation, voiceovers and editing could take 2–3 hours per video. AI tools can potentially reduce this to 20–30 minutes, saving approximately 60–80% of production time, depending on the workflow,” he said.
Bengali-language beauty and lifestyle creator Pallabi Paul Kundu said she had earlier edited videos herself using a paid editing app. Instagram’s AI dubbing feature had reduced production costs and made the results more realistic through lip-syncing.
“People can’t even spot the difference and tell whether I’m actually speaking in another language or not,” she said. She added that her videos had seen a 15-20% increase in viewership.
The revenue test
However, higher viewership does not necessarily mean higher earnings, particularly on Instagram, where creators’ income depends largely on brand collaborations rather than direct payments from the platform based on views, Rajeev said.
Brands have started looking beyond audience size to metrics such as verified engagement, affiliate sales and vernacular resonance, an earlier Mint report noted. This shift comes as more creators from smaller cities enter the brand economy.
The number of non-metro creators participating in brand campaigns rose from around 38,000 in 2020 to more than 4.08 lakh in 2025, according to a report by the Indian School of Business and HashFame, a creator-brand networking platform. The same report said India’s overall creator pool grew from 9.6 lakh in 2020 to 41.2 lakh in 2025.
The commercial value of AI dubbing will depend on whether brands can measure its impact across different language markets, said Rohit Dalmia, chairman and managing director of CineNow, an investment platform focused on intellectual property rights.
“Platforms and creators need language-level measurement of viewership, completion, engagement and conversion so brands can see that dubbed audiences are incremental and commercially valuable,” he said. He added that multilingual distribution would become a revenue opportunity only when brands could link it to actual sales.
Lost in translation
Marathi-language comedy creator Aishwarya Bomble said regional content often relies on cultural references, local humour, slang, accents and a creator’s natural way of speaking. The overall essence of regional content could get diluted when dubbed into another language using AI, she added.
“Around 80% of my audience is Marathi-speaking, and I’ve noticed that my Marathi content consistently performs better. Interestingly, even non-Marathi-speaking viewers engage with my content in Marathi,” she said.
“Especially with conversational or comedy-led content, timing, expressions and delivery are a huge part of the experience. A literal translation might communicate the message, but it may not recreate the same emotion or humour,” she added.
Dutt also pointed to challenges around regional dialects and voice synchronization.
“A translation can be technically accurate but still sound unnatural to someone who speaks that language every day. This can affect how audiences perceive the content and, ultimately, their willingness to engage with it,” he said.
AI dubbing can help regional creators reach audiences beyond their home markets, but the real test is whether that reach translates into meaningful engagement and commercial returns without compromising the cultural nuances that make the original content distinctive.

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

The IPL 2027 auction may be a mini one, but the leadership questions at four franchises are anything but small. Mumbai Indians, Kolkata Knight Riders, Lucknow Super Giants and Delhi Capitals all need to settle their captaincy, and with the next mega-auction expected after 2027, the choice will shape their longer-term plans.
Mumbai Indians: Rohit’s return or a fresh start?
Hardik Pandya’s move to Punjab Kings has reopened the job. Mumbai must decide whether to bring back the man who won five titles or build around a younger leader.
Rohit Sharma is the obvious candidate. He is the most successful captain in the franchise’s history and knows the core of the squad better than anyone.
The case for Tilak Varma is longer-term. The left-hander has long been seen as a future leader, and naming him now would start the transition before the mega-auction. Rohit is the safer pick for 2027; Tilak is the investment. Mumbai must choose between one season of continuity and a head start on the next cycle.
Kolkata Knight Riders: Who succeeds Rahane?
Ajinkya Rahane’s retirement leaves KKR without a captain, and its seventh-place finish in 2026 adds urgency. Vice-captain Rinku Singh is in contention, given his familiarity with the franchise and rising stature. But captaining in a high-pressure T20 league is a different job from being a senior player.
KKR could look outside its leadership group, though an outsider would bring another adjustment before the season. It must decide whether Rinku is the man to build around or whether the immediate challenge calls for someone more experienced.
Lucknow Super Giants: Life after Pant
LSG has the clearest vacancy. Rishabh Pant, who led the side in 2025 and 2026, has returned to Delhi Capitals in a trade involving Kuldeep Yadav. The squad finished last in 2026 and has now missed the playoffs in successive seasons, so another uncertain year is not an option.
Aiden Markram offers international leadership experience and stability. Nicholas Pooran and Mitchell Marsh have also been discussed, though their candidacy depends on the roles LSG want them to play. The franchise could pick an experienced overseas captain or an Indian player already familiar with the squad. Either way, a new captain alone won’t fix what went wrong in 2026.
Delhi Capitals: Axar, Pant or Rahul?
Delhi’s situation is arguably the most complicated. It has brought Pant back, but Axar Patel, who led the side in 2026, is still in the squad.
Pant has led the franchise before and has the personality for it, but his return shouldn’t automatically mean another stint as captain. Delhi must judge whether it is the right cricketing call or merely the familiar one. K.L. Rahul is another option, though his leadership credentials and place in the side would have to be weighed against Pant and Axar.
The new coaching group of Sourav Ganguly (head coach) and Yuvraj Singh (assistant and batting) is likely to have a big say in the decision.

Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.
Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.
The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.

India wants positive ties with Bangladesh, says MEA amid Hasina extradition row
India reaffirmed its commitment to constructive ties with Bangladesh as consular talks were postponed. Sheikh Hasina, 78, was removed from power in August 2024 after violent student-led protests.
India has said it wants a "positive, constructive and forward-looking" relationship with Bangladesh amid diplomatic friction between the two countries and the postponement of their bilateral consular dialogue, the Press Trust of India reported.
Ties came under renewed strain after former Bangladesh prime minister Sheikh Hasina took part in a virtual media interaction in New Delhi on August 5. The consular dialogue, scheduled for next week, has now been postponed.
"India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh," External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a regular media briefing on Friday.
"Accordingly, initiatives have been taken and meetings held under our structured mechanisms in such areas as trade, railways, water resources and border management, among others," he said.
Jaiswal said the next round of the consular dialogue, which will also cover matters related to the revised travel arrangement, would be held on a mutually convenient date. "India remains ready to discuss all bilateral issues with Bangladesh through these existing mechanisms, including at the technical level," he said.
Following Hasina's virtual media interaction, Dhaka reiterated its demand for her extradition. India distanced itself from the event, saying New Delhi had neither played a role in it nor endorsed Hasina's comments.
Bangladesh's foreign ministry reacted sharply to the interaction and said the country was "outraged" that it had been allowed despite Dhaka conveying its concerns to New Delhi about the likely impact on bilateral relations.
Hasina, 78, was removed from power in August 2024 after violent student-led protests. She has been living in India since fleeing Dhaka on August 5 that year, according to PTI.
Amid the continuing strain in ties, India invited Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for a bilateral visit and to attend the outreach session of the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September. Rahman, however, did not attend the summit, and there is no clarity on whether he will visit India soon.
Asked about Bangladesh's repeated demand for Hasina's extradition, Jaiswal said it was a legal matter and would be handled accordingly. India has maintained that bilateral issues can be discussed through existing mechanisms, while the postponed consular dialogue will be held on a mutually convenient date.

One in three students across the globe experiences bullying every month, while one in 10 faces cyber bullying, the UNESCO said, warning that AI is accelerating new forms of technology-facilitated violence (TFV).
UNESCO's new policy brief, ‘Connected and Safe’, shows that nudification apps, voice cloning, automated harassment and AI companion apps used for grooming are now surfacing in school-based incidents across multiple regions.
The United Nations agency has called upon countries to invest in digital safety measures, teacher preparation, and mental health support for students, in coordination with technology companies.
According to Khaled El-Enany, director-general of UNESCO, one in three learners experience bullying every month, while one in ten face cyber bullying. Behind these figures are millions of children whose education, health and well-being are at risk, with consequences that can extend far beyond the classroom.
"Online and technology-facilitated violence (TFV) is no longer a peripheral concern for education systems. It is part of the reality of school life for many learners, with direct consequences for safety, well-being, participation and learning. Around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyber bullying, and across 44 countries in Europe, Central Asia and North America, prevalence rose from 12 to 15 per cent between 2018 and 2022, among both boys and girls," the policy brief said.
"Some learners are more exposed than others. Girls, learners with disabilities, learners of diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, and those marginalised by socio-economic status or geography face distinct and often more severe forms of harm," it said.
In the context of bullying, data shows that girls are just as likely as boys to experience bullying, although the types of bullying differ.
"Boys are generally more exposed to physical bullying and violence, while girls are more exposed to psychological bullying, particularly through cyber bullying and appearance-based bullying. Sexual bullying (sexual jokes, comments and gestures) affects boys and girls at similar rates.
"Physical sexual violence (assault, harassment and rape) can affect both boys and girls, but girls are more likely to experience this form of violence. Corporal punishment and all forms of violent discipline are also influenced by gender, with boys more likely to experience physical corporal punishment than girls and learners likely to be punished to reinforce expectations regarding behaviours deemed socially appropriate for each gender," the brief said.
UNESCO argued that responsibility for safer digital environments for students must be shared between governments, technology companies, platforms and regulators, as schools alone cannot face this issue.
"Safer schools require sustained investment in teacher preparation, mental health and psychosocial support, reporting and response systems, digital safety measures, and coordinated action across education, child protection, health and technology sectors.
"UNESCO recently launched the process towards a new global recommendation on young people and digital environments in the age of AI, to ensure that these technologies protect children's rights and well-being, strengthen critical thinking and empower them to shape their own future," it said.

Windows 11 is testing eight upgrades in Insider builds to reduce daily friction. Key updates include flexible taskbar positioning, faster Windows Search with inline actions, a Battery Status widget, phone-to-PC integration, per-app privacy controls, smarter Windows Hello, anti-glare tools, and enhanced File Explorer previews.
I can’t count how many times I’ve had to drag the window to full size, squint at a bright screen, or open Settings just to turn on dark mode. Each one takes a few seconds, but you repeat them all day. Thankfully, Windows 11 is about to trim a lot of that. Microsoft seems to have noticed, and over the past few months, it has been stacking up small but genuinely useful changes for Windows 11. The best part is that all these features are coming with future updates.
With new optimized features, Windows now feels up to 20% more responsive, with the gains showing up in Start, File Explorer, Search, and more. With the latest Windows Insider release notes, you are in for a eight-feature treat you should know about. One heads-up before we start: not everything is available to everyone yet. Many of these are still being tested in the Windows Insider Experimental channel, so I’ll tell you where each one stands.
Table of Contents
Taskbar customization
For years, the Windows 11 taskbar has been stuck to the bottom of the screen. There was no way to change its position. That is finally changing. Microsoft’s Windows Insider blog confirms that, with the current insider update, users can now park the taskbar on the top, bottom, left, or right edge. Here’s what you can do:
- You can choose icon alignment for every position. On the sides, icons can be top-aligned or centered. On the top or bottom, they can be left-aligned or centered.
- Start, Search, and other flyouts follow the taskbar. Meaning, if you put the taskbar at the top, Start opens from the top.
- On a vertical taskbar, when you choose “Never combine” and turn on labels, every app window gets its own labeled button, so you can see all your windows at a glance.
Moving the taskbar to the side can give you vertical space, handy for developers who want to see more code. To tweak the taskbar, you need to navigate to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. You can also choose to make the taskbar smaller, optimal for small screens. Simply choose the “Show smaller taskbar” option to Always, and you get smaller icons and a shorter bar. No restart or sign-out needed.
Things may not work perfectly, though. Auto-hide and the tablet-optimized taskbar don’t work in the new positions, touch gestures are still in progress, and the search box shows up as a plain search icon for now. Aside from this, the Recommended section is getting renamed to Recent, and you can hide your name and profile picture. There are also separate toggles to show or hide Pinned, Recent, and All.
Smarter Windows Search
This one might be the biggest everyday upgrade. Microsoft has confirmed that a new search built on WinUI 3 is incoming and says it makes it faster and lighter on resources. Windows Search also understands you better. Typos and synonyms are matched more intelligently, so a sloppy query is more likely to give you the right result.
The main highlight is inline actions. So, instead of finding a setting and then opening Settings to change it, you can enable/disable a setting from search. This means you’ll be able to:
- Switch to dark mode, turn on night light, or turn on Bluetooth
- Dim your screen or mute your PC
- Minimize all your windows or arrange windows on screen
Phone actions are coming soon too, allowing you to quickly do things like sending a text through a Phone Link-connected device. Search is soon expected to get inline previews of files, richer file details, web answers (think weather or “how tall is the Eiffel Tower”) and filters. This new experience is also expected to arrive for the Start menu, but only next year. Other features are expected for broader availability later this year.
Battery status widget
This is not a big update, per se, but if you want to know what the battery level is on your wireless mouse? Your headphones? Your laptop? Or any other connected device, usually you’d have to hunt through different menus for each answer.
With the Windows 11 26340.9616 release, Microsoft introduced a Battery Status widget that shows the battery levels of your PC and your peripheral devices in one view. To get it, you need to open the Widgets board > Add widgets > Battery Status. It is rolling out to Insiders on newer builds. Widgets are also getting lighter. Microsoft says on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets now load only when you open them. This helps free up more than 200 MB for your apps.
Phone to PC continuity
Microsoft seems to be making sure that your phone and PC act like one setup. With the upcoming updates, Windows 11 could allow users to reply to messages, answer calls, and open phone apps without picking up their phone. Here are all the features, reportedly available in the insider build:
- Messages and notifications: You will be able to preview them from your Android phone or iPhone right in Start. When you want to reply, you can open a window focused on that chat.
- Quick Settings: Put your phone in silent mode or ring a misplaced phone right from your PC.
- Phone apps on your desktop: Supported Android phones can open phone apps in separate, resizable windows.
- Files: You will be able to browse your phone’s files in File Explorer.
- Photos: You can snap a picture on your phone, and your PC shows a notification that you can open with one click.
- Resume: Pick up supported activities where you left off when you switch devices.
One thing to note is that this requires a compatible Android phone or iPhone, and features vary by platform. The rollout date, similar to other features, isn’t confirmed, but it may arrive by next year.
Better privacy controls
Until now, regular desktop apps were controlled by a single device-wide switch for things like your camera, microphone, and location. That was not something one would want, especially when you want to have granular controls. According to the 28120.3302 release notes, Insiders can now allow or deny access for each desktop app individually. For that, you need to head to Settings > Privacy & security, then open Camera, Microphone, or Location.
The rollout is gentle on your existing setup. All the apps that were granted access will continue to keep it, and apps that were denied stay denied. Nothing will reset. Apps that haven’t asked yet will prompt you the first time they request access.
Smarter Windows Hello
According to Microsoft, with the latest insider builds, it has introduced faster Windows Hello sign-ins, made them easier, and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. There’s also a very practical new trick for face sign-in. If you’ve ever tried to unlock your laptop in a dim room, you know the struggle. You have to turn on the light so that your face is detected correctly.
The 26340.9750 release notes say Windows Hello facial recognition can temporarily brighten your screen to help you sign in when the lighting is poor. To use it, go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello) and turn on Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition. This one is currently in the Experimental channel.
Anti-glare mode
Although Microsoft doesn’t use the name “anti-glare mode,” that’s exactly what the newly added option does. Notably, it’s a contrast theme toggle inside Magnifier, as mentioned in the 28120.3302 release notes. While many people use Night light or color inversion to calm a bright screen, but the downside of using is that it flips everything, including photos, charts, and videos.
With the new toggle, it will recolor the interface only. This way, your images keep their real colors. The dark theme is the default, and you can pick a different contrast theme under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. You still get the “Color inversion” option, and it isn’t going anywhere if you prefer it.
Magnifier also learned some multi-monitor tricks:
- Zoom per display: With your monitors set to Extend, each screen can have its own zoom level. So, one screen where you are writing can sit at 300% while your reference screen stays at 150%.
- View locking: Press Ctrl + Windows + K while pointing at a screen to hold its view in place, then press Windows + Esc to release all locks.
If you just want a softer tint, Windows 11 is also testing a “Screen Tint,” which lets you pick a color overlay and adjust its strength.
File Explorer previews
You might already be using third-party software for file previews inside File Explorer, but wait. Microsoft is also cooking the same feature, and it may arrive very soon for Windows 11. A couple of preview-related changes are incoming:
- Thumbnails in the Recommended section on File Explorer’s Home page are sharper, so they’re crisper and easier to read without needing you to open them.
- You can now preview and install fonts from File Explorer and desktop right-click menus.
If you work with fonts, that second one saves a few steps. For everyone else, it’s a polish update, and it’s good to see File Explorer getting some attention.
Can everyone try these features?
Unfortunately, these features aren’t available for everyone, for now. Most of the features above live in Windows Insider builds. If you’re comfortable with a few bugs, you can join through Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program. You will see most features in builds 26340.9616, 26340.9750 and 28120.3302 in the Experimental channels.
These builds can be unstable, and features in them might change, be removed, or never ship. Many are also rolled out gradually to a subset of Insiders first, so you may not see everything right away. For those who are using Windows 11 on their primary device, you should probably wait.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

The day may have been wet, but Chennaiites still went all out to bring in light and sparkles on Deepavali day, which fell on Sunday (November 8, 2026). While awareness about safety has increased, ophthalmologists in the city have once again called for caution and reiterated protective measures, as they have received dozens of cases of cracker-related injuries.
The Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital received around 50 cases, with about 10 cases having to be admitted, a senior official said.
Also Read: Firecracker-related eye injuries more serious than they appear, claims eye doctors
Over the Deepavali weekend, the emergency clinic at Sankara Nethralaya saw 45 cases of firecracker injuries at its main campus. Two underwent wound repair surgery, while two others were scheduled for surgery on Monday, November 9, according to T.S. Surendran, its chairman..
At Dr. Agarwals Eye Hospital, nearly 20 patients came in with cracker-related injuries, said S. Soundari, regional head, clinical services. One of these, she explained, was a very serious case that had been taken up for surgery. Another patient lit a firecracker, but it did not blast. He went near it to take a look, and it blasted in his face, injuring both eyes. The remaining injuries were mostly small, and would be treated medically, she said. Four cases involved children; the rest were adults, mostly in their 30s and 40s.
At Rajan Eye Care, about 15 patients have been seen over the past three days or so, said Mohan Rajan, chairman and medical director of the hospital. One patient had to undergo a surgery, while minor injuries were treated as outpatients.
Doctors have reiterated caution. Dr. Soundari called for wearing protective eye gear while bursting firecrackers, supervising children properly, and importantly, not trying to touch the eye or take objects out by oneself. “Come to a doctor immediately if there is an eye injury,” she stressed. Dr. Rajan noted that bystanders often got hurt and should be careful to maintain an adequate distance..
