Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
- Published
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
- Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' 
  - Published1 day ago
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

A former Hamas bodyguard convicted of knife crime in the UK is wanted in Germany for allegedly plotting to murder Jewish people.
Details of the alleged plot can now be reported after Mohammed Alfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was found guilty on Friday of a knife attack on a bailiff outside his home in Birmingham.
The 40-year-old was found guilty by a majority verdict of unlawful wounding, possession of two knives and criminal damage. He was cleared of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.
He was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit when he attacked the bailiff last year.
Alfatih, the son of a senior Hamas official, could not be named during his trial because of reporting restrictions.
He had been photographed working for a former leader of Hamas before being granted asylum in the UK in 2015 and British citizenship in 2020.
While detained for the attack on the bailiff in Birmingham, he was rearrested after authorities in Germany said he had been part of an alleged plot to attack Israeli targets in central Europe.
Alfatih, who was born in Germany, is expected to be extradited to the country after he has served his sentence in the UK, with his connection to Hamas stated in the German extradition request.
German prosecutors charged seven suspected Hamas members in September over an alleged plot to target Jews or Israelis in Germany or Austria around the second anniversary of the 7 October attack on Israel.
They said “Mohammed A” played a prominent role in transporting and storing weapons but was being prosecuted separately after UK authorities arrested him in London and noted he had not yet been returned to Germany.
German authorities said he was connected to Hamas’s leadership and was said to have produced a video in advance to take responsibility for the attack on its behalf.
The attack was disrupted by Germany’s domestic intelligence service after a tipoff from the Mossad, Israel’s secret service.
During a two-week trial at Birmingham crown court, the jury was shown video footage of Alfatih lashing out with a knife at the broken window of a van on 14 October 2025.
The bailiff, Kevin Bucknall, was left with cuts to his head and required hospital treatment. The defendant pleaded not guilty on the grounds of self-defence.
The jurors, who convicted Alfatih after being shown footage of him brandishing two large kitchen knives outside his home in Kings Heath, Birmingham, were not told of his links to Hamas.
They were also not told Alfatih was under surveillance by a counter-terrorism unit after being released on bail on suspicion of a terror offence days before the bailiff was attacked.
A government source said: “This is a staggering example of the loss of border control under the last Conservative government, who granted his asylum claim and gave him citizenship.
“This Labour government has just introduced reforms that ensure those who gain citizenship must first show they are a good citizen and have contributed to this country.”

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

Eight people have tested positive for Shigella infection in Malappuram district, with five cases linked to a wedding feast at Korakkuthu in Elamkulam panchayat near Perinthalmanna.
The outbreak has prompted the Health department to step up surveillance and preventive measures in the area.
The five patients attended a wedding held on October 31, 2026, in ward 12 of Elamkulam panchayat. Around 80 people who attended the function have since reported symptoms of diarrhoea. A child from the area is also suspected to have Shigella infection and is under special observation.
The other confirmed cases include a four-year-old girl who ate food from a snack shop at 5th Mile at Amarambalam near Nilambur, and two people who ate mandi rice from a restaurant at Palunda near Chungathara, Nilambur.
The girl and the two patients from Chungathara are undergoing treatment at Government District Hospital, Nilambur. Several others, including the girl’s mother, have also reported similar symptoms.
The Food Safety department has collected samples of food and drinking water served at the wedding and sent them for testing. Stool samples of those affected will be examined at the laboratory at Government Medical College, Manjeri.
A special health team has begun surveillance and field-level interventions. The Health department has advised people to drink boiled and cooled water and eat properly cooked food. Drinking water sources should also be superchlorinated using bleaching powder, said health officials.
The health authorities, in coordination with the panchayat, will intensify inspections at local establishments and public functions. Event organisers have been asked to follow public health guidelines.

Yacht captain on reality show 'Below Deck' arrested in Turkey after teenager dies
A participant from the U.S. reality TV show “Below Deck” has been arrested in Turkey following a fight in Bodrum that left a 17-year-old dead
ISTANBUL -- A participant in the U.S. reality TV show “Below Deck” has been arrested in Turkey over a fight in the resort city of Bodrum that left a 17-year-old dead, local media reported Thursday.
Joao Franco, 36, and his brother Carlos allegedly became involved in an altercation with shopkeepers in Bodrum last Saturday evening, according to the private Demiroren News Agency.
Franco, whom the agency identified as a yacht captain, appeared in the Bravo channel’s “Below Deck Down Under” and “Below Deck Mediterranean” from 2018, as well as “The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City.”
“Below Deck” follows the lives of crew members aboard luxury yachts as they interact with each other and their guests.
The brothers were intoxicated and an argument broke out when they started swearing, Demiroren reported. During the subsequent fight, teenager Muhammet Koyabakan fell and hit his head on the ground. He was taken to a hospital but died on Monday.
The Franco brothers, who are Portuguese nationals, were detained and later formally arrested.
News reports did not specify the charges against them, but Demiroren said they told police they were attacked and acted in self-defense. They denied hitting Koyabakan.
Bodrum, a port city on the Aegean Sea, is a favored spot for wealthy yacht owners. Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos are among the billionaires who have visited in recent years.

An eight-year-old boy diagnosed with Type II achalasia – a rare disorder that affects the ability to swallow food and liquids – has undergone a Perora-l Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM) procedure at Rela Hospital.
Achalasia affects the nerves controlling the muscles of the oesophagus, causing the lower oesophageal sphincter – a muscular valve connecting the food pipe to the stomach – to remain abnormally tight. This prevents food and liquids from passing normally into the stomach. The condition is estimated to affect 0.1 to 0.18 children per 100,000 annually.
The child had progressively worsening difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Following the procedure, he was able to resume consuming clear liquids and subsequently, a soft diet, within 24 hours.
POEM involves passing an endoscope through the mouth and creating a small tunnel within the oesophageal wall to reach and divide the muscle fibres causing the obstruction. Unlike conventional surgery, the procedure does not require external incisions or stitches.
S.N.K. Chenduran, senior consultant and endoscopic surgeon, Department of Medical Gastroenterology, performed the procedure, which took about 50 minutes. He said performing POEM in children required particular precision because of the smaller dimensions of the oesophagus and the delicate tissues.
Dinesh Jothimani, director, Hepatology and Medical Gastroenterology, said persistent swallowing difficulties, regurgitation, vomiting, and unexplained weight loss in children warranted medical evaluation.

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.
Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.
Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.
Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.
“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.
“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.
The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.
“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.
Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.
While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.
There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

Phage therapy, which uses bacteriophages to selectively eliminate harmful bacteria, holds significant potential in combating antimicrobial resistance (AMR), said Dr. Kalyan Chakravarthy Koganti, sepsis and infectious diseases specialist at SHRI Hospital, Guntur.
He said this while sharing his research experience during a press release, after presenting his team's scientific findings at an international symposium jointly organised by the Chinese University of Hong Kong and reputed biomedical research journals.
Dr. Kalyan said his team's research presentation on phage therapy received appreciation from participants at the symposium. Dr. Sutharsan Govindarajan, associate professor and phage biologist, SRM University-A.P., also presented research conducted by the team.
He described the event as an enriching learning experience, particularly the discussions on the wider applications of bacteriophages in diagnostics and therapy, including cancer research. Chuanbin Mao, chair of the symposium, has been researching bacteriophages for 25 years and has contributed extensively to scientific literature, he said.
Dr. Kalyan noted that bacteriophages selectively target disease-causing bacteria without harming human beings, making them promising alternatives when antibiotics fail.
His team has administered phage therapy to a few patients at its centre with encouraging results. In collaboration with SRM University-A.P. and Szeged University, Hungary, the team has been working to advance its availability in India.

The Greens have retaliated against Labor’s decision to run an open ticket in a key inner-city seat by refusing to direct preferences to the party in 15 electorates across the state at this month’s Victorian election.
The move has sparked a war of words between the two parties, with each accusing the other of striking a “dodgy deal” that could help the Liberals and One Nation get elected on 28 November.
On Friday, the Greens confirmed they would only be directing voters to number the Greens one and One Nation last across 15 electorates.
The decision follows Labor’s decision on Tuesday to run an open ticket in the inner Melbourne seat of Prahran, where the Greens had been counting on Labor preferences to win it back. It has been held by the Liberals on a tiny 1.3% margin – after the Greens lost it at a byelection in 2025.
At the time, the Victorian Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, told Guardian Australia that Labor’s “unforgivable” decision could hand the upcoming election to a Liberal-One Nation coalition.
A Labor spokesperson turned the accusation back on the Greens on Friday, mirroring Sandell’s language.
“In one of the most consequential elections in Victoria’s history – the Greens have done a dodgy deal to help elect a Liberal-One Nation government,” the spokesperson said.
“This is unforgivable and Victorians won’t forget it’s Ellen Sandell and the Greens to blame when Jess Wilson cuts our hospitals and schools – and One Nation winds back our nation leading reforms on women’s rights and Treaty.”
The Greens responded by accusing Labor of “lying to Victorian voters”.
“The Greens will be putting One Nation last in every single electorate across Victoria,” their spokesperson said. “We always encourage people to vote in line with their values.
“After months of scaremongering about a Liberal-One Nation government, it is Labor who have done a dodgy backroom deal with the Liberals that could help elect one.”
The 15 electorates where the Greens will issue these how-to-vote cards are: Albert Park, Ashwood, Bellarine, Bendigo East, Bendigo West, Essendon, Euroa, Gippsland East, Mildura, Mornington, Point Cook, Polwarth, South Barwon, Tarneit and Werribee.
Labor fears the decision will particularly hurt their chances in Albert Park, Ashwood, Bellarine, South Barwon and the two Bendigo seats vacated by former premier Jacinta Allan and speaker Maree Edwards.
The Coalition is quietly confident it is improving its chances of fending off One Nation and snatching seats from Labor.
However, Tony Barry, the Liberal strategist turned pollster with Redbridge and co-host of Guardian Australia’s Back to Back Barries podcast, said most Greens voters don’t closely follow their party’s how-to-vote cards.
“Historical preference flows from past state and federal elections shows about 85% of exhausted Greens votes flow to Labor and about 15% leakage to the Coalition, and that rarely changes regardless of the particular circumstances,” Barry said.
But he said in Essendon, where Labor candidate Kat Theodosis is contesting the seat following Danny Pearson’s retirement, in a complex race involving the Liberals, One Nation and three independents candidates, it “might be enough to flip the seat to the Liberals.”
Meanwhile, the conservative Family First party is directing its preferences to Labor candidates affiliated with the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees’ Association (SDA), placing them second on their how-to-vote cards.
The cards feature an image of a baby next to the Labor candidate name with claims they have a “pro-life voting record”.
It prompted Pasoce Vale MP Anthony Cianflone, who is in a tight race against the Greens’ Angelica Panopoulos, to post a statement on social media saying he supported “women’s right to make their own decisions about their bodies and healthcare”.
“That’s why I have supported the Victorian Labor government’s reforms protecting these rights,” Cianflone said.
Family First have also preferenced Matthew Guy last in his safe Liberal seat of Bulleen.
The Family First state leader, Moira Deeming, was disendorsed as a Liberal candidate after alleging Guy had placed her in a headlock earlier this year. Deeming later conceded she misunderstood the technical meaning of “headlock”.

Around 86% of the spending on measures against tuberculosis (TB) in 2025 came from domestic sources, the recently released Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 by the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, even as the reduction in international donor funding to combat the infectious disease remains a cause of concern.
TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025. The report notes that $22 billion is needed annually for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care to achieve the global targets agreed on at the 2023 United Nations high-level TB meeting by 2027.
In absolute terms, Brazil, China, India, the Russian Federation, and South Africa accounted for $3.7 billion (65%) of the total of $5.63 billion provided from domestic sources in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
The report notes that international donor funding fell by 14%, from $1.1 billion in 2024 to $0.94 billion in 2025, having been relatively stable at about $1.1–1.3 billion per year between 2015 and 2024.
Financing for TB research and innovation, at $1.2 billion in 2023, also continued to fall far short of the global target of $5 billion per year. Progress to date has been constrained by the overall level of investment, said the report.
“TB mostly affects adults in their most productive years. However, all age groups are at risk. Over 80% of cases and deaths are in low- and middle-income countries. In 2025, the largest number of new TB cases occurred in the WHO South-East Asia Region (35%),’’ said the report.
South-East Asia Region
The WHO on Friday (November 13, 2026) called on countries in the South-East Asia Region to accelerate action to end TB. The latest TB estimates show the region accounts for 3.6 million people who developed TB in 2025 — 34% of the global total — and 4,00,000 TB-related deaths, or 35% of the global total. "These numbers are a stark reminder that TB remains one of the Region’s most pressing public health and development challenges,” said Nilesh Buddha, officer-in-charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.
A release issued by the regional office added that in 2025, $1.03 billion was available for TB prevention and care in the region, with 91% from domestic sources. Yet this represented only around 16% of global TB funding, despite the region accounting for 34% of global cases. "Closing this gap in resources is critical to sustaining progress," the WHO said.
“Ending TB is not simply a health sector responsibility. It requires leadership across government, sustained investment, strong health systems and communities at the centre of the response. We have tools to prevent, diagnose and treat TB. What is needed now is the commitment to ensure they reach everyone who needs them, without delay or financial hardship,” said Dr. Buddha, adding that ending TB by 2030 will depend on countries turning political commitments into measurable action, with greater urgency and scale.
Far from target
Meanwhile, the Global TB Report said that across the world, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (more than 20% of total household income). This is far from the target of the WHO End TB Strategy of zero.
In 2025, globally there were an estimated 0.96 million new TB cases that were attributable to undernutrition, 0.92 million to diabetes, 0.73 million to alcohol use disorders, 0.69 million to smoking, and 0.55 million to HIV infection.

Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
Tyler's opioid addiction began in his early 20s, and when he decided he wanted to quit, he used kratom leaf powders to help ease withdrawal symptoms.
Tyler, now 38, told NPR he thinks kratom helped him stop using opioids for a decade.
Tyler asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma attached to his history with drug use and addiction.
In early 2025, he saw a new product at a gas station called 7-OH. He hadn't heard of 7-OH, but said the tablets were advertised as "kratom products." He decided to try them, since the kratom powders he'd taken in the past "can be hard on your stomach," he said.
At first, 7-OH gave him a feeling of euphoria he described as similar to opioids, which "felt like a kind of a miracle," he said.
Nearly a year and a half later, he was in a rapid detox program in Michigan, where he was sedated to sleep through the withdrawals he experienced when he tried to stop taking it.
In the past few years, highly concentrated products with 7-OH — sometimes alongside other semi-synthetic opioids — have popped up online, and at many smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. They can come in the form of tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolate.
7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine, is one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom, which comes from a tree in the coffee family. It's naturally found in kratom in very small amounts, and seems to act more like an opioid in the human brain than kratom leaf products. Kratom is used by some people with opioid addiction to maintain long-term recovery. Some people say it makes them feel energized or focused. Others describe the effects of kratom like those of opioids, and say it can relieve pain, feel calming or even create euphoria.
"More potent than I imagined"
Some users of 7-OH and kratom show classic signs of addiction, researchers and policy officials say. But the products are not always clearly labeled, so it's difficult or impossible for users to know what quantity of the substances they are consuming.
"I did not know at all what I was in for. It was much more potent than I had imagined," Tyler said.
Estimates of how many people use kratom and 7-OH in the U.S. are wide-ranging. Some suggest over 5 million people have used kratom in their lifetime. David Epstein, a senior investigator at the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Intramural Research Program, says he's seen estimates of kratom use as high as 15 million. Those estimates don't usually distinguish between whole leaf kratom, 7-OH or other related products.
In the last decade, the U.S. government has attempted to restrict both kratom and 7-OH products, but strong opposition to those moves by the public and powerful advocacy groups backing the substances have kept them federally legal.
That's started to change in the last few months.
A federal crackdown is likely on the way
No federal actions have been taken against "traditional botanical kratom," but a new federal restriction on some 7-OH products could go into place as early as Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
The path there has not been straightforward. In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) restricted the making and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids derived from 7-OH and other related compounds: MGM-15, MGM-16 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). Those compounds were listed under the Controlled Substances Act alongside the most highly restricted drugs, like heroin and LSD.
That caused backlash from kratom advocates who worried the rule would affect products with "trace amounts" of the semi-synthetic opioid, MGPI. One kratom advocacy organization, the American Kratom Association, filed a federal lawsuit on Aug. 26 against the DEA. It asked the DEA to ensure natural kratom products with traces of MGPI would remain legal.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) then issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI on Oct. 9, and the DEA changed its course. They now plan to restrict a narrower range of 7-OH and MGPI products: ones that contain higher concentrations of 7-OH and/or MGPI.
HHS and the DEA say they are not focusing on natural kratom products.
The research on kratom and 7-OH
Many people who oppose the restriction say kratom and 7-OH products have kept them away from traditional opioids, and helped them manage chronic pain, mood and mental health. Some also point to the fact that opioid deaths in the U.S. are decreasing. In 2023 alone, a KFF report found there were over 79,000 opioid deaths, and in 2024 there were 54,000.
A recent report of data from 53 U.S. poison control centers shows reports of calls related to kratom increased about 1,200% between 2015 and 2025. Chris Holstege, a physician and a professor of emergency medicine and pediatrics at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, is one of the authors of that report. He said he and the other authors "were a bit stunned" by those findings, which do not distinguish between kratom or products like 7-OH.
The report included 233 deaths associated with kratom during 2015–2025, with 79% of those deaths involving multiple substances. The most severe outcomes were linked to people using multiple substances alongside kratom products, like opioids, stimulants and benzodiazepines.
But Holstege points out over half the reports of calls, 62%, involved people using kratom without other drugs.
The authors used data on kratom from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), which includes calls from the public, healthcare professionals or medical examiners, and medical records.
For some, a "life-changing" dose
Still, there are people who report benefits of using kratom or 7-OH, said Epstein, the NIDA investigator.
NPR spoke to one mom in Delaware, Angela Wilson, 44, who said 7-OH has helped her manage excruciating chronic pain related to endometriosis, and symptoms of depression she's had since she was a teenager.
She said she's been taking 32 to 40 milligrams of 7-OH a day, split into three doses, for the last year and a half.
Wilson said kratom powders made her feel anxious and shaky, and 7-OH seems to work for her without those side effects.
"It's been truly life-changing for my family situation, my personal life," she said.
Wilson doesn't have health insurance, and said losing access to 7-OH under new restrictions would be "devastating" for her and her family.
"We're not really sure, you know, what I'm gonna do when it's not available," she said.
"It was game over." Dangers of addiction
Epstein has also heard stories like Tyler's. He said people can become addicted or dependent — and some of his ongoing research suggests that risk is higher with 7-OH products than with whole leaf kratom.
He said for some people, their 7-OH use "seemed to go nicely for the first couple of days, but then they found that they had to keep using to avoid withdrawal," Epstein said. "And some of them, not all of them, but some of them, even said they had to, you know, they couldn't make it through the night. They had to get up in the middle of the night to take more."
He said other people were happy with the effects they got from taking 7-OH and didn't feel like it caused problems for them.
Tyler told NPR that 7-OH tablets gave him more energy at first. He works a job where he's on his feet a lot, and with 7-OH, he said, " I can go, go, go, go, go, you know?"
He began taking around 300 to 400 mg of 7-OH a day, about ten times the dose Angela Wilson takes. In the next year, he said he made a few attempts to stop, but the withdrawals were debilitating.
"The best way to put it, I think, is to imagine having the flu, the worst flu you've had, you know, multiply that by at least three times," he said. "And then just know that all you gotta do is take one pill, and it's gone in seconds."
Another former kratom and 7-OH consumer, Brian, 41, told NPR at the height of his use, he was using much more 7-OH than both Angela Wilson and Tyler. Brian also asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma associated with drug use.
Brian used 1,200 mg of 7-OH — and estimates he spent around $150 each day — on the substance. He'd quit using opioids in 2016, but found kratom at a gas station in 2022. He said it claimed to help with energy.
"And 'cause literally right next to the register, nothing taboo about it, looks like those 5-Hour Energy shot type things," he said.
Brian said within minutes of taking it, he realized he felt "exactly" like he did when he'd been taking opioids.
"I was like, 'What is this?,'" he said. "'Like, are you telling me I found a legal, you know, healthy opiate that f***s you up and, you know, you feel great and no consequences, like the legality of it and everything?"
"I was like, 'This is it,'" he said.
Brian tried to stop taking kratom multiple times, but couldn't. One day at a smoke shop, he said the clerk offered him a sample of 7-OH. The clerk described it as a "version of kratom" that Brian could take in lower doses to get the same effects.
"Once I found these little tiny tablets — that I had to take one and it felt like I had taken an Oxycontin — you know, that was it," Brian said. "It was game over."
An uncertain future
Researchers say more research should be done to understand the potential benefits of kratom and 7-OH products, including whether they can help treat addiction. On their website, NIDA says, "early studies suggest kratom and kratom compounds warrant further study as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder."
In the meantime, Holstege, at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, says current marketing around kratom products seems to attract users for other reasons.
"I find it a little hard to believe that all the shops that are popping up around my campus right now are trying to advertise to people who are addicted to opioids," he said. "So the question is, what else are they advertising this product for?"
" I certainly have a growing list of patients in addiction clinics who are addicted to this, and in withdrawal, that we're having to manage," Holstege added.
Brian stopped taking 7-OH in April 2026, when he said he decided to "quit cold turkey." He said he experienced more debilitating withdrawals from 7-OH than he had from quitting opioids. He noted, though, he'd had a much easier time accessing 7-OH, and took it more frequently than he'd taken opioids.
When stopping 7-OH, he said he felt fearful, anxious, and had gastrointestinal issues. He lost the desire to leave his house.
"It was a nightmare," Brian said.
Tyler told NPR he hasn't used 7-OH or kratom since he traveled to the Michigan detox program in March. He said he doesn't think he would have been able to stop using 7-OH without that program.
"There's no chance," he said. "It's just too addictive and too accessible."
He said the road to feeling like himself again has been even longer than when he stopped using opioids. With opioids, he said, it took a few weeks to feel like he had energy again.
With 7-OH, he said the process has taken months.
"Kind of just this week I'm starting to feel kinda great," he said in October. "But it's been a long journey of getting my energy back."

'I sincerely apologize': Blue Jays outfielder Santander apologizes days after anti-Muslim social media posts
Conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful, he says
Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander apologized Friday for sharing anti-Muslim social media posts, saying the content caused hurt and fell short of his own convictions.
In a statement on Instagram, Santander said reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared and the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.
He expressed respect for the Muslim community and pledged to avoid sharing content that promotes hate.
Santander shared the posts on Nov. 4 and deleted them the next morning. They included a video of a Christian preacher disparaging Muslims and another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the United States after Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the Senate in Michigan.
His apology came a day after Blue Jays president and chief executive officer Mark Shapiro apologized to the Muslim community and fans following a meeting with community leaders, and after general manager Ross Atkins asked Santander to publicly address the controversy.
The 32-year-old Venezuelan signed a five-year, $92.5-million US contract with Toronto in January 2025 but missed the entire 2026 big-league season because of injuries. It remains unclear whether the team will discipline him over the posts.

Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
- Published
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

Last week’s blue tsunami carried a lot of white coats: At least seven newly elected Democrats have medical degrees or nursing careers. Pediatrician Annie Andrews of South Carolina scored one of the most shocking Senate victories of election night for Democrats, while Abdul El-Sayed (who earned a medical degree before working in public health) won the all-important Michigan Senate race. In the House, Democrats will soon welcome pediatrician Richard Pan of California, emergency room physician Amish Shah of Arizona, surgeon Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, emergency nurse Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, and oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio.
How the 7 healthcare workers who just got elected to Congress plan to fix our broken system
Abdul El-Sayed, Annie Andrews, and Kristina Knickerbocker aren’t just new members of the House and Senate — they’re also medical professionals.
Like many Democrats, these candidates campaigned on lowering costs, expanding health coverage, and confronting the drugmakers and healthcare corporations that they accuse of putting profits ahead of patients. They have endorsed big ideas to make healthcare better, from a public insurance option to Medicare-for-all, alongside targeted changes to drug prices and health insurance denials.
With President Donald Trump still in the White House, Democrats’ healthcare agenda faces obvious obstacles in the short term. But I spoke with Pan and Shah this week to learn how they hope to influence the healthcare conversation in Washington going forward.
They may be politicians, but they have seen America’s broken healthcare up close. They’re hoping to help some of their new colleagues, who may not have those same experiences and may be prone to thinking of policy issues in abstract terms, understand the urgency and the human toll of our messed-up medical system. And as lawmakers try to come up with solutions to fix those problems, they’ll be there to make sure those policies actually make sense in practice.
“For us, these policy discussions are not abstract,” Pan said. “As a practicing physician, I know what it’s like to be on the front lines and have to look a patient in the eye and even tell them that, well, these programs either exist or don’t exist, and we’re not going to be able to get you help. And those are the types of things I have to deal with each time I see a patient.”
What practicing medicine teaches you about politics
The new members will join a small but notable group of providers-turned-politicians: The Congressional Doctors Caucus, founded last year, had six Democratic members before last week’s midterms. Shah, who previously served in the Arizona legislature, told me that he believed his medical career had given him a valuable outlook for thinking about how to serve in political office.
“The core function of practicing medicine is to care for people,” Shah said. “The same should really be true about politics.”
He’s experienced the shocking inequities of US healthcare, and seen its impact on people’s well-being, firsthand. Earlier this year, Shah said, an uninsured woman came into his emergency room department with an allergic reaction. His team treated her successfully. But she was worried about the bill, asking if she might have to pay a $10,000 charge after she was discharged. And Shah told me that he had to be honest with her that she might.
That’s when he learned that his patient was her family’s breadwinner — and that she actually worked in a nearby emergency department. Somebody who helped provide emergency care to others couldn’t afford it herself.
“It’s a tragedy that those of us who actually go out to help others and be part of the team that saves lives can be left without insurance,” Shah said.
Pan, a former California state senator, described a similar experience while treating kids in primary care. He has seen all the ways US health care is lacking: children who don’t get the mental health support they need to excel in school, families that struggle to afford stable housing or find healthy food. His ability to help depended on decisions made well outside his examination room.
Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here.
“These are all things that certainly have potential policy solutions, but it’s not just theoretical,” he told me. “It is very real and tied to very specific patients that I’ve seen.”
But while these experiences have made them eager to change things, the newly elected physicians are also mindful about how proposed changes could disrupt ongoing patient care. Pan said he wants to push his colleagues about both the intended and unintended consequences or new policies: Who will get help? What happens to people whose needs don’t fit neatly into boxes? As any doctor will tell you, every patient is unique.
That’s especially true for people with chronic conditions, he said, who may have spent years finding the right doctors and treatments. Lawmakers have to strike a balance: identifying ideas that will improve the health system in the long term, without jeopardizing the care that people need right now.
Shah said he hopes his experience as a physician can help Congress find a middle ground between the patients demanding reform and the providers who are wary of big changes. After decades in medicine and a stint in the state legislature, he knows the different players and their concerns.
“I speak the language of healthcare,” he said. “I’ve earned the trust of a lot of those stakeholders that I will not take an axe to the system, but rather reform it in a way that really improves it and centers the patient. So that gives me a unique ability to improve this at the congressional level.”
What the new doctors and nurses want to change
These Democratic doctors, like their party’s leaders, have a clear No. 1 priority when they take office next year: reversing the $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that Republicans passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.
“Given all the damage the Republicans did in the past two years, first we got to triage to stop the bleeding,” Pan told me. He wants to repeal the OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements, restore the lapsed Affordable Care Act tax credits that helped reduce premiums for millions of Americans, and protect Medicare payments. Those were common themes across these physician-politicians: Andrews, Berman, and El-Sayed endorsed the same policies as part of their campaign platform, while Knickerbocker likewise pledged to protect Medicaid, Medicare, the ACA, and children’s health coverage.
Beyond reversing the Republican cuts, the newcomers want to cover more people, though they have different ideas about how to do it.
“You have these real stories that then drive the legislation, and give you the ideas to solve the problems for people.”
— Amish Shah, emergency room physician elected in Arizona
Shah said he supports letting people buy into Medicare. Andrews, Berman, Knickerbocker, and Shah have also endorsed a public option: a government-backed health insurance plan that would compete with private plans. El-Sayed and Hamawy, meanwhile, say they favor Medicare-for-all, guaranteeing comprehensive coverage without premiums or out-of-pocket costs.
“I want to see every United States citizen covered, and I’d like to see the premiums drop,” Shah said.
But even the people who have health insurance often struggle to pay for medical care. Andrews, Berman, El-Sayed, and Hamawy have all proposed expanding the government’s negotiation of prescription drug prices. Andrews and Berman want to extend Medicare’s $35 insulin cap to private insurance. Andrews, Berman, and Hamawy also want to crack down on private equity ownership and consolidation among healthcare providers.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, these doctors were not afraid to get into the weeds of healthcare policy on the campaign trail. Andrews’s detailed plans include limits on some hospital prices and changing Medicare payments so the same service costs the same regardless of where it is performed. Berman’s agenda draws on his own nursing experience: He wants nurses to help set staffing standards, more funding for nursing education, and enhance workplace safety for medical workers, a goal he shares with Shah. In Arizona, Shah worked on protections for healthcare workers, and he wants Congress to focus on the problem too.
Pan also wants to figure out how to restore trust in public health after two years of US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. undermining faith in vaccinations and other medical science. He helped write California laws tightening exemptions from school vaccination requirements; in Congress, he wants stronger oversight of the administration’s healthcare agencies, including probing any possible corruption, and stronger protections for scientific decision-making. He told me that lawmakers may want to consider creating new safeguards into law so future administrations have less latitude to overhaul public health policy.
“The American people need accurate information from their government,” Pan said. “We might want to rethink how to put better guardrails so that someone like an RFK Jr. in the future couldn’t…basically upend everything.”
Andrews and Shah have also placed a lot of emphasis on fixing prior authorizations, one of the most common frustrations for patients and providers alike.
Shah recalled that he once met a Republican constituent who said he was completing prior authorization paperwork on behalf of the doctor treating his son, who had muscular dystrophy, because the doctor’s office was overwhelmed. He was shouldering an absurd administrative burden as a layperson, just so his child could get the care he needed.
And so, Shah worked on legislation to streamline the prior authorization process. A 2021 law standardized prior authorization forms and limited their length to two pages, excluding supporting medical documentation. He sees his state work as a possible model for federal legislation.
“We really need to start looking at these denials,” he said. He wants more scrutiny of decisions that are later overturned and of automated and increasing AI-driven systems that reject people’s claims without meaningful review.
It’s another example of how these freshman members will be ready to dive into the weeds of fixing healthcare. The question will be whether the new lawmakers can translate their direct experience with patients’ frustrations into changes that make getting healthcare care easier.
“You have these real stories that then drive the legislation,” Shah said, “and give you the ideas to solve the problems for people.”

Washington – Cade Cunningham racked up 52 points as the Detroit Pistons edged a double-overtime thriller 144-140 against Washington on Thursday.
The Wizards twice extended the game with clutch scores in the dying seconds, but could not repeat the trick a third time as the Pistons held their nerve to claim an epic road win.
Cunningham became the first player in NBA history to score 50 points and add 10 assists with zero turnovers, while Ausar Thompson had a triple-double with 17 points, 11 assists and 11 rebounds.

Srinagar, Nov 13: Kashmir Divisional Commissioner Anshul Garg on Friday reviewed winter preparedness in the Valley and called for timely and coordinated response to ensure uninterrupted essential services.
The divisional commissioner chaired a meeting to review winter preparedness across the Kashmir division, emphasising the need for coordinated efforts, timely response and adequate arrangements to ensure uninterrupted essential services during the winter season, an official spokesman said.
During the meeting, the divisional commissioner reviewed snow clearance action plans of various agencies and directed prompt snow clearance and clear demarcation of duties to avoid confusion.
Garg stressed optimal utilisation of available machinery and manpower and directed concerned agencies to complete all pending contracts to strengthen the snow clearance mechanism.
Garg assessed electricity demand and supply, availability of buffer stocks of transformers, transformer oil, and DG sets in Gurez, besides the status of tree trimming operations.
He was informed that the average electricity demand in the Valley during winter is around 1,700 MW against an average supply of 1,300 MW, while peak demand reaches 2,400 MW, the spokesman said.
The divisional commissioner directed the authorities to augment the capacity wherever required, complete the remaining tree-trimming work at the earliest, strictly adhere to scheduled power curtailment timings and ensure prompt repair of damaged transformers.
While reviewing the availability of essential commodities in remote and snowbound areas, including Gurez and the Karnah-Machil-Keran belt, the divisional commissioner directed the food and consumer affairs department to complete the advance stocking of LPG cylinders, petroleum products, rice and wheat within one week.
He stressed that adequate stocks of essential commodities be ensured in far-flung areas to prevent any shortage or inconvenience to the public during road closures.
Taking note of delays in the commencement of winter air sorties in Bandipora and Kupwara, the divisional commissioner directed the civil aviation department to operationalise the facility by December 1 to facilitate emergency transportation from remote and inaccessible areas.
Regarding daily flight operations at Srinagar airport, he directed the director, Airport Authority Srinagar, to ensure timely dissemination of information to passengers and the public about changes in flight schedules due to adverse weather conditions.
The divisional commissioner also reviewed healthcare preparedness across districts, including heating arrangements in hospitals, availability of essential medicines, deployment of medical staff in far-flung areas and the requirement for four-wheel drive (4x4) ambulances.
He directed the National Health Mission to provide 4x4 ambulances to the Directorate of Health Services Kashmir for further distribution among districts. Garg stressed their advance shifting to temporary shelters, wherever required, to ensure uninterrupted access to medical care during heavy snowfall and road closures.
Reviewing the preparedness of the Jal Shakti department, the divisional commissioner directed officials to ensure uninterrupted functioning of all schemes, including lift water supply schemes, and adequate arrangements for the deployment of water tankers wherever required.
He also directed the forest department to ensure adequate stocking of firewood at depots across the Valley.
To strengthen interdepartmental coordination, the divisional commissioner directed all district administrations and departments to ensure round-the-clock functioning of respective control rooms, including the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC).
He also instructed appointment of nodal officers and sharing of their contact details to facilitate timely assistance, coordination and dissemination of information.
Stressing the importance of timely weather-related advisories, Garg directed concerned departments to ensure prompt sharing of information regarding weather and avalanche forecasts with the public to minimise risks.
He also directed the Srinagar municipal commissioner to identify waterlogging hotspots across the city and ensure deployment of adequate de-watering pumps to address any eventuality during winter.
During the meeting, deputy commissioners briefed the chair about winter preparedness measures undertaken in respective districts and highlighted critical issues requiring intervention and resolution.
The divisional commissioner called upon all departments to maintain close coordination and ensure that all necessary arrangements are put in place well in advance to minimise public inconvenience and ensure the safety and well-being of people across Kashmir division during winter.

A lengthy layover may seem like a blessing in disguise, allowing travellers to explore a city rather than spend hours waiting at the airport. For one passenger transiting through Delhi, a 14-hour stopover appeared to be the perfect chance to take a quick tour of the capital. However, her plans hit an unexpected hurdle when she realised she needed a visa to leave the airport, which forced her to find other ways to pass the long wait. A woman identified as Brooke, according to her Instagram profile, was recently travelling from Hong Kong to London when she booked a flight with a 14-hour layover in Delhi. She assumed she could use the time between flights to explore the city. However, she ended up spending the extended stopover inside the airport. In a video shared on social media through the account 'Followmytrackz', captioned ‘Longest 14 hours of my life’, the travel creator, said, “I booked a flight from Hong Kong to London with a 14-hour layover in Delhi because I thought it'd be so cool to just see it for the day." She added, “What I did not know until boarding my flight this morning is that even to do the day out of the airport on your layover, you still need a visa.” What was meant to be a day exploring Delhi instead turned into a lengthy wait at the airport. “I now have 14 hours stranded in Delhi airport, and I am about to just go and kill some time, I guess,” she continued. Rather than spend the entire time waiting for her next flight, Brooke decided to make the most of the facilities available at the airport. After discovering a massage parlour, she opted for some relaxation, saying she needed it after spending the previous night sleeping on the floor at Hong Kong airport. She later shared details of the experience and how much it cost, describing the foot massage as “unreal”. She revealed that she paid £32 (approximately ₹4,000) for a combination of foot-and-calf and back, shoulder and hip massages. Shopping was next on her itinerary. With around six hours still to go before her connecting flight, the travel creator decided to browse the shops before taking a nap and grabbing something to eat. The experience even left her wondering whether booking another flight for several hundred pounds would have been a better option than spending so many hours at the airport. Social media users were quick to offer suggestions and comment on how Brooke spent her time at the airport. One user suggested that she pay for lounge access, while another praised her for making good use of the long wait. A third user commented, “I can kill 13 hours in Delhi.” Another person shared a similar experience, saying, “The same thing happened to me. You can actually get a transit visa at the airport, but the people there are so clueless and unhelpful that I gave up, booked the hotel in the airport, and slept.” Another user commented, “Delhi domestic terminal is actually better than international with the refurbishment. I was stuck for 14 hours as well.” Brooke's experience offers an important reminder for international travellers: a long layover does not automatically permit passengers to leave the airport. Those planning to explore a city during a stopover should check the destination country's visa and transit-entry requirements before booking their itinerary. Three things remain constant at every Brazilian Grand Prix: tributes to the beloved Ayrton Senna, intense wheel-to-wheel action and Max Verstappen mounting a back-to-front recovery drive.
For the third consecutive edition, Verstappen charged through the field at the Autodromo José Carlos Pace to finish on the podium.
In 2024, he won another rain-marred race after starting 17th on the grid. A year later, he finished third despite starting from the pit lane. This time, he converted 21st place into a second-place finish.
Recovery drives through the field generally take place with a tyre offset in high-grip conditions. What made Verstappen’s foray through the pack more impressive was that all the cars began the race on intermediate tyres, with the track still wet from an earlier downpour.
By the end of Lap 5, the four-time champion had surged to eighth. “I think the first few laps, of course, were very important. I overtook a lot of cars, and actually, that first stint, I think on the intermediates, was really, really strong,” Verstappen said after the race.
The Dutchman was, however, unhappy with his car’s balance, which he indicates scuppered him from challenging Lando Norris for the win. He eventually finished more than 14 seconds behind the 2025 world champion.
“Once I got into P2, I couldn’t really make any inroads. So we have to understand what went wrong there. I don’t know if we picked up some kind of damage because the car felt like the complete opposite to anything that I’ve felt the whole weekend, with some really weird balance,” he explained.
Fighting back
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix marked Verstappen’s eighth consecutive podium and his 10th in 11 races. He is now second in the drivers’ standings, 17 points ahead of George Russell. All this in a car that was, for much of the year, the fourth-fastest on the grid.
The FIA’s Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) measurements rated Red Bull Powertrains as the best-performing combustion engine on the grid this year. However, that classification did not translate into on-track performance for the Milton Keynes-based outfit.
Verstappen had complained about the car’s oversteer throughout the season. High tyre degradation further affected the race pace. The team recovered some performance in medium- and high-speed corners through its mid-season upgrade package in Austria.
But with four retirements in the first half of the season, Verstappen was never really in contention for the drivers’ title, particularly with Kimi Antonelli blazing to the championship lead with five consecutive wins.
Right on track
After the back-and-forth with the pit wall earlier in the season, Verstappen seems to have settled into his sweet spot. His confidence in the car is at its peak.
During the 90-minute break at the start of qualifying in Brazil, the Dutchman said he was more invested in the Premier League matches, knowing he would start from the back of the grid. Verstappen bringing out this laid-back demeanour augurs well for Red Bull.
Three wins in the final three races would take his tally to 354 points, his lowest since 2020. But if the team continues to improve its current development cycle, Verstappen could be the main challenger to the Mercedes pair.
Red Bull has the best driver on the grid. After extended speculation linking him with the Silver Arrows, the team has tied him down to a contract until 2030. Now the ball is in the engineers’ court to give him the tools to fight for a fifth championship.
