More than 46 years after his big-screen debut in the slasher classic “Friday the 13th,” hulking horror icon Jason Voorhees is about to prove that his machete cuts just as deep in animation. The hockey-masked killer returns in “Never Hike Alone: Ghosts in the Fog,” a new 10-minute animated film from independent production company Womp Stomp Films.
Premiering Friday, Nov. 13, at 5 p.m. PT, and streaming for free on the Womp Stomp Films YouTube channel, the story follows an unlucky trio of friends whose relaxing weekend camping trip takes a gory turn when they become lost in the fog surrounding the infamous Camp Crystal Lake.
Founded in 2016 by filmmaker Vincente DiSanti, Womp Stomp Films has built a devoted following with its ambitious series of “Friday the 13th” fan films. The saga began with DiSanti’s 2017 short “Never Hike Alone,” followed by the winter-set prequel “Never Hike in the Snow” in 2020. The feature-length sequel “Never Hike Alone 2” arrived in 2023, featuring “Friday the 13th Part VI: Jason Lives” actors Thom Mathews and Vincent Guastaferro reprising their original roles as Tommy Jarvis and Sheriff Rick Cologne.
The “Never Hike Alone” films have relied on crowdfunding campaigns to help finance their increasingly elaborate productions. The fan-supported approach has allowed DiSanti and his collaborators to expand the saga while making the finished films available to watch for free online.
Although the “Never Hike Alone” films feature copyrighted characters, settings and storylines from the official “Friday the 13th” franchise, Womp Stomp Films operates independently of the studios that own the Jason Voorhees property. The company follows a set of self-imposed guidelines designed to avoid copyright disputes, including making its films available for free, using crowdfunding exclusively for production expenses and not turning a profit. Each film includes an on-screen disclaimer acknowledging that the rights holders can challenge the production. So far, the franchise owners have not taken action to stop the films.
“Ghosts in the Fog” marks the fourth installment in the Womp Stomp series and its first venture into animation. The short arrives amid a resurgence of activity surrounding the “Friday the 13th” franchise. Peacock debuted its A24-produced prequel series “Crystal Lake,” starring Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees, in October. Meanwhile, it was announced Friday that Steve Miner, who directed 1981’s “Friday the 13th Part 2” and 1982’s “Friday the 13th Part III,” will return to helm the franchise’s 13th feature film, scheduled for theatrical release in 2027. The new movie will mark Jason’s first big-screen appearance since the 2009 reboot.
“Ghosts in the Fog” was produced in collaboration with Mako Animation Studio, a Mexico-based company specializing in 2D animation. Founded in 2015 by Juan Rivera, who co-directed the new short alongside DiSanti, the studio’s previous projects include the animated YouTube series “John Death.”

HistoriCity: Guru Padmasambhava and the Nyingma Tradition in Arunachal Pradesh
Arunachal’s Buddhist traditions unite in an exhibition of Buddha relics from Piprahwa, returning to the state after 13 years.
In November this year, Arunachal Pradesh’s two Buddhist traditions are coming together in an exhibition centered around relics of the Buddha himself. The relics come from the Piprahwa stupa in Siddharthnagar district, Uttar Pradesh, a site linked with ancient Kapilavastu and the Buddha’s Shakya clan. They were excavated in 1898 by William Claxton Peppe and are kept at the National Museum in Delhi. The exhibition marks the return of Buddha’s relics to the state after 13 years. In the land where Padmasambhava is honoured as a second Buddha, devotees are now venerating relics of the first.
High in the mountains of western Arunachal Pradesh, prayer flags, whitewashed chortens (stupas) and cliffside monasteries mark the landscape. Ask the Monpas who brought this faith to their land and most will name Guru Rinpoche, better known as Padmasambhava.
Across the Himalaya he is revered as a ‘second Buddha’ and as the founding figure of the Nyingma, or ‘Ancient’, school, the oldest of the four major traditions of Tibetan Buddhism.
From Nalanda to Tibet
The Nyingma story begins in India. Between the 5th and 12th centuries, Nalanda, and later Vikramashila and Odantapuri (in present-day Bihar), developed Vajrayana, the ‘Thunderbolt Vehicle’. In it, wisdom and compassion took the form of deities, to be realised through mantra and meditation.
Padmasambhava is traditionally said to have come from Uddiyana and studied at Nalanda. In the 8th century the Tibetan king Trisong Detsen invited the Buddhist guru Shantarakshita to establish Buddhism in Tibet. Tradition says hostile local powers blocked him, so Padmasambhava was called in to subdue them. Together the two teachers founded Samye, Tibet’s s first monastery, and the king and the two masters are honoured as the founders of Tibetan Buddhism.
When “schools arose from the 11th century, those who kept the older lineages became known as the Nyingmapa. They are known for Dzogchen (Great Perfection) teachings and for terma, treasures the Guru hid for later discovery, among them hidden valleys called beyul. Relics of Padmasambhava are believed to rest at Hajo in Assam.
Two Roads into Arunachal
Buddhism reached Arunachal via two separate routes, and neither climbed up from the Assam plains. Following the route from Tibet to Bhutan, Buddhism came to the remote valleys of Arunachal. The Monpa and Sherdukpen of Tawang and West Kameng follow Tibetan Vajrayana. It was born in India, but it reached them only after travelling to Tibet and coming back south through Tibet and Bhutan.
Tradition credits the Guru Padmasambhava with an 8th-century visit. The historical record begins around the 15th century, when Nyingma lamas from Bhutan founded temples in Monyul. Gelug monks from Tibet followed along the trade routes to Tsona. Assam, the ancient Kamarupa, was itself a Buddhist centre, but no evidence suggests that plains Buddhism carried the faith into these hills.
The second Buddhist inroad was via Myanmar. The Tai Khamti are a Shan people from Bor Khamti in the upper Irrawaddy valley of Myanmar. In the late 18th century, they crossed the hills and settled near Sadiya with the Ahom kings’ permission, later spreading into Namsai, Lohit and Changlang in Arunachal Pradesh. They brought Theravada Buddhism with them from Burma, and every Khamti village keeps a chong (temple) and a kongmu (pagoda).
The Singpho, who also came from Myanmar, took up Theravada later. Myanmar was the source; Assam’s Sadiya frontier was only the doorway.
Padmasambhava’s legacy in Arunachal
Caves at around 14,000 feet, and rock marks venerated as Padmasambhava’s footprints, attract pilgrims. Taktsang Gompa, the “Tiger’s Den”, about 45 kilometres from Tawang, is built around the cave where he is said to have meditated. He is also said to have foretold three temples, the three ling, which tradition identifies with Urgelling, Sangeling and Tsorgyeling.
The Chumi Gyatse falls are said to have sprung where his rosary struck a cliff. Further east, Pemako on the upper Siang is revered as one of the greatest beyul. Of the early Nyingma temples, Khinmey Gompa, founded in 1440, remains Nyingma. Urgelling, birthplace of the Sixth Dalai Lama in 1683, later passed to the Gelug.
In 1680–81, Tawang Monastery, Gaden Namgyal Lhatse (“divine paradise of complete victory”), was founded by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso. He was a Monpa who had studied in Lhasa under the Fifth Dalai Lama and was sent home to build a monastery among his own people. Legend says his horse wandered off and halted on a ridge, where he built the monastery; the name is read as ta (horse) and wang (chosen). The Dalai Lama ordered the local people to help, and gave a thangka that the monastery still keeps.
Tawang belongs to the Gelug school and is tied to Drepung Monastery in Lhasa. Its founding made the Gelug dominant in Monyul, despite resistance from the Nyingma lamas. For nearly three centuries it was also the seat of Lhasa’s authority in the Tawang tract. In 1959 the 14th Dalai Lama fled into India through this region, and in 1997 he consecrated the monastery’s rebuilt assembly hall. Standing at over 10,000 feet, it is the largest monastery in India, and its library holds manuscripts lettered in gold.
Nyingma practice lives on around it, in village temples, ani gompa nunneries and masked cham dances. The anthropologist Verrier Elwin, Nehru’s adviser on the region, described the Monpa as apeople who lived their religion rather than theorising about it.
Was Arunachal Part of Tibet?
The link with Tibet was real but limited to one area. Lhasa administered the Tawang tract from the 17th century. The 1914 Simla Convention’s McMahon Line, agreed by British and Tibetan representatives without China’s assent, placed Tawang in British India. Even so, Tibetan officials remained until February 1951, when an Assam Rifles column under Major Bob Khathing took
control. Most of present-day Arunachal, home to communities such as the Adi, Nyishi, Apatani and Mishmi, was never under Tibetan rule.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

As Delhi continues to battle toxic air, one home in the national capital is drawing attention for maintaining an indoor Air Quality Index (AQI) of around 10-15. The residents, Peter Singh and Neeno Kaur, have created a green living space with approximately 15,000 plants, filtered air and an aquaponics-based farming system. The couple's home has come into focus again amid worsening pollution in Delhi-NCR, where restrictions under Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) remain in force. According to an India Today report, the couple have developed a clean-air ecosystem inside their home, using air filtration, extensive greenery and a system that allows them to grow much of their own food. Peter Satwant Singh, 81, and his wife Neeno Kaur, 72, are Delhi-based urban farmers who live in Sainik Farms, South Delhi. The couple moved to the locality in 1989, after Neeno was diagnosed with chronic leukaemia and needed treatment at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), according to The Week. Their journey towards sustainable living began with Neeno's health struggles. After chemotherapy affected her lungs, the couple explored ways to improve their living environment and adopted an organic lifestyle. They later developed an extensive home-based farming system using aquaponics, which combines fish farming with soil-free plant cultivation. Singh holds a PhD in topology in mathematics from Delhi University’s St Stephen’s College, as per Hindustan Times. The couple describe themselves as urban farmers and also conduct online classes to share their knowledge of aquaponics, growing vegetables and composting. The couple's home in South Delhi's Sainik Farms has around 15,000 plants, which form a major part of its green ecosystem. Their approach combines traditional construction techniques, indoor greenery and systems designed to reduce dependence on external resources. A report by The Better India in 2024 stated the house maintained an AQI reading of around 15. It also highlighted the couple's use of aquaponics, a method that combines fish farming with soil-free plant cultivation. Their aquaponics arrangement includes four large fish tanks. Water containing nutrients from the fish tanks is circulated to the plants, which absorb the nutrients and help filter the water before it returns to the tanks. The system reportedly uses around 1,000 litres of water daily, with water being recycled. The couple also grow vegetables, maize and herbs at home. Kitchen waste is converted into organic fertiliser, while rainwater harvesting and greywater recycling help reduce water wastage. Neeno's health concerns were among the reasons behind the couple's decision to change their lifestyle. The Better India reported that the initiative began after she was diagnosed with cancer. The couple subsequently focused on creating a healthier environment and growing organic food. "We want to show that this is how we live. If we can do it, anyone can do it," Neeno told The Better India. The couple's clean-air home stands in contrast to the pollution situation across Delhi-NCR. On Thursday, Delhi recorded an AQI of 321 at 7 am, placing it in the 'very poor' category, according to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data cited by ANI. Several monitoring stations recorded readings above 350. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage III of GRAP across the entire NCR on November 6, after Delhi's daily average AQI reached 382. The commission said forecasts from the India Meteorological Department and the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology indicated that air quality was likely to deteriorate into the 'severe' category in the following days. Stage III measures include restrictions on non-essential construction and demolition activities, in addition to measures under the first two stages. The CAQM also urged residents to use cleaner transport, combine journeys, avoid coal and wood for heating, and follow work-from-home and hybrid-schooling directions where applicable. Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): A tug-of-war has begun in the Congress over the leadership issue just two years before the assembly elections and after former chief minister Digvijaya Singh's Yatra.
There were speculations that Singh launched the Yatra to promote former minister Jaivardhan Singh, who also looks enthusiastic about it.
But to lay all such speculations to rest, Singh said the Congress should fight the 2028 assembly elections under the leadership of MPCC president Jitu Patwari and the Leader of Opposition Umang Singhar.
Singh's statement has set off discussions across the state. On the heels of the state, Patwari said, ''Singh's money belongs to Jaivardhan, but his political legacy remains with me.'' His remark ignited the debate.
Amid the discussions, former MP Nakulnath has planned to show his strength in Bhopal. He plans to organise an event in the state capital on the occasion of former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's birth anniversary and before the birthday of his father Kamal Nath.
Supporters of Nath have started gathering in the state capital to participate in the event and put up hoardings containing the pictures of Nakul.
A few supporters of Nakul removed the pictures of Digvijaya, Patwari, and Singhar from the hoardings.
Kamal Nath sent a message about Nakul's event, indicating his support for his son's event.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Following discrepancies found about 8.5 lakh students who have either dropped out of school or whose enrolment details have not been updated on the Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE) portal, Rajya Shiksha Kendra (RSK) has ordered physical verification of student records in private schools across the state. The exercise has been ordered to be completed within 10 days.
The RSK has issued guidelines directing block resource centre coordinators (BRCCs) and cluster academic coordinators (Jan Shikshaks) to verify student enrolment data on the UDISE portal and Education Portal 3.0 against the admission, scholar and attendance registers maintained physically by private schools.
According to the guidelines, despite repeated instructions, the progress of enrolment-related data verification through UDISE and the portal has not been satisfactory.
Records will be verified with attendance register
During the verification, officials will match student details available on the portals with the school's admission register, scholar register and attendance register.
Any discrepancies will have to be rectified immediately to ensure that the online records match the physical registers.
In cases where major discrepancies are found, officials will seek a factual explanation from the school regarding the admission status of students in each class and submit the details to the District Education Centre.
The exercise will also cover students marked in the drop box on the UDISE portal. Officials will review their updated status and seek clarification from schools wherever required.
The RSK has warned that indifference or failure to complete the verification within the stipulated period will invite disciplinary action. A proposal for action against the responsible officials will be sent to the collector-cum-district mission director.
Enrolment drops by 8.5 lakh students
Schools across the state have recorded around 8.5 lakh fewer students enrolled in Class 1 to 12 in the current academic session compared with the previous year, raising concerns over student retention and the updating of school records.
According to UDISE data as of October 13, the state's enrolment fell from 1.42 crore in 2025-26 to 1.34 crore in 2026-27.

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”
ALSO READ: Suvendu calls firecracker critics communists as Kolkata chokes on Diwali pollution
The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”
#WATCH | Delhi: On air pollution, Dr Vijay Hadda, Professor, Department of Pulmonary Medicine & Sleep Disorders, AIIMS, says, “These green crackers reduce emissions by only 30%. As far as the gases and particulate matter are concerned, 70% of the emissions remain the same as those from conventional firecrackers. The AQI, which used to be in three digits, has now reached four digits. If you compare Delhi’s air quality with that of other cities, you will find that there is almost a 50% difference. Obviously, life is not going to be easy for the people living here. You keep inhaling this poisonous smoke, breathing it in continuously. Every minute, you breathe at least 20 times, taking in at least half a litre of air with each breath. I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival. I am absolutely certain that as time passes, we will begin to see its effects. Many of my colleagues who are otherwise completely healthy have been calling me and saying, “I am unable to get rid of this irritation. It feels as though something is stuck in my throat.” We saw patients during our last OPD session, and they have returned again today. This happens every year, but somehow, we all forget. The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it…”
— ANI (@ANI) November 9, 2026
In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

A 54-year-old man was arrested by the Veppankuppam police on charges of setting on fire his daughter’s house at Agaram village near Odugathur town at foothills of Jawadhu Hills in Vellore on Friday.
Police said the accused R. Anandan, 54, a wage labourer, was upset over his daughter Vaishnavi marrying Rajesh, a milk van driver, against his wishes. In a fit of rage, Anandan allegedly set on fire Rajesh’s father Kumar’s house in Agaram village. Residents alerted Veppankuppam police, who rushed to the spot with firefighters. The house, which was unoccupied, was gutted. A case was registered and Anandan was arrested.

France hold nerve to edge past South Africa in thriller
- Published
Nations Championship
France (21) 21
Tries: Grandidier-Nkanang, Attissogbe, Bielle-Biarrey Cons: Lucu (3)
South Africa (7) 19
Tries: Wessels, Reinach, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu (2)
France held on to end their five-match losing run against South Africa at Stade de France with an enthralling 21-19 victory in Paris.
The victory dents the world champions' hopes of reaching the Nations Championship final and puts Les Bleus in a strong position to top the northern hemisphere standings.
The hosts, inspired by their captain Antoine Dupont, showed their class and skill to score three tries in a frantic first half.
France's back three of Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, Theo Attissogbe and Louis Bielle-Biarrey all crossed in a thrilling opening 40 minutes, with Jan-Hendrik Wessels scoring off the back of a maul for the visitors.
The Springboks thought they had a second try on the stroke of half-time but Kurt-Lee Arendse's try was chalked off after he strayed marginally offside.
Number eight Jasper Wiese was shown a 20-minute red card early in the second half - the third of five cards shown in an incident-packed game - for a dangerous shoulder charge, but it had the opposite effect to derailing the world champions.
With South Africa's set-piece power proving too much, replacement scrum-half Cobus Reinach and hooker Malcolm Marx scored to set up a thrilling finale.
However, Manie Libbok missed the vital conversion to Marx's try that would have levelled the game.
With South Africa pushing for a winning score, Bielle-Biarrey produced a huge defensive tackle to force the ball loose, before Dupont, who was named player of the match, gathered possession to help seal the victory.
The result will come as a blow to both England and Ireland, who are in direct competition with France for a place in the Nations Championship final at the end of the month.
Les Bleus, who are six points clear at the top of the northern hemisphere standings, now face Argentina next Saturday, putting them in a strong position to reach the inaugural final at Allianz Stadium on Sunday, 29 November.
Dupont wears 10 but excels from nine
Injuries to France's three first-choice fly-halves - Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack and Antoine Hastoy - left France coach Fabien Galthie with little option but to deploy his captain and talismanic scrum-half at number 10.
Despite wearing the France number 10 shirt for the first time, Dupont lined up at scrum-half, as Galthie played Rassie Erasmus, who had swapped his entire front row an hour before kick-off, at his own game.
It was an electric start from the hosts, as a clever move sent Kalvin Gourgues through a gap, with Grandidier-Nkanang eventually crossing in the corner.
A monstrous left-footed 50:22 from Dupont, with South Africa lock Lood de Jager in the sin-bin for a high tackle, gave France field position, before the ball cannoned off Gourgues' head and Attissogbe crossed for a fortunate try.
Dupont supplied more magic, grubber kicking through on his stronger right foot for Bielle-Biarrey to race over.
South Africa's power told as they scored their opening try from a maul, before Erasmus changed his entire front row again, five minutes before half-time.
Creativity, intensity and physicality - it was a first game that felt remarkably similar to the epic quarter-final of the 2023 Rugby World Cup in Paris.
Despite losing Wiese to a 20-minute red card early in the second half, the world champions took advantage of Grandidier-Nkanang's sin-bin for a deliberate knock-on.
Tiredness and poor discipline made the game loose and chaotic, before the Springboks turned to their scrum to regain control.
A succession of scrum penalties resulted in another sin-bin, with replacement France prop Regis Montagne yellow carded as the hosts were left clinging on for the final 10 minutes.
Stunning scramble defence and sheer grit showed a side to the back-to-back Six Nations champions France that has often been questioned.
Despite their scrum crumbling, France held firm, continuing to chase kicks and compete for loose balls.
A draw would have felt a fair result given the contrasting nature of the two halves, but Libbok - as at the 2023 World Cup - badly shanked a kick that will once again raise questions over his ability to deliver under pressure in the biggest Test matches.
For once, the fine margins went against South Africa, who won every knockout game of the last World Cup by a point.
They face Ireland in Dublin next Saturday and will now likely need a favour from England, who take on New Zealand earlier that same day, if they are to reclaim top spot in the southern hemisphere standings.

Johnny Depp has been a superstar since the 1980s, and he's been paid like one.
From the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise, which paid him tens of millions, to a seven-figure deal with Dior, Depp has used his paydays to live a lavish life: He once bought an island in the Bahamas and spent $30,000 a month on wine.
Here's a breakdown of Depp's wealth and how he's reportedly spent it.
Over a 13-year span, Depp earned $650 million, according to his former management firm.
After finding fame on the hit late-1980s TV series "21 Jump Street," Depp became a bona fide movie star thanks to performances in offbeat Tim Burton movies like"Edward Scissorhands" and "Ed Wood."
Depp was paid handsomely for his efforts.
According to his former management firm, The Management Group, Depp earned over $650 million in the 13 years they worked together from 1999 to 2016.
A large portion of that is paydays he received playing Captain Jack Sparrow in the "Pirates of the Caribbean" franchise.
After the success of "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," Depp started routinely banking $20 million per movie.
The first "Pirates" movie, "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," made over $650 million at the box-office worldwide. With that, Depp's asking price soared. On top of taking in $20 million pre-picture in the franchise, he got around 20% of the back end per picture, according to The Hollywood Reporter.
So not only was he paid upfront, but Depp was cut another check after the movie broke even.
Depp earned more than $40 million on each "Pirates" movie thanks to his back-end deal.
Thanks to the success of the "Pirates" sequels, including 2006's "Dead Man's Chest," which earned over $1 billion worldwide, Depp's earnings from the movies became astronomical.
The actor brought in north of $40 million per sequel on the back end of the movies alone, per THR. Again, that doesn't count the $20 million base pay for each.
But not all of that went directly into Depp's pocket. His agents got 10%, managers took 5%, and there are deductions for taxes and expenses.
However, the paydays only got bigger from there.
The back-end deal for "Alice in Wonderland" was even larger: $55 million.
Taking a pause from playing Captain Jack in 2010, Depp teamed up with Tim Burton again for the latest adaptation of "Alice in Wonderland."
On top of his $20 million base, THR reported that he took in $55 million on the back end thanks to the movie's successful box office run, which brought in over $1 billion.
Thanks to the "Pirates" movies, "Alice in Wonderland," and 2014's "Into the Woods," in which he played the Big Bad Wolf, all getting prime home entertainment releases and cable play, Depp took in $25.7 million in residuals in 2016 and 2017 thanks to his profit participation deals on those movies.
In 2016, he even landed on Forbes' list of highest-paid celebrities. He reportedly took in $48 million that year.
Depp has earned millions as the face of Dior's Sauvage fragrance for men.
The actor has been the face of Sauvage for years. Depp was reportedly taking in $3 million to $5 million in the deal.
In August 2022, Business Insider confirmed that Depp signed a seven-figure, multi-year deal with Dior.
Depp was paid $16 million for just one scene in "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald."
Depp was asked to step down from "Fantastic Beasts 3" days after losing a libel case against the publishers of the UK newspaper, The Sun, over a 2018 article that described him as a "wife beater."
However, because he had a "pay-or-play" deal on the movie, meaning he would get paid regardless of if he appeared in it, he was paid his $16 million fee.
Depp only filmed one scene as Grindelwald. Mads Mikkelsen took over the role for 2022's "Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore."
Depp bought an island in the Bahamas for $3.6 million.
The actor first set eyes on the 45-acre island located 60 miles from Nassau in 2003 while filming "Curse of the Black Pearl." He purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay for $3.6 million in 2004.
He's since outfitted the island with solar-powered buildings, including a house with stunning 360-degree views.
He spent $5 million to shoot the ashes of his friend, author Hunter S. Thompson, out of a cannon.
Depp befriended famous gonzo journalist Thompson around the time he played him in the 1998 movie "Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas."
They stayed friends until Thompson's death in 2005. Thompson had spoken about wanting his funeral to be an extravagant affair involving his ashes shot out of a cannon and a red, white, and blue fireworks show to end the event.
Depp said he spent $5 million to fulfill his friend's wishes.
Depp had $2 million in monthly bills, including $100,000 a month for addiction issues.
Depp had huge daily spending habits to live a lavish lifestyle, which led to him spending $2 million a month on bills, according to his former management firm.
At one time, the actor reportedly paid:
- $300,000 a month for a 40-person staff
- $10,000 a day to his former security manager
- $350,000 monthly to maintain his 156-foot yacht (which he has since sold to J.K. Rowling for $27 million)
- $30,000 monthly for wine (Although Depp told Rolling Stone this was a conservative estimate. "It's insulting to say that I spent $30,000 on wine," he said. "Because it was far more.")
- $100,000 a month for a doctor to treat his addiction issues
Depp commented on his spending in 2017, telling the Wall Street Journal, "It's my money."
"If I want to buy 15,000 cotton balls a day, it's my thing," he said.
The actor's spending habits were first revealed in 2017 when he filed a $25 million lawsuit against his former business managers at The Management Group. TMG countersued; the parties reached a settlement a year later. No details were made public.
Depp was awarded $15 million in the defamation suit against Amber Heard.
Depp filed a defamation suit against ex-wife Amber Heard in response to a 2018 op-ed she wrote for The Washington Post that detailed her experience with domestic violence.
Depp's name wasn't mentioned, but the article was widely interpreted as being about him.
The 2022 trial lasted for six weeks, in which both Depp and Heard took the stand. The jury awarded Depp $15 million in damages from Heard, and Heard $2 million from Depp.
Depp's $15 million reward was reduced to $10.35 million to comply with state limits for punitive damages.
Depp sold $3 million in artwork.
Since the verdict, Depp has been spending more time playing music than getting back to making movies.
It's unlikely he'll land the kind of paydays he got before his legal battle with Heard, but the actor still has a loyal fanbase.
In July 2022, Depp announced on his Instagram that he would be selling his artwork at a gallery in England. All the pieces sold within hours, and the actor pocketed around $3 million in total.
Depp was reportedly paid $5 million to star in "Ebenezer."
"Ebenezer," Paramount's horror-tinged retelling of the beloved Charles Dickens holiday tale, marks Depp's first major studio release since 2018's "Fantastic Beasts: The Crimes of Grindelwald."
To star as the title character, Depp reportedly got paid a fraction of the paydays he commanded in his "Pirates" years
According to Variety, Depp is getting $5 million for the role. But the trade notes that he is in line to receive bonuses if the movie hits certain box-office milestones.

Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.
On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
Turning a Windows defense against itself
The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.
By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.
Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.
“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote. “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.
Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.
On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.
She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
Ms. Bhati told the Bench that stubble burning accounted for 14% of Delhi’s pollution on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Bench said it will pass some orders and take up the plea on November 16 after the court reopens following the Diwali vacation.
A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday (November 6, 2026) as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the ‘severe’ category, with the overall AQI settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality at 9 a.m., while the remaining were in the ‘very poor’ category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472, official data showed.

Himachal Cabinet clears Rs 1,500 monthly aid for women, 300 units free power
The Himachal Pradesh Cabinet approved monthly financial assistance for eligible women and free electricity for families. The decisions also expand reforms across water, energy, transport, healthcare and public services.
The Himachal Pradesh Cabinet on Friday approved the launch of the Mukhya Mantri Apna Parivar Sukhi Parivar Yojna, under which eligible women aged between 18 and 59 will receive Rs 1,500 a month, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The scheme will also provide 300 units of free electricity to eligible families. An official statement cited by PTI said 3.5 lakh women had been identified as beneficiaries.
At a meeting chaired by Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu, the Cabinet decided to adopt a uniform state policy to determine and periodically revise rates for surplus raw water sold to neighbouring states, government agencies and industries. It set an initial benchmark rate of Rs 100 per 1,000 cubic feet for all state projects, including inter-state water projects.
The Cabinet also decided to launch the Khelo Himachal Chitta Mukt Abhiyan 2026. The initiative seeks to involve young people in sports, strengthen drug prevention efforts and promote a healthy lifestyle, discipline and positive community participation.
Amendments to the Swaran Jayanti Energy Policy 2021 were also approved. The amended policy provides for free power royalty at a 50 per cent rate for the first 10 years after commissioned projects of central public sector undertakings complete 40 years of operation. The projects will be transferred to the state government free of cost after 50 years from their commissioning date.
The Cabinet decided to cancel the allotment of 222 solar power projects that had not been implemented despite considerable time having passed. The allotment of 13 hydroelectric projects with a capacity of more than 25 MW will also be cancelled for failure to comply with norms, while 20 projects will be offered for fresh bids.
Under the Rajiv Gandhi Swarojgar Start-up Yojna 2023, the subsidy for purchasing diesel buses will be raised from 30 per cent to 40 per cent. The subsidy is meant for operating passenger buses on identified routes within subdivisions.
The policy will also provide a 50 per cent subsidy for purchasing electric buses and a 40 per cent subsidy for diesel buses with more than 10 seats. These buses will operate on the Hamirpur Bus Stand-Dr Radhakrishnan Medical College, Jolsapper route and the New OPD, IGMC Shimla-Atal Institute of Medical Super Speciality, Chamiyana route.
The Cabinet approved an increase in the minimum support price of naturally grown ginger from Rs 30 to Rs 40 per kilogram. It also approved the engagement of 1,000 Rogi Mitras in the health department to provide affordable and quality health services.
Approval was given to create and fill 561 Junior Office Assistant (IT) posts in government medical colleges, dental colleges and the Directorate of Medical Education.
The Cabinet granted a one-time relaxation under Rule 11 of the Himachal Pradesh Police Department (Recruitment of Constables) Rules, 2024, allowing the written examination for constable posts to be conducted offline instead of online. According to PTI, the Himachal Pradesh Public Service Commission will make arrangements to conduct online examinations within six months.
The Cabinet also approved the Registration Sewa Kendra Project to modernise existing sub-registrar offices on the lines of Passport Seva Kendras. In the first phase, the project will be launched in Solan, Shimla, Kangra and Sirmaur districts.
The decisions cover financial assistance and free electricity for eligible families, water pricing, sports and drug prevention, energy projects, transport subsidies, farm support, healthcare staffing, government recruitment and the modernisation of registration services.
